The House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of the Hon. Mr. Fielding :
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty.
['I see no objection to this motion.']

Mr. Speaker, I must in the first place congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) on the very excellent speech from his standpoint which he delivered yesterday. That the hon. gentleman always makes the best of the situation we will all acknowledge, and while yesterday he had even a larger number than usual of very sharp corners to turn, he on the whole accomplished it as well as could be expected. And, whenever he did upset he gathered himself up quickly again and he went on in as smiling a way as ever. Now, while the speech was received by the House in a very appreciative and attentive manner, I was astonished to see what a singularly soparific effect so good a speech had on some of his colleagues. I noticed that there was not the attention given to it by some of the members of the cabinet which we might have reasonably expected. In fact, I do not think that I have ever before witnessed in this House a budget speech of interest) delivered while four of the Finance Minister's colleagues were sound asleep; and one of them enjoyed it so much that he woke up at six o'clock to protest against the debate being adjourned.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend the Finance Minister congratulates the country upon its prosperity. We. on, this side of the House, shall not be behind hand in

congratulating the country upon the prosperous conditions at present existing', and ill that respect we offer a somewhat differ-rent spectacle to that which was presented in days past, by the Liberals when in opposition, some of whom were good enough to offer net only to this country but to the mother country a style of literature which was found very useful indeed by American immigration agents.
Hear, hear.

The Minister of Finance did not quite so strenuously as on some past occasions argue that our prosperity is due to the government, he treats of that phase in very moderate terms indeed. In fact, the terms of liis speech hi that regard are in very strong contrast to a recent deliverance of the Minister of Marine (Hon. Mr. Prefoutaine) in Montreal in which he remarked that the prosperity of Canada was entirely due to the Fielding tariff. Coming from a gentleman of the position of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that was hardly a worthy statement -it partakes more of the character of a patent medicine advertisement than of the utterance which we might hope to hear from a gentleman occupying the high position of head of one of the departments of state in Canada. It is perfectly evident that in the view of the Minister of Marine, the right hon. Mr. Chamberlain has taken an entirely erroneous view of the condition of affairs in Canada. At the recent colonial conference Mr. Chamberlain referring to the prosperity of Canada and the increase of Canada's trade from 1890 to 1902 spoke in this way :
The total imports ot Canada increased in that period 14,500,000 pounds sterling, or at the rate of 62 per cent. That shows the enormous increased prosperity in the Dominion ; it shows how the energy of its inhabitants is developing its trade.
And when you come to think of it, 1 suppose some credit is due to the business capacity and energy of the people of this country. For my part 1 have never been able to find out the exact nature of the changes in the tariff of 1897 to which the prosperity of Canada during the past few years has been due. I have inquired as to that across the floor of the House on a great many occasions and I have never got a definite or satisfactory reply. I believe that the people of Canada are entitled to some of the credit for the Increased trade and the increased prosperity of this country during the past six years, although it is quite true that speakers on the other side of the House, both in this Chamber and throughout the country affect to believe in an entirely different reason for our prosperity. If the government does not adopt my view on this question; if their friends do not adopt that view; if they do not agree Mr. BOKDBN (Halifax).
with the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who said that the prosperity of Canada was due to causes beyond the control of any government; if they do not believe in that, then Sir, they are altogether too modest, because while they have increased the trade of Canada by $184,000,000 since 1890, look what the Fielding tariff lias done for the world. I do not suppose, speaking in sober reality, that any of these gentlemen across the floor claim that the increases in these different countries fire due to the tariff brought down in 1897 by the Hon. Mr. Fielding. But may it not be truly claimed with regard to these different countries, that the advent of the Canadian Liberals to power in 1896 is as much responsible for the improved condition of trade in the whole civilized world as for the prosperous condition which fortunately has prevailed in Canada from 1896 t>
1902.
Let me make one more observation to my hon. friend the Finance Minister. He seems to take it for granted that as the imports to this country have increased to an enormous extent since 1896, we are to find in that a necessary indication of prosperity. Sir, I take issue with my hon. friend on that point. I say that increased imports may accompany but do not necessarily indicate increased prosperity. Look at the condition of affairs in Canada to-day. We produce from $750,000,000 to $800,000,000 of manufactured goods, counting everything as a manufacture in the production of which motive power is employed. The long delayed census returns have not yet furnished us with a statement of the annual value of our agricultural products. If our home production should be decreased by $50,000,000 in any year, that might result in increasing our importations by twenty-five, thirty or forty million dollars. To this extent the manufactures and products which are now furnished by the Canadian people would be brought in from foreign countries. Would not my hon. friend the Minister of Finance stand up in the House and point to the increased revenue resulting from that condition of things and say : Look, the trade of Canada has Increased, not $184,000,000, but

$225,000,000, and our surplus is not $13,000,000, but $25,000,000. And yet, is there any hon. gentleman in this House who would say that such a statement would indicate a healthy condition of affairs in this country ?
.My hon. friend has gone very fully into what I may call the business returns of this country, and I will endeavour, in my figures I give to the House, not to duplicate those which he has furnished. I have some documents to present in a tabulated form, and, with the permission of the House, I will follow the example of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and hand them to the reporters without reading them in full.

My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was very warm indeed on that point ; he was more than warm, Mr. Speaker, he was almost tearful when he spoke of the sorrows of the farmers and the burden of taxation laid upon them by an extravagant and corrupt government. 1 will present to the House a comparison of the taxation during the past six years with that of the previous six years under Conservative administration ; because I think it is right, when statements of large trade and abundant revenues are laid before the House, that we in the opposition should show the reverse side of the shield.

I might point out to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as a culmination of this statement, that according to the estimate of the hon. Minister of Finance we shall have imposed on the people of Canada during the present year no less than $47,520,160 of taxation. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he contemplates these figures, should really, for very decency's sake, pump up a few of the briny tears which he shed in the old days.
A few years ago the hon. gentleman contributed a very strong article to the 1 North American Review ' on the subject of protection and free trade, in which he said :
In 1878, the actual taxation of Canada was $17,841,938, though, as there was a deficit in that year, the necessary taxation might be placed at $19,000,000. In 1889 the actual taxation was $30,613,522, being an increase of $11,613,522.
Let us pursue the comparison. In 1896 the actual taxation was $27,759,285, in 1902 it was $43,389,112 ; being an increase of $15,629,S27, or considerably more than fifty per cent of an increase. What was the comment of the hon. gentleman when he wrote this article on the melancholy condition of affairs in 1889 :
Comment is hardly necessary, nor, indeed, does space permit me to point out the enormous mischiefs which result in a young and poor country from absorbing so large a proportion of the earnings of the people, in defraying the charges of the federal government, as is now being taken in Canada.
Well, if no comment was needed then, is it not needed now, upon an increase in taxation of between $15,000,000 and $16,000,000 in six years ? I trust that when the hon. gentleman comes to address the House on this occasion lie will give his views on the question of taxation, and explain wherein they differ from the views he held at the time he wrote this article. I referred to this same article last year or the year before, but my right hon. friend was not good enough to make any allusion to it, in the speech he then addressed to the House. I thought I might possibly have been mistaken in the identity of the gentleman who wrote the article. Although it purported to have been written by one Sir Richard John Cartwright, it might possibly have been some other gentleman than my right hon. friend who occupies the position of Minister of Trade and Commerce.
There is another consideration which I would like to present to the House. If, as members of the government claim, the pre-

sent tariff is a revenue tariff, why is the taxation continued at so abnormal a figure ? Why does the government take from the people, for example, $1,000,000 more in excise duties ou tobacco and $500,000 more in customs duties on sugar than would have been taken under the tariff before 1896 ? And why does the Minister of Finance retain the duty on breadstuff's which he regarded as so unjust and oppressive that while premier of Nova Scotia he moved the following resolution with regard to it:
That while it is as a rule inexpedient to deal with Dominion questions in this House, in view of the obnoxious character of the duty on breadstuffs, the House must firmly protest against the imposition of such duties.
And the same view was entertained by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, referring to Sir Leonard Tilley's surplus in 1882, said :
I asked how it was got. $1,100,000 was derived from two of the most odious and oppressive taxes which were ever imposed in any civilized country before, under similar circumstances at least, the taxes on breadstuffs and fuel. If he really wants to relieve the people, let him remove the taxes on breadstuffs and coal.
My hon. friend the. Minister of Trade and Commerce sits unmoved in his chair while a surplus of $13,000,000 is announced in this House, and forgets the commiseration he expressed some years ago for the condition of the people of this country labouring under two of the most odious and oppressive taxes which were ever imposed in any civilized country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the revenues have indeed been abundant during the past six years. There has been an increase of more than $60,000,000 over those of the previous six years, but let my hon. friend the Minister of Finance bear in mind that if the duties on tobacco, sugar, coal and breadstuffs had been removed, the condition of affairs would be very different. If my hon. friend had the courage to carry out his financial convictions, his boasted surplus would not exist by a good many millions. In making this point I do not wish to be understood as advocating the removal of the duties on these articles, but as merely contrasting the present position taken by the Minister of Finance with the former professions of himself and colleagues and asking them at present what they have to say about those promises and professions made in days gone by. I think I am warranted in putting that question by the language used by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. I have here a statement of his views with regard to the pledges and promises of public men, which I think will commend itself to the judgment of the House :
If a public man can hold one set of principles out of office and another set in office, responsible government is a farce.
You have the right to hold the politician to his pledge, just as much as you would the man Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
of business. The man who obtains goods from you under false pretenses is a cheat and swindler. What should you call the men who obtain votes by means of pledges which they never intended to keep ? I say again, if you are prepared to overlook these things then you have no right to ask for fidelity from any man who hereafter represents you.
I credit these words to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. I am told that he uttered them in days gone by. But whether he uttered them or not, I do not think he will challenge their soundness, and I ask him to apply those words to the record of himself and his political friends during the past six years as contrasted with the promises and professions which they held out to the people during the eighteen years they were in opposition.
The total expenditure of the country is a matter about which, standing on this side of the House, I think I should have a word to say. The total expenditure during the six years, beginning with 1891 and ending with 1896, reached the sum of $251,682,027. During the six years beginning with 1897 and ending with 1902, it amounted to $314,520,785, or an increase during that period of no less than $62,838,758 over the previous six years.

The average annual expenditure of the present Liberal government during the past six years, amounted to $52,420,131. Compare this with the average annual expenditure of the previous Conservative government, which amounted to $41,947,005, and you have an average annual increase under Liberal administration of no less than $10,493,126.

I could not get my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce to pay the slightest attention to that celebrated article when he addressed the House two years ago. Might I not ask from the hon. gentleman the favour of passing reference to that published statement of his. Might I not ask him to make a comparison between the figures of our present exependiture and that which he denounced 'in those days, and especially draw attention to the fact that he attributed all the wretchedness and misery and maladministration in Canada to what do you think. To the fact that in Canada at that day protection existed. Of course we know that, according to the right lion, gentleman's view, no protection exists in the present tariff, and I think we are entitled to some other argument from the right hon. gentleman to show that that which was food for comment and criticism so severe in days gone by, is now a matter of indifference to the hon. gentleman, even though it is exaggerated a hundred fold.
Let me now, Mr. Speaker, deal with the expenditure on a per capita basis. I am not objecting to fair and even liberal expenditure. We have a young and growing country, which needs to be developed, but I must say that a good deal of public money in this country is not used for very wise purposes and not expended in a very statesmanlike way. In making the comparisons which I do to-day, I wish to be understood as not carping at fair and reasonable expenditure, because I am always willing and ready to support the government in its expenditures, so long as they are made on some systematic plan and for some wise purpose, in the true interests of our country. But it is only right that I should bring to the attention of the country, in these times of growing trade, increasing revenues and prosperity, the fact that our expenditure is also increasing by leaps and bounds ; and we may well bear in mind the words which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, uttered only two or three sessions ago, that we cannot always expect to have these prosperous times, but must look for lean years in the future, years when the public revenue will not be by any means abundant. I should be glad to see a larger increase for the lighthouse and coast service, for I think that if there is a department of the public service which has been neglected more than another during the past six years it is this one. I should be glad also to see a greater increase in the expenditure for the government of the North-west Territories. Judging by the accounts I heard of the inadequacy of the public revenues for the purposes of the country during my recent trip to the west, I think that the grant that is made for this service might very well have been supplemented. But I bring this Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).

As to the public debt, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has dealt with that very fully in his speech. It is quite true that he shows a very good record so far as reduction of debt is concerned, if we are to conclude that his sentiments of fifteen or twenty years ago are absolutely wrong, and the sentiments he expressed only yesterday are absolutely right. But, if any importance is to be attached to what he said about surpluses in the old days, he cannot congratulate himself as much as he felt at liberty to do on the handling of the pub-

It will thus be seen, Mr. Speaker, that during all these years of the present administration there has been an enormous increase in revenue. Sly hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in making his comparison in this regard, will bear in mind that if the Conservative government from 1891 to 1896 had had the same revenue which the hon. gentleman has enjoyed from 1897 to 1902, the public debt of this country could have been decreased by no less an amount than $45,000,000. My hon. friend thinks he is able to congratulate himself because, up to the end of last year, it was increased $13,000,000, and by means of the so-called surplus of the present year he will decrease it, I believe, by about $5,000,000, leaving a net increase of some $8,000,000.
Now, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was, as I said, particularly jubilant over the fact that he had a surplus, and I have no doubt that my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce shares 47
that jubilation to the greatest possible extent. Would it be out of place, Mr. Speaker, for me to call to the attention of this hon. gentleman some utterances of by-gone days
that seem to have in them possibly a spark of good sense, and to invite the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he comes to address the House, to tell us what he thinks of these utterances of the old days, and whether he is prepared to take the same view which he held from 1876 to 1896. I am afraid that my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in the touching words of the old ballad, will have to say :	.
I cannot sing the old songs I sang long years ago.
Now, the editorial utterances of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who was almost as good an editor as he is a Minister of Finance, are also worthy of attention. In the columns of the Morning ' Chronicle ' some years ago he made this criticism of a Conservative administration :
If these surpluses were created by the government in some magic way there may be in them a cause for thankfulness to Sir John Macdonald and his followers, but when it is considered that every dollar of the surplus Is money taken out of the pockets of the people without a shadow of an excuse, money not required even by the reckless expenditure of the government, there is not much cause for re-ioicing.
Now, would my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce do his best to digest the utterances of his colleague, and let us know, when he comes to address the House, what he really thinks of the views which were then entertained. But that is not all. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance broke out in the following year, when there happened to be another surplus, and this is the way in which he bewailed the unhappy lot of a country that was afflicted with a surplus :
That millions of dollars should be unnecessarily taken yearly from the consuming classes of the country, and this, without being absolutely necessary, is a cardinal principle of the Finance Minister, to which even his best friends do not unreservedly assent.
They see that a surplus of millions at the capital is just so much money withdrawn from the trade of the country. How long can the Dominion stand the drain ? Certainly not many years longer.
There were no cheers, of course, because it was a newspaper article, but we can well understand how the cheers resounded, we can even remember how the cheers resounded, when sentiments of this kind were heard on every public platform of the country. But, Mr. Speaker, let me not neglect my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because I am always pleased when I quote any utterance of his; he has so terse and vigorous a way of expressing himself that it is really delightful to hear him, because he puts in half a dozen

words these matters more forcibly and more eloquently than most of us could do by
speaking fifteen- minutes. This is the way the right hon. gentleman expressed himself in the old days :
Taxation is an evil that nothing but the requirements of government can justify.
And the requirements of government this year do not justify the present taxation by some $12,000,000 or $13,00,000. Yet my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce seems to be pleased with the announcement of his colleague. I do not know how he will look upon it when he comes to address the House on the subject. But It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is cqnsiderable force in the views of the Minister of Finance, which I have read to the House, as well as in the very terse statement which the right hon. gentleman the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave to the House and to the country years ago, in the single sentence I have read from his utterances. Is there not some attraction to a certain class of people in this country when a surplus of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000 is announced ? There are people in this country as well as In every other, whose chief concern about the public revenue is to appropriate some of it to their own use under the guise of a par-lamentary vote. Sir, it seems to me that our policy in Canada should be to accomplish the following objects
1.	To so arrange our tariff that all legitimate industries at present established in this country should be so protected as to insure as far as possible permanency under conditions of depression as well as in times of commercial expansion.

2.	To invite capital and attract labour to the establishment of other industries which the resources and raw material of our country amply justify.
3.	To preserve by means of an adequately protective tariff our own home market for our own people and to have the policy of the government so declared and understood.
4.	In framing our tariff to have regard solely to the interests of Canada which have been committed to our charge although recognizing that in consulting our own interests we must not be unmindful of the tariffs raised against us by other countries.
5.	To so frame our fiscal policy that labour in Canada shall be paid a fair living wrage remembering always that our labouring classes and therefore our producers and manufacturers cannot be expected to compete on even terms with countries in which the condition of life among the labouring classes is altogether different. We do not desire to reduce our labouring population to the low standard of living, to that hard fierce struggle for existence which prevails in many countries. We do not want our labouring classes to compete without protection against the pauper labour of any country.
6.	To utilize the labour of our own people in conversion of our own raw material into finished products required for use in our own country. It is surely bad policy to export our raw material, to send our labouring-classes abroad to another country to find work in its manufactories and to send after both our money to pay for the finished product which we require.
Canada is bound to become a great agricultural country and her farmers are entitled to every possible protection and assistance. But we have enormous and varied resources the reasonable development of which will build up, not only in the east but in the west as well, great industrial centres of population which will afford a home market better than any foreign market for very large portions of our agricultural products. We know now that one of the matters of regret among the Americans who are coming by thousands into our great North-west is that they do not have in the west of Canada the home market which they had in the United States by reason of the great industrial centres which have been built up in the Western States. I believe that by a policy of adequate protection, such as the Liberal-Conservative party has advocated, is advocating and will advocate in this country, we will build up, even in the west of Canada, great industries and great industrial centres. The value of our home market cannot be placed too high. We know the value which has been placed upon it in the United States of America. We know that the United States have always carefully guarded their home market and it is apparent from the utterances of her public

We say that it matters very much who produces that which the American people consume. American people shall have the first opportunity to supply the American market. As I have said before in this House, Canada, since entering upon her period of commercial development, finds herself peculiarly situated. She lies 4,000 miles alongside the greatest manufacturing and agricultural country in the world. She has a sparse population spread over an enormous area. She lies alongside of a country which protects by an almost prohibitive tariff its own home market. Canada, with 5.500,000 people lies alongside of the United States with a population of 80,000,000 and a home market absolutely protected. What is the result ? Look at the enormous manufactures of the United States; look at the enormous agricultural production of the United States. In times of great commercial expansion the home market of the United States takes nearly everything that is produced in that country ; at all events, the amount they export, although absolutely large, is relatively very small. They exported in 1900 only three and one-half per cent of the manufactures and eight, or nine, or ten per cent of the agricultural products. Well, things will go on all right during a time of commercial expansion when the home mar-

ket is capable of absorbing nearly the whole product, but when a time of depression comes, when the consuming power of the people of the United States is decreased, what will happen? A good deal will happen. Canada lies alongside of the United States, Canada is her best customer in manufactured goods, as the hon. member for North Norfolk truly says. Canada is her third best customer in all classes of goods. When the surplus of the United States comes to be dealt with, where will it be dealt with ? It will be dealt with in Canada and Canada may reasonably expect in the first instance to be the dumping ground of the American surplus. Canada, to some extent, is the dumping ground of that surplus at the present time. It is argued gravely by some people in this country that it is' a good thing for the people of Canada that Canada should be the slaughter market for the manufactures and agricultural products of the United States." The argument seems to be this : It is said that if these goods are sold in Canada at less than the cost of production we get them cheap and therefore, upon the old free trade argument of years ago, it must be a good thing for the Canadian people to buy these goods in the cheapest market. What if the advent of these goods into the Canadian market closes up Canadian factories ? What if Canadian farmers leave their farms and go to the United States and find the employment which they cannot find at home ? I believe that for another reason a policy of free trade such as was advocated years ago can never be an acceptable policy in Canada. Free traders in Great Britain, possibly men who might be described as doctrinaires so far as this country is concerned because they do not realize the conditions which prevail here, regret that Canada has not followed the example of the mother country and adopted free trade. It seems to me that these gentlemen really do not know that of which they speak. If Canada had adopted the policy of free trade and opened her markets to the United States, our trade relations, bad as they are with the mother country, would be far worse and further than that, I believe that the commercial supremacy of the United States which would undoubtedly then have prevailed in our markets would have been coupled eventually with political supremacy. Therefore, I do not think, looking at our situation, that we can ever have anything like a policy of free trade in Canada, and if we are going to adopt the policy of protection, let us have a declared and pronounced policy so that the people may know what to expect and let us adopt a policy which will adequately protect all the interests of the country.

Now, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party believes in a policy of adequate protection ; a policy of such adequate protection as will maintain and strengthen Canadian industries ; such a policy as will give our own market to our own people That policy we have declared in all parts of the country. In the western states the policy of protection has found favour with the farmers, because they see built up in all that western country great industrial centres ; because they feel the advantage of a protected home market, and because they know that without the protection of that home market they would get very much less for their products than they do at present As I said before, I believe that the farmers in the western part of Canada will have the same experience, and that they will learn, even more than they do at present-and they do very largely realize it at present-the advantages of our home market; the advantages to this country of the protection of the home market so far as all classes of the people are concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. GEORGE BALL (Nicolet) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 30) respecting the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company. He said : Mr. Speaker, in presenting this motion, I would like to draw your attention and that of the House to the facts of the case. This Bill was on the Order paper a short time ago, and my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) thought he would render me a service by presenting it in my absence. My hon. friend from Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil), lacking knowledge of parliamentary procedure-being, like myself, a new member of this House-thought he would propose the six months' hoist. Fortunately or unfortunately, I do not know which, the Bill had not been printed in French, and my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) raised the point of order. In this way the Bill remains on the Order paper, and comes up for its second reading to-night. Since the last occasion, I have made some inquiries, and I find what I am about to read to you :
The consent given by the House to the second reading of a private Bill does not necessarily commit the House to the principle of the Bill. The expediency of a private Bill being mainly founded upon allegations of fact which
have not yet been proved. The House in agreeing to the second reading affirms the principle of the Bill conditionally and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
Since 1868 no private Bills have been defeated on the second reading. It was done, however, before confederation but then Council could be heard at the Bar for or against the Bill.
In 1880 objection was made to the second reading of the Bill concerning the Credit Valley Railway Company. A long discussion took place on that objection and the Hon. Mr. Holton, who has always been considered as a high authority on parliamentary procedure, said that a private Bill should always receive its second reading, and Sir John Macdonald, in spite of the fact that objection was raised by one of his political friends, expressed the same idea as the Hon. Mr. Holton.
In 1879 Sir John A. Macdonald expressed the same principle on a Bill concerning the Saskatchewan Colonization Railway Company, and this Bill was also® read a second time and referred to the committee.
In 1889, Sir John A. Macdonald, on the Ottawa and Montreal Boom Company said, it is greatly to the advancement of public business that private Bills should be sent to the various committees to be dealt with and then on the reports of the committees the great question whether the Bill would become law or not conies up. Though the objection made to the Bill which was then under consideration was because it was a Bill of public nature.
Now, the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), represents the Prime Minister in that right hon. gentleman's absence and leads this House. I would ask him kindly not to allow such attempts to be made to kill a Bill at its second reading. And for various reasons. Supposing that this principle were adopted to-day, what difficulty might we not look for in the future. There are on the list here a good many private Bills. All private Bills are generally read the second time in about half an hour, no matter what the number may be. Supposing that on each of these Bills, an hon. member should raise objection and seek to prevent the second reading, you can see what difficulty there would be. I would ask the protection of the leader of this House. I would like him to treat me as he treats every one else. I want British fair play.

subtopic: PRIVATE BILLS. . ATLANTIC AND LAKE SUPERIOR RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Before this motion is put, I beg permission to say a few words. The hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Ball) has certainly made out what appears to be a very strong case regarding the precedents in the second reading of private Bills. There is not the least doubt that it is in the interest of the House and of parties applying to the House that private Bills should be sent, as a matter of course, to committee to be discussed. But, in this case, we are dealing with a most extraordinary set of people; and I feel it to be in the interest of my county and the people I represent and only just to 1 myself to bring the matter before the House,



so that I may explain the peculiar position in which we stand. This application of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway-the name is not unfamiliar to the old members of the House-is connected with the old Baie des Clialeurs Railway, which, as most members are aware, has been before this House on several occasions during the last ten or fifteen years. The Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company was originally incorporated in 1893, for the bunding and operation of a line of railway from GaspO Basin in the county of Gaspfi, to Sault Ste. Marie. It was made up of eight different sections of road, including the Baie des Clialeurs, the Great Eastern, the Montreal and Sorel, the Montreal Bridge, the Ottawa Valley, the Pontiac and Pacific Junction, the Ontario Pacific and the Intercolonial section. The year following this incorporation, an Act was passed fti this parliament authorizing the transfer of the Baie des Chaleurs and the Great Eastern to this company and the system was operated under the name of the Atlantic and Lake Superior. For some years the promoter of this company, Mr. C. N. Armstrong, who is well known to the members of this House, attempted in various ways to bring about the successful completion of the undertaking. The charter of the Montreal Bridge Company was discussed last session in this House, and on that occasion, I believe, the House gained an insight into the methods that were employed. But for the moment I wish to limit myself more particularly to what happened in the county of Bona-ventnre. Tnis new company, the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway, took over the Baie des Chaleurs Railway, and constructed some eighteen miles from Caplan down to New Carlisle. In 1900, when I had the honour of being elected to this House, the powers of the company were lapsed, and the subsidies which had been voted were also lapsed. But fo-day we find this company coming again before parliament and asking for a renewal of its powers, and asking that we should extend for five years the time during which this undertaking may be completed, not only from Gasp 6 Basin to Sault Ste. Marie, but to enable this company to be incorporated and purchase the roads which are mentioned in the Bill, which would enable it to reach as far as the Pacific ocean over the unbuilt Grand Trunk Pacific.
I desire, Mr. Speaker, before they are given these powers that the House should be made acquainted with the manner in which they have dealt with the people of Bonaventure. The Minister of Railways, in December last, at my request, and to give effect to the law which had been adopted here in 1900 reviving the subsidy, issued a circular calling upon the people of Bonaventure county more especially, and the public at large, who had claims on the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway for the last section of thirty miles thereof, to send
Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure),
in their claims to the Department of Railways to enable him to distribute pro rata the $10,000 which had been reserved from the subsidy for the payment of labour, board bills and material. What was the result ? The Minister of Railways received, during five or six weeks, claims amounting to $226,000, a tabulated list of which has been prepared. These claims were sworn to, and were produced for that amount on thirty miles of the road. The claims that remain on the other seventy miles of road, not coming within the purview of the subsidy bill, were not filed. We have therefore reasonable cause to believe that this company owes $300,000 in the county of Bonaventure, to Liberals and Conservatives, poor men for the most part, labourers, local merchants, widows keeping boarding houses, and so forth. In spite of the fact that this company owes to-day $300,000, they have the audacity to come before this parliament and to ask for what practically amounts to a transcontinental charter. This company, Mr. Speaker, is practically out of business. In 1900 it transferred its charter to the trustees for the bondholders who are now operating the road. These trustees are represented in Montreal by Senator J. P. B. Casgrain, and the chief of these trustees is Mr. Joaquin Galindez, of London. These people do not make the application themselves, but it is the old company which has gone out of business, which has transferred its road, and which owes $300,000 in my county alone, and who wish to comprise in this scheme the Montreal bridge, the charter of which has expired, and a portion of the Montreal and South Shore Railway, which has been transferred to other hands. All these are comprised under the general name of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway.
I therefore feel it my duty, in justice to my constituents to inform the House of this state of affairs. Last year I had no opportunity of doing so, because the Bill was killed in committee without being discussed, since the very mention of the name was sufficient to cause the Bill to be thrown out. The year before, the trustees of the road, rather than take advantage of the two years extension of time which we had given them in which to build the two miles of road, introduced a Bill in the Senate, and which was passed in the Senate, extending for five years the time during which they could complete two or three miles of road. To-day the Private Bills Committee of Quebec was called upon to consider another Bill introduced by these same people under the name of the Quebec and Oriental Railway Company. These people ask for power from the legislature of Quebec to build a railway from Riviere du Loup to Metapedia parallel to the Intercolonial Railway. They ask for power under a simple resolution of their board of directors to transfer the Atlantic and Lake

Superior and the Baie des Chaleurs Railway over to the new concern. If that should happen, Mr. Speaker, I wish to know in what position the unfortunate people of Bonaventure will he if this road is so transferred. Under all these circumstances 1 thought it my duty to call particular attention to this Bill. My county is not the only one interested, all the counties to the south of the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec are interested, in fact almost every county up to Montreal, and thence across tiie river, and from Montreal up the Ottawa valley, on to Sault Ste. Marie, and by their connections out to the Pacific coast. 1 think that before these people are allowed to leave Bonaventure they should settle with their debtors there. At the request of the government I will willingly consent not to move the six months hoist, because I know it is somewhat contrary to precedent. Now that I have laid down the lines upon which I oppose this Bill, I am satisfied to leave it to the Railway Committee, confident that ample justice will be done in the matter. For these reasons I will consent to the second reading of the Bill.

I have no objection at all to the Bill going to the committee, but I may say to my hon. friend that I am sufficiently acquainted with the transactions of this company and with the condition to which their affairs have fallen to make it impossible for me to consent that this Bill should become law. I am of the opinion that not only the Bill in some portions is objectionable, but that the Bill as a whole should be rejected by this House. I think that would be the sense of the committee which will have to deal with the matter if it should go to the Committee on Railways and Canals, but if the House feels that it knows enough about the transaction to say that it is useless to send it to the committee because there can only be one result of the reference, then, I think, my hon. friend will at once yield to the reasonableness of the position which is taken in regard to it and allow us to dispose of the matter now. We have a great deal of business to go before the Railway Committee and sending it unnecessary work is a thing, which, I think, we ought to avoid doing. I am quite sure the committee cannot look with favour upon the passage of this Bill. The company is in an absolutely demoralized condition and it has left things in such a shape that great difficulty is experienced in unravelling its affairs for the purpose, not of trying to save something for the company, bub of trying to get some small percentage of the wages for the labouring people who have worked on the road. That is the condition in which this company stands. I do not think anything like it has been known in the history of railway construction in this country. My own experience is that of the hou. gentleman. I never got anything or asked anything from the government. But he was mistaken about the election. There was no election on when the vote was authorized by parliament.
The hon. gentleman was incorrect in stating that when the vote was passed that there was no opposition on this side.
I did not say that. What I said was that parliament did authorize the work and that a contract was entered into by virtue of that authority, and I am only asking a vote to carry it out.

In view of the strenuous opposition offered last year, when the vote for this work was originally submitted, we are justified in making comments on it today. Tlie facts were these, as shown by * Hansard.' The hon. member for Stan-stead (Mr. Lovell), who is always out of the House when the question comes up for discussion, invested in some timber limbs in that locality. It is not an arable section,
its chief value being the standing timber. Here then we have the hon. member for Stanstead wanting the Crown to aid him in his enterprise and taking the government and the Minister of Public Works by the throat, with the result that the government pledge themselves to an expenditure of $70,000 for the sole advantage of his lumber company. We should have the assurance that this will be treated as a business enterprise. It is true that the hon. gentleman was not in charge of the Department of Public Works when the vote for this work was first taken, and is consequently not personally responsible for its inception, but he should pledge the House and country that the government is going to tax the hon. gentleman from Stanstead and his company a rental which will give a fair return on the outlay. Let me read, for the benefit of the House, a list of these docks built at the expense of the public exchequer. Here is a list of decks in the province of Quebec, built at the expense of hundreds of thousands to the people of Canada, showing receipts from those docks for the last year :
Carleton, $28.07 ; Cedars, $17.10 ; Coteau du Lac, $27.84 ; Greece's Point, $10.24 ; Isle aux Grues, $0.12 ; Lacolle, $9.76 ; Perce, $24.71 ; St. IrenSe, $55.69 ; St. Thomas de Montmagny, $2.62.
In view of the fact that these docks are used by public corporations and private parties and that they have cost the country hundreds of thousands, I think the hon. minister, before this item passes, should promise the House that there shall be a fair return of at least $500 from the docks now under discussion. This should be done especially because the company, when they have completed their lumbering operations will leave it in the hands of the people, a work from which no revenue can be obtained.

The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) is evidently not familiar with the timber trade of the eastern provinces, or he would not make the statement he has made. When he speaks of the spruce timber being cut off in a few years, he is completely outside the facts. Price Bros., for instance, have been cutting on their limit for over sixty years. Spruce reproduces itself in from sixteen to twenty-five years, and operators claim that they can cut indefinitely from the spruce forests of the province of Quebec. If the limit that has been referred to is of such large extent as has been alleged-and it would need to be pretty large to make it worth the money spoken of-no question arises as to that timber ever being cut out. There seems to be a disposition on the part of certain speakers on the opposition side to reflect upon an hon. member of this House because he had an interest in this property. So far as that hon. member is concerned, he is not now interested in this property. It is well known that he sold out to a large company of which he is not a member.
Sold out at an enhanced value, I suppose.

The value may he enhanced or it may not. But the plain fact remains that there is no danger, if this is a large spruce limit, of the timber being cut out; this dock will be as useful twenty, or forty or fifty years from now as it is to-day.

We on this side must thank the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) for the information he has given. His statement is-and I accept it as true, I know he would not make the statement unless it were true-that the hon. member for Stanstead was either sole or part owner of this property and was desirous of unloading on some company, and, to increase the value, he gets his party friends to spend $70,000 of public money there, of which he gets the benefit. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schell) did not say so directly, but I am sure he is blaming the government for this action and I say he is quite right in doing so. The hon. minister is taken to account by the member for Glengarry. What does the hon. gentleman complain of ? He is complaining that after this great amount of $60,000 or $70,000 for this dock was appropriated, the owner unloads it on an incorporated company and gets the benefit. I agree with the hon. member for Glengarry that the minister and the party should be censured for having made such a grant. Another point brought out by the hon. member for Glengarry-and I must thank him for it also-is that if it were true that the timber could be cut out in fifteen years or so it might be a hardship on the hon. member for Stanstead to ask him to build a dock; but it would not be a hardship to ask him to build the dock instead of having it built by the public, because the timber constantly reproduces itself in from sixteen to twenty-five years. It will be seen, therefore, that the hon. member for Stanstead had a more decided advantage that I thought he had. In view of the complaint made by the hon. member for Glengarry I am sure the hon. Minister of Public Works will agree not to allow the dock to be used by the company that has purchased the rights of the hon. member for Stanstead-at least the hon. member for Glengarry says they have done so-without giving the country a rental of at least eight per cent on the expenditure, and also keeping the dock in repair.

I do not see how I am to make an agreement contrary to the law. These people will have to pay dues according to the rates fixed. There is a large business done, and the dock ought to yield a good revenue.
What are the dues ?
I have not the rates here; they are under another department.

It is evident from the list read by the hon. member for East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett) either that the dues are very small or, in the case of many of these docks, no business is done. I cannot but feel that there has been a great deal of public money spent in these public works without ministering to any real public need. No man can convince me that a revenue of from twenty-five cents to twelve dollars from works that have cost thousands can indicate anything but that the money spent on these works has been almost wholly wasted. When I think that along the shores of Lake Ontario, in such ridings as that I have the honour to represent, where millions of bushels of grain are shipped and large quantities of goods imported, there are towns whose post offices give a large revenue to the country, yet where not a dollar of public money has been spent, I am convinced more than ever that there must be something radically wrong in such a vote as this. The proposition now before us seems to be one of the most absurd ever submitted to the House since I have had the honour of being a member-that we are to spend something like $60,000 at a point where the minister tells us there is not a town. I venture the assertion that if we were to look at the Postmaster General's Report we should find there is not even a post office there.
There is not-I have looked it up.

I have no objection to hon. members of this House buying timber limits, but the objection that I raise is to the expenditure of public money for the benefit of corporations or private individuals. And against this the minister should set his face determinedly. I believe that the minister feels deep down in his own heart that there has been a wrong which it will be his duty to make right at the earliest opportunity.

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Sir. Slonk) was obliged to go to Slontreal this evening. He left in my hands a copy of the estimates with some items marked to be reserved, and amongst them I find the item now under discussion. If there was an agreement that this and other items should be allowed to stand until the House goes into Supply again, I do not think we should discuss the matter at greater length. I presume the hon. Slinister of Public Works will allow these items that are marked to stand.

I am most anxious to meet the wishes of the members of this committee, but the proposition I have to make is better for the hon. member for Jacques Cartier than that presented by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and it is in accordance with the arrangement I entered into with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier before

Lie left. We all lmve rights in these matters. This is the third or fourth time the items have been allowed to stand on account of the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Monk's) absence. To-day, when he was going away I agreed- and I am anxious to carry out that agreement, and I submit it is more generous than what the hon. member for West Toronto is asking-that the general vote for the province of Quebec should stand with the understanding that when it comes ul>, any item in the Quebec list can be taken up and discussed. This will give greater latitude than would be given by merely picking out four or five items and passing the others. This carries out the understanding we had with the hon. member before six o'clock.

I hope the minister does not mean that he will pass all these items, because I think it is possible that a motion will be made to strike out this item. I think the time has arrived when jobs of this kind should be stopped. I am satisfied that the minister, if he wishes to make a reputation for himself in his new office, will see that this sort of thing is ended. Here we have a member of this House engaged in the lumber business, going down there where there is not even a post office, where there is not even a resident, and gets thousands of dollars nominally expended on a wharf. Has anybody inspected that wharf ? Is there a report of the inspector of the work ? Is there a wharf in existence ? rossibly this is the stuff which sailed down the Bay of Fundy, and formed a portion of some of the money spoken of by Senator Ellis which was sent from the Dominion government to assist the Liberal party in New Brunswick elections. We may as well look these things squarely in the face. So far as I am concerned. I have no hesitation in saying that I would like to see this item stricken out, unless we get some more satisfactory data in connection with it.
If my hon. friend had paid careful attention to the discussion
I listened to every word that was said. I object to the hon. gentleman's insinuation that I did not pay attention to what was said. I can tell him everything that transpired in the conversation.

I did not intend to offend the hon. gentleman. What I meant to say was that he could not have understood the situation, or given it that thought that it requires. I said that parliament some three years ago had committed itself to this contract. I be lieve the matter was discussed at considerable length on a previous occasion, I am not sure but that there was a vote on this question on a previous occasion. If the item was struck out of the estimates now,
it would not save the country from paying the amount already expended, with the added cost of a suit brought against the Crown. The government are legally bound to the contractors to carry out the work. Perhaps about one-half the money has already been spent; therefore no member of this committee under these conditions would feel disposed to vote to strike the item out of the estimates. The contract has been entered into and the amount will have to he paid; if the vote is cancelled, then the country will have to pay such damages as the court may find in favour of the contractors, in addition to what they have already earned.

Will the minister tell us from whom this dock was purchased, who are the contractors, who owned the timber limit ? Let us have the names of the people in connection with this matter. Don't be afraid to bring out the names of the men.

I do not think it is within the province of the department to have all the information the hon. gentleman asks for; but all that we have and all that is reasonable, I am ready to produce. It has been stated here, though I have no personal knowledge of it, that the member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) was largely interested in timber limits in this district. I would like to know how many business men there are in this House who have not business interests in various parts of the country where public works are constructed, and whose property will be more or less affected by our legislation. It is quite true that there may be extreme cases where the money expended will benefit an individual or a corporation rather than the public at large. In this particular case, all I know is that statements have been made that an hon. member of this House was interested largely in timber limits in that district. There are many men sitting in this House at present, and have sat in it in the past, who have greatly benefited by the expenditure of public money in different parts of the country where they happen to be owners of timber limits, or who may be engaged in other business. The development of the country would not go on unless men of their energy and ability engaged in business. The argument that no money should be spent in a locality because certain individuals will benefit from it more than others, I do not think any one giving it serious thought would endorse. We have spent something over $80,000,000 on our canal system, which has directly benefited certain parties along the rivers, and certain large centres more than other parties and other centres. We have lately gone so far as to free the canals of the dues that were charged to people using them, believing that it was in | the general interest of the country to do

so. In this case, I know that in 1901 or 1902 a vote was taken committing parliament to this expenditure, and a contract was entered into. The hon. gentleman wanted to know the names of the contractors. They are Heney & Smith, of Ottawa. This contract was entered into on the 29th of June, 1901; and, as I have already stated, about half the money has already been paid to the contractors.
When was the first vote taken ?

I have not heard the name of the party from whom this property was purchased. The minister told us the government had purchased this dock and had a deed of it. From whom was that deed obtained ?
The MINISTER' OF PUBLIC WORKS. I have not the deed here, nor could it be expected that a minister should have these documents.
The minister should have all this information at his fingers end.
All reasonable information, but not unreasonable information. I have stated on the authority of the deputy minister that a grant of the land required here has been made over to the Crown.
Was there any deed of it ?

Yes, I am informed there was a deed. Of course, it could not be a legal grant without a deed. Supposing that this property belonged to an individual member, the deed would come from him. That seems to be the insinuation. I do not know, the deputy minister does not remember. But the point in which this committee and the public are interested is to know whether the Crown has been granted the property and at what price. In this particular case the grant was made free.
Was the contract entered into before any vote was passed by this House ?
I have given the date of the contract.

The minister says that what the committee is interested in is to know that we are committed to the contract. Is it to be said that if we have allowed, without knowledge, an item to pass whereby we become committed to a contract that is unwise and injudicious, in which the country's money is spent to no good purpose, and because a portion of the money has already been expended, that we are bound to spend the rest, or, in other words, to throw Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
it away ? On the very face of it, this seems to be a job, and not a very creditable one at that. If the information we have got out peaeemeal be correct, an hon. member of this House goes down and buys a large timber limit in a comparatively unknown forest, and by some kind of understanding with the government, I presume come to beforehand, he is promised that he will get a dock there, and the country is going to spend $70,000 or $80,000 to benefit his property. There is no business to be done, no boats running there, no trade; but the government commences an expenditure. For whose benefit ? Simply for the purpose of benefiting a member of this House. That seems to be the whole story so far as the Information goes at present. Now, the country had better know that. Then the minister went on and told us that the very fact that this man sold his interest in that timber limit at such an enhanced value is no evidence that it was a vote of this House which made the place valuable. It was nothing else which made the place valuable. There was no trade to be done, it was a forest, it was on the river, I presume. And when the government agreed to make an expenditure of $80,000 to build a wharf, it is no wonder that the property has become valuable. The result is that an hon. member supporting the government helps to vote the money and then sells out at a greatly advanced price, and we are told that because we are committed to it we must go on and make this expenditure. The country had better know this, because, so far as we know, or so far as any information is vouchsafed to this House, this is a most discreditable transaction throughout, unjustifiable, and I was going to say corrupt. I think I would be quite justified if I did so. I want the people of my part of the country to know this. They have tried very hard to get a few thousand dollars spent to improve harbours and to build wharfs where there are large and enterprising manufacturing towns surrounded by a prosperous farming country and where an extensive trade is being done. Yet, they cannot get this government to provide proper facilities to carry on their trade. But, the government will go to the province of Quebec and start to build a wharf where there is no trade, where there is nothing but a timber limit, the property of a member of this House, where there is not even a post office, or a settlement, not even a trade to be done, not even a boat calling there, and yet we are committed to an expenditure of $80,000, and because we inadvertently became committed to it, not having this knowledge when we committed ourselves, which, if we had had it we never would have submitted to vote the item-because we have been committed to it without proper knowledge, then, it is said, we must go on and carry it out.
Why does the hon. gentleman say that the cost will be $80,000 ?
That which has been already done the hon. member tells us, must cost $59,000.
The work is under contract, and there should uot be any mistake. The cost is $59,500.
I would like to get an answer from the hon. minister to my question. Which came first-the vote or the contract for the erection of this wharf ?
The vote came first.
When was the contract let ?
29th June, 1901.
And the first vote was last year ?
No, the first vote was in 1901.
How much was that vote ?
Five thousand.

What is the amount of the contract ?
The MINISTER OF'PUBLIC WORKS. Fifty-three thousand nine hundred.
Was it intended with that vote of $5,000 to build this wharf ? Had the engineers gone down there and estimated that $5,000 would be sufficient to build the wharf that was afterwards to cost $59,500 ?

I think the hon. gentleman now leading the opposition (Mr. Sproule) will see that it is hardly fair to say this matter was done without the knowledge of the House. There was a very full discussion last year, and if I am not mistaken a vote was taken on this very item.
No.
Well then I have been misinformed. I could not vouch for that statement, but I was under the impression a vote had been taken. However, ' Hansard ' will show.
There was no discussion when the item was brought up in the first instance, and that is what the opposition complained of last year.
I think it Is wrong for this House to grant a vote of money without having knowledge of the total amount of the cost.
That is our contention.

I quite agree with hon. gentlemen. I have no fault to find with that proposition. I think it is right. It should be the duty of the minister of the department to furnish that information to the House. I think it is due to the House and the country that when a vote is taken of a small amount for the reason that it would not be spent within the current fiscal year the estimated cost of the undertaking should be submitted so that parliament would know what it was committing the country to.

I am glad to see that the hon. minister takes that view. It seems to me that as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, this smells very strongly of jobbery. It seems that in order to get a candidate in a certain county in the province of Quebec, it was necessary for a deal of this sort to be made. The deal was, as appears from the statements that have been made, that in order to get this gentleman to run in a certain county in the province of Quebec it was necessary to make him a promise that this property which he had bought and which was not valuable from the fact that there were not then the necessary facilities for carrying on the lumbering business, would be made the object of a large expenditure of money. Then an arrangement was made for the vote that was passed in this House. The thin edge of the wedge was put in at first. The small amount of $5,000 was put in the estimates for the purpose of committing the House to the greater expenditure which was to follow and without any estimate whatever from the engineer and without any information being vouchsafed to the House as to the expenditure.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) say what authority he has for making the statement that there was an agreement in regard to this matter ?
Does the hon. minister dispute that ?

Certainly, as far as I am concerned and on behalf of the government, I am prepared to take the responsibility of saying that there is no knowledge on the part of any member of the government of any such thing. I have admitted the statement of hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the interest of an hon. member in the landed property and in the timber limits, as I could not dispute it, but I do desire to say on behalf of myself and on behalf of the government that there was no arrangement previous to the election, cr any discussion in regard to the matter whatever. Unless the hon. gentleman has some authority for a serious statement of this kind, he is not justified in mak-

ing it. He as a lawyer, and as a member of this House will see tlie necessity for giving some authority for such a statement.

There is a very strong rumour in the county of Stanstead that such an arrangement was made, and I may say further to the hon. minister that the facts of the case, as disclosed to-night and in the debate of last year when this matter was up, show clearly that there is a very strong ground for the rumour that prevails in Stanstead. What do we find ? We find that one hon. member who knew that this matter was coming up, and who should have been here to stand up and explain it is conspicuous by his absence. I speak of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell). The first vote was a small vote of $5,000, when, if there had been any examination at all, it must have been known to the department that it would require a very much larger amount of money to build that wharf there. Now, the hon. minister comes down aud asks for $60,000.
that some one has given a deed to the department. In view of the fact that last year there was considerable discussion with regard to this, it is very surprising that the deputy minister should say that some one gave a deed of the property, but who he does not know. The hon. gentleman from Glengarry (Mr. Schell) says that the property belongs to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell), and we are much obliged to him for that information.

I beg to correct the hon. gentleman. Personally, I do not know anything about the circumstances, and I did not say that I did. The member for Simcoe said that the timber would be cut off in a few years, and I rose to correct that statement". I went on further to say, as the name of the hon. member for Stanstead was mentioned in connection with this, that I had seen in the ' Canada Lumberman ' where this property had been sold for a certain sum.	[DOT]
How much ?
They asked for $25,000 last year.
And how much this year?
Thirty-six thousand.

Making upwards of $70,000 for this purpose. We find that they are making this expenditure of public money in a place where there are no people to serve except the one individual who owned tlie property, not even a post office in this place, while there are important towns and harbours all over the country requiring an expenditure of public money. Take the great city of Toronto, where it was impossible to get a grant of any-size from the government to provide the necessary facilities for the great metropolis of this country ; yet $70,000 of an expenditure is to be made in an obscure place where there is no post office, simply to enable this gentleman who had made a bad bargain in his purchase of this property to unload it. The facts of the matter have been clearly shown by the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell). The committee must be grateful to the hon. member for Glengarry for the exceeding amount of light he has thrown upon the question.
During the discussion last year I think the amount of the contract was given to the House.

I do not remember whether it was or not, but I know that a great part of the discussion last year was with respect to the deed to the property on which the wharf was going to be built, aud we found the Minister of Public Works first declaring that no one owned it, and then that he thought it was Crown land. Now we find that it was private property, and Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
I cannot tell you now, but you can get the paper in the reading room. I mentioned these two points, and if hon. gentlemen attribute any further statements to me, they are mistaken.

The hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) has just confirmed what I said. He stated that the property belonged to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell), who hjtd since sold it to a corporation. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schell) tells us that he read that statement in the ' Canada Lumberman.'
It has not appeared in tlie 'Canada Gazette' yet.
Perhaps it will appear there next. I must congratulate the minister that he has come around to our way of thinking, and has promised that there will be no more jobs of this kind while he is minister.

I want more than that promise from the minister. We must have the papers showing who first applied for the building of the wharf and upon whose advice the expenditure was undertaken. It would be better that the minister should leave the vote over, and get the information in the meantime.
Would it not be the part of wisdom to allow this item to stand until the hon. member for Jacques Cartier is present ?
Everything that was said to-night was said last year.

Of course, I could get the [DOT] Hansard ' and read what was said last year, but if the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) understood that this

item was to be reserved, that understanding should be carried out.
I would be very particular indeed to carry out any arrangement I made with any member of the opposition.
I believe that.
The arrangement which I propose is much broader, and I might be found fault witli if I narrowed it down to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke).
If the narrower arrangement suits us and suits the hon. member (Mr. Monk), no fault can be found with the minister if he agrees to it.

My proposal is that the general vote for the province of Quebec should stand, with the privilege to any hon. member to discuss any and every item as fully as he wishes. If hon. gentlemen look at the * Hansard ' of last year they will find that the amount of the contract, the names of the contractors, and all other information was given, and that parliament has committed itself to this work. We cannot set up against the contractor that parliament did not possess full knowledge, and we are under obligations in the highest sense to pay the contractors for the work that has been undertaken.

It is due to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) that this item should stand until he is present. Last year the statement was made in the House that the only condition under which he would be a candidate was that the government would expend a large sum of money at this place, and that, when the government promised that, he consented to be a candidate. That charge was made last year in the House, and it is made again this year. I remember distinctly that when the matter was up last year the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lovell) was in his place that day, but when this discussion came on he was not in his seat. It is due to that hon. gentleman (Mr. Lovell) that he should be in his place in this House to say whether or not the rumour is well founded. So far as I am concerned, putting one piece of information I have received with another, I have no doubt in my mind that this was an inducement held out to the hon. gentleman to be a candidate. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lovell) had not been a member of tiiis House before ; he had large interests at this place, and we find that here, where there are something like 314 souls, men, women and children, the government is going to expend a sum of nearly $60,000. Last year we objected that the government had no title to this property, and to-night the minister is not in a position to give us any information on that point. Last year we were told that Rocky Point,, where the pier is being built, was Crown land, and now
we are told that some private person has given a title, but who that private person is the government does not seem to know. Last year we complained that the government came down with a vote for $5,000 for a work that would ultimately cost $60,000, and to-day we say that parliament had not the information before it necessary to consent to the work in the first place. We are told that we should ask this information in the first instance, but every one knows that from time to time certain items may slip through because the opposition feel that they do not want to carp over every item. We want to find fault only with the items which we think we are justified in finding fault with, and this is one of the items. Let this item stand until the member for Stanstead can tell us whether or not there is any truth in the rumour that he would not be a candidate until it was promised that this money would be expended.

There are two points which the hon. gentleman makes. The first is that the Item ought to stand. The agreement with the hon. member was that one item should stand and that all the items in this vote might be discussed under that item at a future time. I do not think the hon. gentleman could say that any broader or fairer proposition could be made.
I confess that I am very much against that principle, because when we have passed items in that way, we have been stopped from discussing them on the ground that they have passed the House.
Not if we made an agreement that they might be discussed.
But we are practically committing ourselves to the vote when we have not the information properly before us.
The other point the hon. gentleman makes is that the information was not properly given. If he looks in ' Hansard,' he will find that the information was given.
The hon. member for Stanstead, it is stated, refused to be a candidate until it was agreed that this money should be spent for his benefit.

That is not the point I am referring to. If any hon. gentleman has a charge to make against the ex-Minister of Public Works, who proposed this vote and explained it, there is a proper way to make that charge. We are now passing an appropriation to pay the balance of this contract. That is what is "under consideration.

The hon. gentleman's predecessor did not take the same view of this question that the hon. gentleman is now taking. He said that the hon. gentleman

with the rest of his colleagues were as responsible for this matter as he was.
That is perfectly correct. Every gentleman acquainted, with our constitutional system knows that.
The hon. gentleman's predecessor in office stated the position; and, as the Minister of Justice has passed over * Hansard,' I will read what his colleagues said last year.

The hon. gentleman need not read it, because I admit that the government is responsible for this contract. The majority in parliament are also responsible. As Minister of Public Works, I am committed, the ministry is committed and parliament is committed to this contract. There is no doubt about that.

I would like to ask the minister why it was necessary to get a deed of this property, because on page 1034 of ' Hansard ' of last year, the Minister of Public Works is reported as having stated that no site was purchased, because it was not necessary to purchase a site, the work being built on a rocky point that did not belong to any one. If the minister says there is a deed of the property, I would like to know wiiy this deed was obtained, and from whom it was obtained.

The hon. gentleman must see that that is an unreasonable proposition, because parliament voted the money last session to carry out this contract. In view of the statement then made by the late minister that the government did not own the property, we are now in a much stronger position, because I have made the statement that the deed has been procured. As to whom it was purchased from, I have promised to bring down the document so that every man can see it.

That is the strongest reason why the vote should not go through now, because we have not that information. I cannot understand why the hon. gentleman wants to press it, in view of the rumours that are floating about in regard to the connection of the hon. member for Stan-stead with this transaction, and in view of the fact that a deed has been obtained when it was said last session that there was no need of obtaining a deed. I think we should have this information.
The passing of this item does not prevent any hon. member from bringing that up.

Then the minister coflld use the same argument that he has used already. He has stated that we committed ourselves so far last year and the year before that we cannot back out of this transaction now ; and yet he wants to take the vote Mr. CLARKE.
and still further commit the House. Then he will say, you passed this vote without the information, and now, what do you want the information for, when you have committed the House to the whole expenditure ?

I think the minister ought to let this item stand for the present and furnish the information we require. We should have the deed of the property, we should be informed who applied for this dock to be built and who recommended it, and should have all the papers connected with it. We should be informed what the engineer's estimate of the cost was before the work was undertaken. We require all this information to enable us to judge of the matter before we commit ourselves any further to it. Then, the hon. member for Stanstead is not present, neither is the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who wished to be here when this matter was discussed.
