These are strong reasons why this item should be held over.

I will answer the hon. gentleman's questions seriatim. He says the item should stand until we are informed who recommended this vote. I have already stated that it was recommended by the Minister of Public Works.
There must have been some one who applied for it.
I have stated that there was no further information about it in the department. How can I bring down information that is not in the possession of the department ?
Is it possible that there was no application made for the expenditure ?
I have answered one question. The next is as to the report of the engineer. Parliament authorized the expenditure after the minister had stated that there was no report of the engineer.
Could the minister submit it without a report of the engineer 1

I am only giving the facts as they are. 1 have nothing to keep back. There is no reason for letting the item stand in order to bring down what does not exist. The minister admitted that there was no report, and still parliament voted the amount.
Against the wishes of the opposition.
The opposition did not oppose it.
They protested against it.

They did not vote against it, and parliament passed the item. I cannot agree to the suggestion that this should stand because either

the ex-Minister of Public Works or the hon. member for Stanstend is not present. If there was not the fullest opportunity given to bring the matter up when they were present, I would say there was some reason for the request; but under the circumstances I can see no reason why this item should bo delayed further.

It seems to me that the very fact that there is no request from any person in the records of the department, as the hon. minister has just told us, for the erection of this wharf, is a confirmation of this very rumour, so prevalent through the county of Stanstead, that the hon. member for Stanstead became a member of this House on the understanding that he was to have the value of his property enhanced by the building of this wharf at the public expense. If such were not the case, there would be some recommendation or some petition to the department showing the desire of the people of that section for the construction of this work.

In the absence of the hon. member for Stanstead, who should be here to defend himself, 1 notice that there are two members present from the adjoining locality of Bonaventure and Restigouche. These hon. gentlemen could throw some light on the question.

We are now called upon to vote $36,000 in connection with a certain pier at Grande Valve. While I have no desire to embarrass the hon. minister and wish to expedite as far as possible, the work of the session, I feel bound to call attention to the fact that while at this place there are only three hundred people.
Three hundred and fourteen.

While at this place, with a population of only three hundred and fourteen, we are called on to spend $36,000, in the province of Prince Edward Island, where we have a population of 100,000, the government are only spending $34,000 on public works. That is not right and I protest against it in the name of the people I represent. If you cannot spend more than $34,000 in Prince Edward Island, you can surely have no justification for spending $61,000 in Grand Valve. In the interest of fair play and justice, this item should be allowed to stand until the hon. member from Stanstead is here to explain the facts. If he thinks that by absenting himself, he is going to escape being called to account we should prove to him that he is mistaken. Any hon. member who gets a timber limit from the government should be prepared to stand up in this House and defend himself against the criticisms made on such a transaction as the present, but the hon. gentleman does not want to go
into the facts. He has made his escape by the back door and left this item t:* be dis-t cussed by his friends. I think we should insist on this item standing over.

I wish to show exactly the position of this thing. There is no doubt something wrong in it. The hon. minister lias admitted that the government had no engineer there. The hon. member from Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) is a lumber man. Lumber men do not engage engineers to locate their work but select the places themselves where they require wharfs, and evidently in this case the hon. member interested said to the government :	I want
the wharf at a certain place and you will build it there. According to the admission of the lion. Minister of Public Works, the government did not know anything about the best locality where to build that wharf. Well, who did ? It must be clear to everybody that they were completely in the hands of the parties interested and are eating and drinking their own condemnation.
We have uo evidence whatever that there is any such wharf in existence. No engineer, no officer of the department, has ever seen the wharf.
I did not say that.
Let us have the wharf in the House.
Bring in the wharf.
Since that contract was let, there has been an engineer in charge of the work.

The hon. minister tells us that this wharf is for the benefit of the public. How is it that for the last two hundred years, dowu the gulf of the St. Lawrence, the shores of which are inhabited by fishermen who require wharfs, there never has been a wharf built except at this locality, and that is down in the interests of the hon. member from Stanstead and promised at the time of the election in 1901. That in itself shows that there must be something wrong.

We are making only a reasonable request when we ask the hon. minister to allow this matter to stand over. The discussion to-night shows this to be one of the rankest jobs that ever disgraced this or any other government, and to call on the followers of the government to vote this thing through without the fullest information is putting a very severe test on their party allegiance.
If the hon. gentleman wants information he will get it. What information does lie require ?

East year the ex-Minister pf Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said that the deed of that property was all right and that it did not belong to any body but the government. But when the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) was asked who owned the property where the dock was built, he said that it was owned by the firm of Lovell and Company. The ex-Minister of Public WTorks then said that if he had known that he would not have undertaken the work and that he would not continue it until the government had a proper deed of the land. He must have been misled or he would not have put a dollar into that dock until the deed of the property was given. We would like to know who misled the Minister of Public Works last year when he spent several thousand dollars of public money in building a dock for a private individual who owned lumber] lands in that locality ! If public money is to be spent, it should be expended where the people generally get the benefit and not for the special advantage of one individual. I am in the lumber business myself, and if at any time I require a wharf for my business, I have to build it myself, and that is the case with other lumber men. If the hon. Minister of Public Works will let this item stand over and thoroughly investigate the matter, he will conclude to spend * no more money there. We have spent more money on that dock than the country can afford, taking into consideration any benefit the country will get from it. The hon. minister would do well if he would stop all proceedings on that work, because I do not think it will ever be of any public advantage at all corresponding with the amount invested. It will be a detriment to the country to keep it up, and the benefit will go to one individual.

The hon. gentleman has misquoted the exMinister of Public Works last year. According to 1 Hansard ' he said :
I quite agree that we should have titles in every ease, and my officers have received positive instructions on that point. They are within hearing of my voice and they know that I have given them the most positive and severe instructions.
Instructions as to what ?
As to the deed.
What page is the hon. minister quoting from ?
Page 1042.
That refers to the Cara-quet wharf.

Perhaps so. But, so far as the point under discussion is concerned, to clear that up, Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
I have informed the Committee that the deed to this property has been procured.
From whom ?
I have not that information.

It might be given as some defence of this scheme if it could be shown that other persons would be served besides this company. But the map shows that this part of Gasp 6 is so rough that the local government have not even surveyed it into townships, or parishes. The place where this work is situated has the suggestive name of * Grand Valley of the Mountains.' It was stated here last year, and the hon. member for Stanstead has had an opportunity to deny it, that he, being the owner of this property in Gaspfi, was desirous of having a dock established there. He was not a member of the House before this parliament, and the facts seem to bear out the rumour current among his friends in his own riding, that he became a candidate upon condition that this large public expenditure should be made for his benefit. It is due to the hon. member for Stanstead to give him an opportunity to contradict that rumour, and I am prepared for my part, to carry on the discussion until the hon. member for Stanstead is summoned to give his explanation of the matter. Why should not the minister allow this item to stand. A reference to the census shows that at the place where this work is to be there are only about thirty heads of families. This saw-mill must be a very small one. I do not know the capacity of the mill or the extent of the timber limit. But I will be bound to say that, when the facts of the case come out, it will be found that the amount paid for the mill and the limit is about equal to the government's expenditure on this work. In fact, as stated by the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell), the government is spending $00,000 to enhance the value of the property of the hon. member for Stanstead. About half the amount has already been expended. Let the hon. minister put down his foot and stop the work on this dock.
You' would not save any money by that.

Why, certainly. The hon. minister will have to settle with the contractor; and he knows that the contractor cannot go into court without getting a fiat from his department through the Minister of Justice. Let the contractor be paid for what he has done, and we may be quite sure the lumber company will finish the dock, ns they are to get the benefit or it. It is plain beyond the shadow of a doubt that the whole thing, from its inception, was a political job. And, now that the country has spent $30,000 to enrich the hon. mem-for Stanstead, I am prepared for one, to vote against any further expenditure.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) suggests that the discussion should be kept up merely for the sake of the discussion. Now, it seems to me that an arrangement made between the parties in this House should be carried out

What arrangement has been made between the parties ? None whatever. There may have been an arrangement between private individuals on
either side

If there is no other reason for further discussion than has already been given, I cannot see what objection there can be to the proposal I submitted. I have offered to allow the general vote to stand with the understanding that when it comes up any special item in the Quebec list can b'e discussed by any hon. member whether he is present now or not.

It is due to the hon. minister to say that I do not dispute the accuracy of his statement respecting the arrangement entered into between himself and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), but I do say that that hon'. gentleman, who is absent, must have misunderstood what the agreement was, because, as I have explained, he left with me a copy of the estimates with several items, including the one under discussion, marked to be reserved. Evidently he did not understand that this item was to pass.

The hon. minister says that an arrangement was made between the two parties. I want to tell him there was nothing of the kind. It has been a fashion in this House-it may have come in before hon. gentlemen opposite took office, but it has been very carefully followed by them-for the government to reserve an item in a given list with the understanding that any item on the list may be discussed when it comes up; then they bring it up at a time when the people interested are not here, and it goes through without discussion. I want to tell the hon. minister that this item is not going to get by in any such way; I give him fair warning of that. We are going to get at the facts in this case, or we will know the reason why.
I was not present in the earlier part of the discussion. May I ask what amount has been spent on this work ?

I happen to be responsible for this work. I was in office when representations were made to us that there was a very large trade to be developed if a wharf was built at Grande Vallee. We had the survey made, and, after a good 49
deal of discussion and, perhaps, of hesitation, the government decided to go on with the work. The expenditure now under discussion is not a new one, and it seems to me rather late to treat it as it is being treated now. The whole thing came up before the House last year. There was some discussion but the item went through. Now a contract has been entered into, and the government of the country is pledged to that work. Whether the House made a mistake or not, the government is pledged. This is the case in two words. But there is not so much mistake as hon. gentlemen opposite seem to believe. It is to my knowledge that, in the past, both long ago and in recent times, the country has built wharfs in places where there was not a large population. It is not necessary that there should be a large population at the place before a work of this kind is gone on with.
The hopes of the future are an element in every public work of importance. But whether we have made a mistake or not, the House authorized the Minister of Public Works last year to go on with the work. There is no answer to that. If we have made a. mistake, well, so much the worse for us. But the country is bound to pay for that work now. It has been said, and I believe truly said, that certain parties, among whom is a member of parliament, will benefit by that work. I do not know of many public works in which some people are not benefited. AVe do not build wharfs for heaven's sake all the time. AVe build wharfs for the people living on this planet, not for those who are in heaven, but for those who are on this very planet that we are so happy to live on. Now this work comes within that category. It is built for people who are living under God's sun, and the hon. member for Stanstead is among them. He has bought limits there. There are many members of parliament who have property in places where wharfs are built. Are they guilty of any job ? Are they guilty of any crime ? It is not a crime against civilization or' against God to build public works for the benefit of people, whoever they may be. Members of parliament, to my knowledge, have often benefited by works which have been constructed in the past, and which are going on now. AA^ell, this work is of some magnitude for Grande Vallee. It may be a little exaggeration of the blessings that we have freely distributed in this country. But this country is prosperous. The Minister of Finance has just told us that we have a surplus of $13,500,000, and out of that surplus we are bound to pay to the contractors of Grand Valffie the balance of the work.

I quite agree with the request of some gentlemen on this side of the House that Mr. Lovell should have an opportunity of explaining his connection with this matter. He comes from a county



adjoining my own in the Eastern Townships. There is in the public mind a scandal connected with this affair that ought to be cleared up in the Interest of the firm of Lovell & Sons, of which the hon. member for Staustead is the head. At the time of the convention when candidates were chosen for Staustead county, Mr. Lovell came to the convention called by the Conservatives, and there it was generally understood that he was desirous of being the candidate, not solely on account of his love of the Liberal party, but for the purpose of furthering some object that he was understood to have in view. That was the general understanding at this meeting. He made a proposition which was accepted by the Conservative party of Stanstead county, that so far as that election was concerned it should be run free from any corruption or expenditure. Whether that agreement was kept or not, it is not necessary for me to inquire. But we were surprised in the first place that Mr. Lovell should be desirous of being a candidate; we were surprised in the next place that he attended our convention; we were surprised in the third place that lie made this proposition, because it has not been the habit of the Liberal party in Stan-stead county to run elections upon that pure and angelic basis. Well, Sir, that was our feeling, and as we prosecuted our iuquiries, we were confidentially told that Mr. Lovell had some axe to grind, and that was the reason he was| a candidate. Now lie bought a limit from the government, a very small piece of land on the lower St. Lawrence. There was nothing else there but a forest, he built a mill and acquired these limits, and then it seems that he wanted a wharf. In Mr. Lovell's county and in the district in which he lives, it is firmly believed, I am sorry to say to his discredit, that this wharf is the price of his candidature for the Liberal party. Now, Sir, I think it is a grave situation, a disgraceful situation, and one that Mr. Lovell should be prepared to stand up in this House and either refute or acknowledge, as the case may be. Therefore I think that when we ask the government to allow this item to stand, it is done as much in the interest of Mr. Lovell and of his character as of anybody else. Since that time the property has been sold. Sir. Lovell and his sons, so I understand by the public press, are no longer owners of that property, it has passed over to other hands, and Mr. Lovell is reputed to have received something like $100,000 out of his property.
How much did he pay for it ?
He paid very little. They are making the price of this wharf out of it. Now', Mr. Chairman, don't you think that this is a most extraordinary situation, that this country should go to work and

spend $50,000 or $60,000 in building a wharf for a property the total value of which is only $100,000 or $125,000 ? It is a most extraordinary position. The expenditure is unwarranted on that basis alone. On a property that is only valued at $125,000 we have no right to expend $00,000 of the public money for its development. I think we have a right to protest against it on that ground alone as a business proposition, to say nothing about the other question that has been raised.
Now, before I sit down I wish to say that, taking all these matters into consideration, the statements that have been made at the very outset of Mr. Lorvell's candidature for Stanstead county that he was to receive some consideration, that he had some object in view in running for that county besides being the candidate of the Liberal party, and when we find this item put in here and this charge made throughout the country, throughout the Eastern Townships, all around Mr. Lovell's home, in the very village where he lives-I say in view of all these circumstances it is a duty the government owes to itself, irrespective of party, that that lion, gentleman should be given an opportunity to stand up in this House and defend himself from these imputations. I say this, Sir, because the name of Lovell & Sons as an honoured business concern has been above-board in our section of the country. Moreover, this gentleman is sitting in his seat here in parliament for * the last time. He is an old man, and whatever the results of the next battle may be in Stanstead county for membership in this parliament, Mr. Lovell will not be the member for Sanstead county. There is not much quesion about that. Now, having had such a business career in that section of the country, I think this is not the way that he should retire from political life, leaving this stain upon his character. Therefore, I say that the minister in justice to Mr. Lovell and his family, in view of his business record, should allow this item to stand until the whole matter is properly explained so far as Mr. Lovell's connection with it is concerned.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that this contract was let in November, 1901. Now if that statement is correct, I would like to know what is the use of the government going through the farce of entering into a contract pledging us to pay $53,000 for a work when the contract was made in November, 1901 ? Is it not a bit of a farce to enter into an arrangement without first coming to parliament and laying before us what the work is supposed to be, what the cost of the work is to be ? But after the government entered into a contract it comes down and, as a matter of form, asks us to pass a vote. They first expend the money aud (lieu come and ask parliament to vote it.

I have already stated

the ex-Minister of Public Works will be able to speak for himself-that he took the responsibility of recommending this work, and the government assumes responsibility for it now. Last session parliament, after full discussion, endorsed the contract after it was made.
Will the minister be good enough to tell us the size of the wharf, how much work has been done on it ? Is there such a wharf in existence ? I have asked that two or three times.

There is no doubt that there is such a wharf in existence. The work has been taken charge of by a special engineer of the department named Mr. Dubuc. The works placed under contract comprise the construction of a breakwater-pier composed of a substructure of seven cribs of ballasted crib-work having a total length of 900 feet and a breadth increasing from twenty-five feet on top at the shore end to twenty-nine feet at the outer end and which are to be sunk flush with the low water level, spring tide, and topped by a continuous superstructure standing eighteen feet above the said low water level, spring tides.
How much of it has been done ? Is there any report of the progress made 1
Did you say eighteen feet above low water ?
Eighteen feet above low water.
Has the hon. gentleman the first estimate made ?
No, I have the total amount that has been paid out.
How much is that ?
$20,000. The material must be on the ground by this time and under the contract the work must be finished within a month or two.
Has the work been continued during the winter months ?
I understand form the reports of the department that the material was got out during the winter, that it is now on the ground and that the work will soon be completed.

Who are the contractors ?
The MINISTER OB1 PUBLIC WORKS. Messrs. Heney & Smith, Ottawa.

I think it is only fair that under the special circumstances in this case the hon. minister should not press the 49J
vote. It is a fact that there is no public interest to be served by this dock save the interest of this lumber company which own the laud adjoining and if the hon. minister stops the work at present and does not do anything more upon it, he knows very well that the lumber company will complete the work. It will not be the first contract that this government have broken after contracts have been let. The hon. minister knows that hundreds and hundreds of contracts equally as binding in point of honour and from a business point of view were broken by this government. When the hon. gentlemen came into power they found from one end of this country to the other a contract solemnly entered into by the Postmaster General with mail carriers. What did the hon. gentlemen do ? Without even giving a cent of compensation they cut these contracts in two, refused to carry them and ' refused to give these men permission to go into court to seek damages to which they were entitled. This is only going to be a case of hardship on this lumber company who own the property if called upon to complete this dock which, if completed, will be serving them and them alone. I think it is fair to ask the hon. minister that no further money shall be spent on this work and let this company complete the work. There are no surveyed lands in the neighbourhood, the dock is not going to serve any public interest after this company get through with their saw-mill operations which appear to be on a very limited scale and thereafter the work will stand ns a monument to this government's waste of public money.

I should be very sorry to shut off any discussion. I have made that proposition over and over again. I think the hon. gentleman leading the opposition will see the fairness of my suggestion because I do not think he can point out any reason why the item should not be proceeded with now. In my opinion time would be gained by disposing of it for the present with the understanding that if any question is asked or any discussion is desired at any future time the subject will again be brought up without any objection from myself or from the government.

Over and over again when we requested that any particular item should be allowed to stand it has been agreed to by the hon. minister at once. Why is this one forced through ? When it is a fact that we have no information in reference to the grave suspicion of the worst kind of jobbery connected with it, I submit that in the absence of that information we are justified in asking it to stand over. The hon. minister asks us to give the vote the approval of this committee by allowing it to go through and reserving the discussion until later, but, we say the time to discuss it is when we get the information we want

from the department and when the hon. members are present who are interested in it. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) are the parties who should be present. Surely the hon. minister will allow the item to stand.

X must protest as energetically as I can against that word ' jobbery.' I did not commit any jobbery when I was in office or elsewhere. I am not guilty of any jobbery. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has been on the Public Accounts Committee for six years. He has investigated the accounts to the best of his ability, which is large, and yet he has not found any jobbery that I have committed. I protest against that word; it is unfair. That work has been carried out in good faith. Whether I made a mistake or not is another question. X was not a party to any jobbery. We have built works elsewhere. In the Yukon we built roads where there was no population. We have been spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in building roads where there were no settlers. We have spent nearly $1,000,000 in building a telegraph line in view of future prospects. In Grande Vallee we have acted on the same principle. I thought in perfect good faith that it would develop that part of the country. The work was recommended to me by several members of xrarliament, especially by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) who, I am sorry not to see in his seat. The work was undertaken in good faith. There was no jobbery. I protest against that word. I hope it has not been applied to the department or to myself. If it has been I must protest against that with all the energy I possess.

I think the statement of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is a little premature. I think it is a little bit uncalled for. If the hon. gentleman had been in this House for the last hour and a half or two hours, during which, as by degrees, we got out the little information we could, and listened to the discussion, he would have known why it was characterized from this side of the House. We were told the circumstances which took place, of the rumours that were prevalent in regard to the transaction, the name of the original owner of the property and the purpose for which the wharf was to be built. In answer to the request I made twice or three times in succession as to who recommended this work,
I was told that there was no record in the department that anybody recommended it. When we asked for the engineer's estimate for the cost of the undertaking, we were told that there was none. I do not say that the ex-Minister of Public Works was in it. He may have been innocently led to do this work but I have not a single word to take back. I say it is surrounded by suspicion, Mr. SPROTJLE.
by more than a strong suspicion of jobbery, and it is the very strongest justification for demanding that this item shall be held over until we get the information from the department, or until we know something more about it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) may take back or not take back what he has said, but there is no jobbery in it, and before a member of parliament has the right to use the word ' jobbery ' he must be in a position to prove what he is saying.
Not at all.

I challenge my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) to prove that there has been any jobbery. The word ' jobbery ' is not parliamentary, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) who is an old hand, knows very well that before he is in a position to use such strong and uncalled for language, he should have some evidence to sustain him. Where is his evidence ? It is not forthcoming and it cannot be forthcoming. The only suspicion is that there is.a member of parliament who has timber limits in the neighbourhood, but perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) himself has some property near some wharfs that have been built by the government.
Not a cent nor never had.
Nor never will.
Nor never will in that kind of business.

There is no jobbery, and my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has no right to use that word. He may not take it back, but if he does not that will not strengthen his position. The work has been given in good faith ; the contract has been awarded and the matter was discussed last year. Let me add that one of the men interested in that work is dead and in his grave.
We cannot get at him.

No, but in view of that sad circumstance it would be a little fairer to let bygones be bygones. The work has been done and the country is bound to pay for it. The hon. gentlemen opposite have made their case last year and this year again. Last year they had some ground for opposition because it was the first time a vote was asked, but parliament has approved of it, and parliament is responsible and the government is responsible for the price of the work. Hon. gentlemen know right well that the contract cannot be cancelled. This whole thing is a tempest without any cause whatever at the present time.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) argues that last year there might

be some reason for a protest. He says that the contract having been let we can do nothing but pay the shot, but last year when the discussion came up the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) told us himself that the contract was let and that we should not discuss it then. He argued in that way last year because in the year previous they slipped in a small vote of $5,000 for a work which they must have known would cost twelve times that amount. The Hon. Mr. Tarte tells us now that we cannot repudiate this contract. Fancy this government talking about not repudiating contracts when they repudiated not only the contracts in the Post Office Department, but contracts in the Militia Department, entered into with the Messrs. Sanford for the supply of clothing, and they did that so hastily that they had to recall their action when they found that no one else could do the work in so satisfactory a manner. Twenty thousand dollars have been spent on this work up to the present time. It would be far better for the country that you should stop the contract ; pay the contractor for the work he has done and pay his estimated profit on the work that is to be done.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that after having spent $20,000 on a useful public work you should let the whole thing go.
And the material for the balance is on the ground.

It would be a waste of money to do that.
* Mr. FOWLER. It would be far less a waste of money to stop the whole thing than to go on spending more of the money of the people for the benefit of a single individual, or the benefit of a corporation who bought out that individual's rights. To hear these gentlemen opposite talk you would think this is a work for the general benefit of the country. Why, the argument which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) uses to defend this could be equally as well used to defend the worst kind of a job that could be perpetrated. There are 314 souls living at this place according to last census, and every adult of them is in the service of the hon. member for Stanstead or his company. It is not for their benefit you are building this ; it is for the benefit of the hon. member for .Stanstead and no other. In view of what has been said by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope), in view of the very strong rumour which I first stated to the House that prevails in Stanstead, and in the Eastern Townships ; in view of the serious reflection there is upon the character, upon the honour, upon the integrity of one member of this House that he has used his position-if it be true, and I do not say it is true, for I do.not know whether it is true or not-in view of all this it seems to
me that if the government had the interests of the hon. member (Mr. Lovell) at heart, they would want to have that hon. gentleman here to stand up upon the floor of parliament and explain to this House anjj to the country his whole connection into the matter. If they were true friends of the hon. member for Stanstead that is the course they would take. I say, Sir, even though the expression may be objectionable to the ex-minister ; I say that while it may not bo jobbery, yet it smells most strongly of jobbery. We find the government spending $00,000 in the interests of a supporter, and spending that money for no other purpose than the private purpose of that hon. member. We find first a vote of $5,000 ; next year a vote of $25,000, and this year a vote for $36,000. We find all this, and we have reason to protest against it. Last year we were told that a contract was let and certain work performed. Last year we were told that nobody owned this property and that the title of it was in the clouds, but this year there is a deed of the porperty although the department is entirely innocent as to whom that deed came from. Why are they so innocent about it ? Surely they knew that we would require information on that point this year, and yet they come here without information and attempt to rush this vote through by means of the brute force of their majority. That is all they have to rely upon. If this is an honest transaction ; if there is no jobbery in it ; if the skirts of the hon. member for Stanstead are absolutely clean, and the skirts of the government clean as well, because one involves the other ; then it would be far more seemly on the part of the Minister of Public Works to let this item stand until the member for Stanstead is here to defend himself from this serious charge. I trust that in the interests of parliament : I trust in the interests of public life in this country, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lovell) can properly defend himself and can clear himself from the very' strong suspicion which at the present time attaches to his name.

If the item were suspended, there would be twice as much noise about it as we hear to-night. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat would point to that fact as the best evidence that there was jobbery. The Minister of Public Works may do as he likes, but if I were in his place I would go on with the item, because there is nothing wrong with it. It is a fair expenditure of money. It may be a little large, I grant. On various occasions different governments have spent large sums of money on works which at their inception did not seem to Be very meritorious. In this case, if the name of a member of parliament had not been connected with the work, there would not have been ten words said about it in the House. But there is a member of parliament who has properties in that neighbourhood. Members of the

opposition are in their right in criticising the item. This is a political game. Criticism is a good thing ; I do not object to it at all ; but criticism does not make black what is white. In this case, I say it again, if ft member of the ministerial party had not properties in that neighbourhood, the item would have passed like a shot. But there is a member of parliament in that position. This is political warfare
This is a political wharf, too.

Well, I grant that politics has a lot to do in the world ; but politics has made at times a good deal worse work than this wharf will be. This work will be a useful one. It will develop a large lumber industry.
Hear, hear ; that is the whole thing.

Where is the objection to developing the lumber industry of this country, even by means of a wharf T We are developing all kinds of industries by means of improvements. If I were the Minister of Public Works, I wonld ask that the item go through.
The hon. gentleman knows as well as anybody that the development of the lumber industry belongs to the province of Quebec, and it gets the benefit.
The province of Quebec has not the right to build wharfs. That is a sacred right of this parliament.

I am delighted to see that the ex-Minister of Public Works does not hang his head in shame. I notice that the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has gone out; the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Reid) has escaped ; and the hon. member for Sitanstead (Mr. Lovell) is not in his place.
Restigouche is 500 miles from this place.

I beg pardon ; it is right opposite Gaspe. I know where the county is just as well as any member on the other side, and I want to tell them that the hon. member for Restigouche cannot be gotten to stand up in the House and defend this job. Bring him in and he will condemn it as well as every man in that part of the country. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) charged the Minister of Public Works last year with building wharfs along the shores of the St. Lawrence river so thickly that there was not room for them on the shore, and they had to hang them on the trees. This is one of those docks, I suppose. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that the great North-west, where settlers from the United States and from the old lands are now going in such large numbers, Hon. Mr. TARTE.
is entitled to legitimate and necessary expenditures, and the territorial legislature should be strengthened by grants of money for the development of that country, instead of throwing it away on the rocks around Gaspe. Perhaps the ex-Minister of Public Works can tell us from whom the deed of this property was obtained. We have been asking that all night.
I think the deed was given by Mr. Lovell himself.
Hear, hear.
Where is the crime in that ?
We have been trying all night to get that information.
I do not see why it was not given immediately. I would have given it immediately.
I wish you had come in sooner, then.
I was better engaged.

I think ' Hansard ' will show that I did say that if the property belonged to Mr. Lovell, the deed must have been got from him. I may say that previous to six o'clock the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) stated that he wished to be absent this evening. I said that, so far as I was concerned, I was willing that the general vote for the province should stand, so that all the Items might be discussed, and the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition was willing that this item should pass, as I had given all the information I had with regard to it. The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works is now here, and has confirmed everything I said. That being the case, if any hon. gentleman on the other side will ask for any information that has not been furnished, it will be given if it is in the department, and there will be an opportunity for further discussion under the arrangement that has been made. Then I ask that the item be allowed to pass.
Not by a long chalk. It might as well be understood that if this item passes to-night and is discussed generally, we cannot afterwards vote on it.

Is it not a most interesting feature of this debate to see a member of parliament like my hon. friend getting up and saying that Restigouche is just opposite Grande Vallee ? It is not even in the same province.
I did not say anything of the kind. Restigouche is in the province of New Brunswick, across the river.

I am very glad that my hon. friend has at last found that Restigouche is in New Brunswick. He should

have known it before. It is not on the same river at ail. There are about 500 miles between the two places. Here is a member of parliament, one of the leaders on the other side of the House, who criticises an estimate on the ground that Restigouche and Grande Vallee are a few steps apart, when there are about 500 miles between the two. We cannot take him seriously. He is good to make war in South Africa, but he is no good to criticise items of this kind ; he is not in it. When my hon. friend speaks of rocks, he again speaks of things lie does not know. Gasp6 is one of the most fertile districts of this country. There is not only lumber there, but fertile lands. We are glad in the province of Quebec to give as much money as is necessary to develop the west, but we insist on having our share of honest public expenditure. My hon. friend reminded the House last year that a member of parliament unwisely said that we had built so many wharfs in the province of Quebec that there is no room for navigation there. Well, a good deal less money has been spent building Wharfs in the province of Quebec than in Ontario. We have not said anything against this ; we do not kick, to use a vulgar expression. We are pleased with our lot, but it seems to me that when we are only asking ordinary favours, amongst which is this Grande Vallee wharf, we should not be treated as if we were a lot of thieves. We ai-e not going to get out of the country with that wharf. It will stay there and will be very useful for the development of an important industry-the lumber industry. Moreover, I repeat, the district of Gaspe is one of the most fertile districts of this country, and that wharf will not only be useful for lumber operations, but also for settlers. Everybody who knows anything of colonization in the province of Quebec knows that the settlers there must go into the forests. We build roads for them. On this occasion we are building a wharf, not only for lumbering operations, but for the settlers those lumbering operations will bring in there. The settlement of Lake St. John's district, in which there are to-day over 40,000 people, is due to colonization and lumber operations. The province of Quebec is not like our North-west. In the North-west a man has only to take a pair of oxen and go on with his work, but in the province of Quebec ve have first to cut down the timber, and the best friend of the settler is the lumber merchant, when he is carrying on his work in an honourable manner. Everybody who knows anything of the way in which the province of Quebec has been settled knows that. I do not see why we Should take up more time discussing this wharf, if the name of a member of parliament were not tnixed up with it, it would not be discussed. This w7ork will be useful from the standpoint of the settlers. My hon. friend should
not forget that there is not a railway there. He has railways in his county, but this section of country has none, and if we do not give the people there a wharf, wbat are they going to have ?

For the last twenty-five years, I have almost sworn by the hon. gentleman, but can have faith in him no longer. When an hon. gentleman stands up in this House and says it is 500 miles from Restigouche to Gaspe, he shows a lamentable ignorance of the geography of his own country.
I make the same statement too.

Nobody pays any attention to what the hon. gentleman says. Nobody would ever charge him with knowing anything even about his own province, but from the hon. gentleman who has just spoken we expected something better.
I move that a go d surveyor be appointed immediately to measure the distance.

In our county we have railways, but we have paid for them ourselves to the tune of $250,000, and we want the province of Quebec to tax themselves in the same way. The ex-Minister of Public Works, who has just skipped out of the Chamber, says that the government have built wagon roads there for the farmers. But that is supposed to be done by the province in the new districts, and we find that that is one of the large corruption funds which the Ontario government uses to corrupt electors. A11 the roads outside colonization roads have to be built by the municipalities themselves, and I object to our spending the hard cash of the people of Ontario in building roads through the bush in the province of Quebec, or in constructing docks for the benefit of private companies. I am surprised that the hon Minister of Finance would allow an item of this kind to go into the estimates and that the hon. Minister of Public Works would permit this kind of thing to go on.

I cannot see that there is anything to get very warm over in this item. Last year the government were asked what amount of trade was to be done at that port and what was the real object of building the wharf, and there was no one present to give the information. I would like to point out to the government that while we cannot expect the present Minister of Public Works, who has but lately assumed the position, to know all the details, but surely it is due to the House that when a public work is being built, especially in a constituency which returns a supporter of the government, the least we should expect is that the member for that constituency should be in his place to give that explanation to the House which the minister is not

prepared to give. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) absented himself from the House last year when this vote was up. He was in this House yesterday and must have known that the estimates of the province of Quebec were to be discussed this evening, and yet we find him still absent. In view of this fact., and in view of the rumours which went the rounds during the general elections, and which have been current since in connection with that lion, gentleman, surely lie ought to have deemed it his duty to remain here for the purpose of explaining what amount of trade is to be done in this place, and what is the object of building this work there. I see no reason why we should not be entitled to this information before passing this item.
What information ?

The information as to what trade the government expect will be done at this point. No explanation has been given us of that. There is no lion, gentleman in a position to give it except the hon. member for Stanstead, and he remains away. I can see no reason why this item should not stand until we get that information. Certain rumours have been circulated against that lion, gentleman, and in justice to himself and to his constituents, he ought to be here prepared to deny them. In view of the very vague information we have in connection with this item and the suspicions circumstances surrounding it, I think that it should be allowed to stand over. Why are we refused this information ?

What information ? I have stated over and over again that all the information which is in the department has been given. But lion, gentlemen are putting questions that cannot be answered. Information was given before the ex-Minister of Public Works entered the Chamber, and he has confirmed what was said. It is alleged that a corrupt bargain had been made between the ex-Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Stanstead
Nobody said that.
If I am mistaken I shall be glad to withdraw what I said. But I certainly understood hon. members to say that there was a corrupt bargain on behalf of the ex-Minister of Public Works.
No, no.
It was said fifty times.
I deny it emphatically It was not said fifty times; it was not said once.
* Hansard ' will show that it was not said.

I am in the judgment of lion, members when I say that the statement was made that there was jobbery or corruption, that there was an arrangement made for the hon. member for Stanstead to become a candidate on the understanding that this work would be gone on with.
That was said.
I denied that on behalf of the government.
You don't know anything about it.

So far as my knowledge went. And the ex-Minister of Public Works is here, and lie denied it emphatically. It is only fair that I should say to the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingrain) that I have offered, particularly in this instance, to give all the information asked for that is in the possession of the department.

I understand the hon. minister to say that, if this item is passed, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who is unavoidably absent, or any other member will be free to discuss this matter on an item to be reserved.
I stated so distinctly, and I think it is only fair that it should be carried out.

I was interrupted in my remarks by the Minister of Public Works, who desired to say that any information desired should be furnished to the committee, if it was in the department. But what we complained of last year, and what we complain of this year, is that the information is not in the department. The only one who can furnish it is the hon. member for Stanstead. No doubt he recommended the work; he was directly interested. There must have been some reason given in support of the application, but he has never communicated it to the House, nor has the government. The minister talks about the amount of trade to be done. Has he ever furnished us any information which would enable us to judge what that trade was likely to be ? Nobody charged the ex-Minister of Public Works with jobbery in this matter. What we said and what we say, is that it was commonly reported in that constituency that he had become a candidate on the understanding that this work was to be carried out.
Would not that be a corrupt job ?

We have stated that that rumour was in circulation. Let the hon. member come here and deny it; if lie does not. lie rests under the stigma of it. If such a charge were made against me I should I feel it my duty to myself and my constitu-

ents to remain in the House when the vote in relation to the matter was under discussion, so as to clear myself. The fact that the hon. gentleman is not here is prima facie evidence that there is something in the rumour. I do not desire to lecture hon. gentlemen opposite, but, when there are works going on in the constituencies, it is only fair to the House that they should give us the benefit of the information they have, which must be more detailed and intimate than the minister can give. We are entitled to all reasonable information; but it seems like pulling teeth, to use the common comparison, to get information we desire. And. if we criticise we are accused of mere carping. Of course, our criticism is regarded by hon. gentlemen opposite as much less lofty than that indulged in by them when they were on this side, when the McMullen's and others carried on the discussion. I am glad to say that the criticism of the opposition has been much fairer since 1890 than it was when hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side. Even with the much greater provocation that we have had, you never hear language used in this House such as they used. If the hon. minister wishes this item to pass, he should have a statement of the trade expected to be done, so that we may understand what is the object of spending this money.

I wish to say a word with reference to the ex-Minister of Public Works, because he worked himself into a good deal of excitement, and it almost seemed to me he was trying to draw a red herring across the trail. Is not Quebec, he asked, entitled to have public money spent within her borders ? No person objected to money being spent in Quebec wherever it was proper to do so. We are quite willing to see expenditures in Quebec, where sufficient information is given us to lead us to believe that the expenditure is in the public interest. But it is because the minister cannot or will not give us the information necessary that we ask the item to be held over. When the item was first read, the request was made, in a good-natured way that it should be allowed to stand in the absence of the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). On the other hand, the Minister of Public Works proposed that some other items should be allowed to stand. To-night, the minister seeks to stop us from discussion on the ground that we are committed to this expenditure. But we were told the same thing last year; and, if we allow the item to go without discussion, no doubt that fact will be quoted to prevent discussion at any time in the future. We asked who recommended this work, and the Minister of Public Works said that he did not know that anybody recommended it.
Oh, no, I did not say that.
The ex-minister stated that it was recommended by members of the House.

I stated that it was recommended by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), who is not now in his seat. If the Minister of Public Works will look in his department, he will find also that there was a pretty large petition from the settlers there. The work was strongly recommended.

Does that not fully justify the position we take ? The hon. minister told us there was nothing in the department. I asked specifically if there was any application from the people in the locality, and I was told that there was not. Surely, if there was urgent need for this work somebody must have applied for it. We asked that the item should be allowed to stand that the minister might look up the informati n. I asked if there was an engineer's estimate, and was told that there was not. Surely there must be such information in the department, but that information is not given to us. Are we doing an improper thing when we ask that the item stand till the information be given us ? I hold that we should be doing much less than our duty as an opposition if we allowed the item to pass until all reasonable information was given us. We urged that other items should be gone on with, so that those items might be passed to which there was little or no objection. But nothing will suit the hon. minister but that this very item which we do not want passed, shall be passed. We only ask reasonable information, that we may know whether we are justified in voting' this money or whether we should move that the item be struck out. We do not want to do that, because we believe the information is available, and if the Minister of Public Works was as agreeable as he usually is, he would allow that Item to stand.

Members of parliament have a right to ask for Information, and I would be the last to decline to recognize such a right. But what I objected to was the strong expression used by my hon. friend. He is a man of long experience and knows the value of words ; and when, on entering the House I heard the word ' jobbery well, I did not like it, it is not a pleasant word to hear concerning a work witii which one was connected. I am sure so far as I am concerned there was no jobbery and nothing improper.
If it is any satisfaction to the hon. gentleman, I may say that I had no reference to him when I spoke of jobbery.

I do not object to hon. members asking for information, but no information in the department would justify the use of that word by my hon. friend.

Now, if our lion, friends opposite insist that this item should not go through, it is for the minister to say what lie will do. So far as the department is concerned, there was the ordinary information. There was a petition, there was a survey made, there was an estimate made. My hon. friend who is now Minister of Public Works is still a little fresh. It is easy to understand that he cannot possibly know all the details of the office over which he presides. But I remember well the facts in the present case. There was a petition, there were the ordinary representations made in such cases. The information is available just as the wharf is available.

The information has at last been vouchsafed to us by the exMinister of Public Works. I do not mean to say that the present minister was withholding it deliberately, although he had his deputy at his elbow, and should have known something about the business.
If the eliief engineer bad been here the whole thing would have been explained.

So it transpires that a member of parliament sitting in this House is the gentleman who has handed over the deed of this property to the government of Canada. What was the consideration given for that ? If there was none, the deed is valueless. If there has been a money transaction, then that lion, member has violated the Independence of Parliament Act. We find that all the circumstances point to the fact that it was through the influence of this member of parliament and to benefit his own property so that he could sell it, that this expenditure has been made. And we have heard to-night from another Liberal who says that there was an enormous rake-off, and this wharf has been constructed and the people are taxed to pay for an expenditure that is not justified. So far as I am personally concerned, I do not intend that this thing should continue. These gentlemen may just as well be given to understand that the people of this country have rights, and members of parliament have rights, and we intend to exercise them, and that this jobbery should cease of building docks along the shores of the county represented by the Finance Minister or along the shores of the St. Lawrence where they are not needed. These things have got to be justified, or else they will not be allowed to pass.

R I) SON.	If there were any
doubt as to whether we were asking for useless information, that doubt has been dispelled by the information given by the ex-Minister of Public Works. We have been told over and over again by the Minister of Public Works that there was no information, or that the information asked for was not available in his department. We are now informed by the ex-minister that Hon. Mr. TARTE.
the information asked for is available and that it is in the department.
It was there when I left.

So we have not been asking for that which does not exist. I myself made use of that very objectionable word, and I think I used it advisedly ; I said that if this debate went to the public without the information which we asked for, it would have the appearance of the rankest jobbery. I did not say it was that, but it would certainly leave that impression. I hope the Minister of Public Works will not call upon the supporters of the government. to vote this tiling through without giving us the fullest explanation that is possible to be had.

The hon. gentleman has spoken for some time, and he lias not submitted one question saying what kind of information he would like to have. I have stated time and again that all the information with regard to this matter has been furnished to the fullest possible extent. I have also stated that last session when this matter was before the House the ex-Minister of Public Works gave all the information in his possession with regard to it.

I must take exception to this statement. In the first place the question was asked : Who is responsible ? I said the Minister of Public Works last session took the responsibility and the government took it with him. The ex-minister last session gave this information, and he was more familiar with it than I could be :
The improvement of the St. Lawrence is one thing and the erection of the wharf at Grande Vallfie is another thing. We are attending to the improvement of the St. Lawrence better than it has ever been done in the past. It is of no use to make so much fuss-for it is fuss that is being made now and nothing else. The hon. member for GaspS (Mr. Lemieux) is not in his seat at the moment. He is one of those who came to the government and represented to us that, if there was a wharf built there large lumbering interests would be fostered and developed.
That answers both questions. Large lumbering interests would be established at that place and for that reason parliament authorized that work.

Mr. SrROULE. Why does the hon. minister say it is not in the sessional papers ?

Every one is liable to be mistaken. I spoke from the information of the official of the department. It is the usual custom to have petitions in these cases, but he was speaking then with the information fresh in his mind.
If I remember right I received a deputation or two.

There is no record kept of deputations as a rule.
1-Ion. Air. TARTE. No.

If there was any information asked for that was held back or was not brought down I would be only too glad that the item should stand. I perhaps would have granted the request of my hon. friend even then had it not been for the arrangement which has been made with gentlemen who wish to discuss the subject. That was the only reason why I desired that we should pass the item. If there was any information in the possession of the department that I could bring down, I would be only too glad to do so. The lion. ex-Minister of Public Works continued :
We considered the case and came to the conclusion that it was a meritorious work. Now it is not fair and it is not good policy to say that improvements must always be made at places where there is a large population. If by the erection of this work you help population to settle there that will be a good thing.
And so on. This information was all given when the hon. gentleman was in office and that large amount was given committing parliament to this contract. I think after this full discussion and in view of the arrangement that the subject may be brought up again this item might be passed for the present. I am placed in a position in which I could not adopt the suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite unless some lion, gentlemen can say that there is some information wanted which has not been brought down.

The hon. Minister of Public Works has put his argument fairly, if he will abide by it. I have refrained, and that is very hard work for me, during the last two or three hours while this has been going on from taking part in it but it has occurred to me several times that we might arrive at an understanding of this animated discussion. The hon. minister says if there is any information that any hon. member of the committee desires it will be brought down and that for that pnrpose the item will be allowed to stand. I submit it is quite evident that there is in the department certain information most valuable to this committee, information that
will probably help the elucidation of the matters in dispute and which should be brought down. For instance, we have the assertion definitely that there was an estimate by the engineer. It was thought at one time that there were two. There was at least one estimate made by the engineer. We have a right to have that document brought down.
I did not understand what the hon. gentleman said.
I understand that the engineer made an estimate of this work.
That has been given.

That estimate has not been brought down to the House.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS It has; that information! has been given to the committee.

I do not argue with the hon. mininster as to what has been given in the past. I understand that when I stand on the floor of this House I am entitled to all the information which is given to the House. As the hon. gentleman has suggested that hon. members should ask for the information they require, I respectfully ask, without reference to whether it has been or has not been given in time past, that it shall be given now.
I hope the hon. gentleman will not think I am interrupting him when I say that I have given that information on several occasions.

The hon. minister misunderstands me. The estimate of the engineer, I understand, to be in writing. It is a document in the department. The examination of that document is important and that document should be brought down to the committee so as to enable the committee to inspect it and form an opinion upon it. Then, we have heard from the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that there was a recommendation. That recommendation may or may not be in writing. If that recommendation is in writing it should be brought down to this committee. It is a subject of information to which we are entitled.
What recommendation does the hon. gentleman refer to ?
The recommendation for the prosection of the work-the recommendation by some important supporters of the government. These things all have to have their inception.
1 have said that there is no such writing in the department.
Tlie lion. ex-Minister of Public Works seems to think there is.
What ?
The recommendation of the hon. member for Gasp6 and several others.
They called upon him, he says.

I am not going to debate that because I may not be right on that point. There is an estimate; that point is clear. That is one source of information that t as a member, do ask for. 1 want the recommendation done in writing if a recommendation exists. If it does not exist that point goes by. The next point I come to and about which I ask the hon. minister to furnish us information is the petition. It is acknowledged, I suppose, that there was a petition sent by a number of persons as stated by the lion. ex-Minister of Public Works.

There was a deputation or a written petition-I do not remember exactly which. I remember very well that the bon. member for Gaspe came on several occasions and with several people to ask for that work. That I remember very distinctly indeed because it was in his own division, but members of parliament do not always write. They come up often and' see the ministers.
The lion. exMinister of Public Works said that there was a petition signed by the people.

There may have been. I know I received a petition or two. As to the engineer's report the policy of the department is that before any work is offered for tender there is an estimate made. There is a survey of course because we cannot prepare plans without having a survey made and it was made in this case as in all other cases. In the ordinary way plans and specifications were prepared.

I was speaking of the petition. The bon. ex-Minister of Public Works seemed to be perfectly clear when be first spoke upon this subject that there was a petition. He repeated that more than once. I noticed also that just a little while ago the hon. Minister of Public Works intimated to the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works that he might be wrong about that and I know that the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works intimated that he still thought he! was right. I am not going to argue that he is right, but to put our position in the weakest possible way we may-say that it is a subject of doubt.' It leaves the probability that there is a petition on file in the department. While the bare possibility remains that there is a document on file in the department it is unfair to this Committee to ask us to pass this item until Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
the hon. minister has ascertained definitely' and conclusively that no such document exists in the department.
Suppose there is none ?

Then it is for the minister
to candidly- say to the committee that there is none.
If there is one he will bring it down.
I do not understand that the minister has stated that he has actually made a search to see if there was a petition.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that I did not inquire if there was a petition ?
I do not know as to that.
I did inquire and there are no papers further than I have explained.
Do I understand the minister to say that since this question has come up a search has been made ?
Yes, you can understand that.
I understand that since this has come up a search has been made in the department. Is that right ?
That is right.

Then I put the responsibility on the minister that it will turn out that he is mistaken in this matter. There is no question, however, that there is a deed, and it is said that deed was given to the government for nothing. It is very important for us to know whether that was a voluntary deed or a deed for a consideration. I submit that the facts show that whether there is an expressed consideration in that deed or not, there was actually a consideration for that deed and a valuable consideration necessarily passing from the government to this Mr. Lovell. It was allimportant to this Mr. Lovell the member for Stanstead, that that work should be executed in consideration of the execution of that deed, and not otherwise. For no other cause moving him to it he gave this deed to the government. It is a consideration passing from the government to a member of this House, and therefore this deed should be submitted to this committee for consideration. We shoidd have such documents as now remain into the custody of the department, we should have a clear expdanation of the absence of this petition in case it is absent, and we should have the plans prepared by the engineer and then we will be in a position to intelligently consider this estimate. Summing it up, I ask the Minister of Public Works does he

not now see-I don't tliinlc he will because he has been pretty candid and courteous to us so far-does he now not see that there are requests for information which ought to be supplied before this item goes through? What difference can it make whether it goes through now and is discussed hereafter, or is allowed to stand over until we get the information ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. I have explained to the hon. gentleman frankly, and I think the ex-minister endorsed it, that no estimate of the work had been made previous to the vote of 1901-2; that afterwards an estimate was made. The hon. gentleman has asked me several questions, and I ask him now, whether the written estimate would be of any value after the contract was made ? The contract was entered into in 1901; that shows the cost of the work, and any estimate made previous to that would be of no value whatever.
It would show a change in opinion as to how this work should be done.
There is no change. The contract was entered into and that was the cost of the work.

It is important that we should have the engineer's estimate because by it we could form an opinion as to whether or not it would be better to continue this work ; whether it would be better to abandon this work, let the money we have expended go, and pay fair damages in equity; rather to further waste public money in this matter.

As I understand, this contract was entered into in 1901 for $53,900, and up to date $20,000 has been expended by the government. How is it that before the $53,000 is expended and paid by the government, the minister comes forward and asks for another vote that will make a total of $61,000 ?

There is a revote of $5,000. The total cost is $59,500. The work is under contract. I am informed that the material is on the ground, that the work is being proceeded with and as soon as the money is voted the progress estimates will be ready. There would still be a balance to be provided of $3,500. The engineer has estimated the cost of superintendence at $5,600, and, as I have explained, it would require $3,500 more to pay for the full cost of this work.

I do not object to the cost of the dock; I never object to the cost of any government work which may be necessary. The point in this case is that a member of this parliament is engaged in a deal with this government. He disposed
to the government of a site for a dock. He has a timber limit adjoining. The government then turns round and builds a wharf to increase the value of his property at a place where there are no settlers except a few meii who are working in his one-horse mill. That to my mind is the serious part of the whole business, and I think the minister should meet the wishes of the committee and let this item stand over until the whole matter is explained., Nothing will be injured by doing so. We want the hon. member from Stanstead to be here and give us a statement of the facts of the case. Is the country going to pay for a private dock for every friend of the government who happens to have a timber limit ? Is that the line on which hon. gentlemen opposite are going to carry on the affairs of the country ? I think the ex-Minister of Public Works is responsible for this, and it is hardly consistent with his usual high standard of morality.
I am responsible for worse things than that. It is a first-class thing.
Will the minister tell us what consideration was paid for that deed ? Is it in the department ? Was it submitted to the Minister of Justice ?

I may say, first, that I would be only too glad if I had any reasonable excuse to grant the hon. gentleman's request; but, after the explanations that have been made, I cannot see that there is any ground why this contract should not be carried out. With regard to the deed, the ex-minister says it was got from Mr. Lovell, or rather from his company, or his son, without consideration. How much interest the present member may have in the company I do not know. I am not in a position to deny all the statements and rumours that have been made here; they have to go for what they are worth; but every possible information that it is in my power to give has been given.
May I ask the hon. Minister of Justice, would this deed be of any value without a consideration ?

I do not know anything about the deed. I have no present recollection of it; but I know the facts, and as we have been talking of this thing for a couple of hours, it might be interesting to get the facts. If my information is correct, the wharf is built on the shore on a site which is vested in the Crown. That which it was important to get from the lumber company was the right of access to the wharf, and I understand the intention was to convey that right of access to the Crown. Whether that was given or not I cannot say, but it was never contended that the site upon which the wharf is situated was ever vested in any one but the Crown.
Do 1 understand the Minister of Justice to mean that the site belonged to the province of Quebec ?

I am not quite prepared to say that. That is a very big question, which has been discussed many times in the courts-whether riparian rights of this kind are vested in the province or in the Dominion. There is a great deal of difference between the right of property vested in the province and the right of user vested in the Dominion.
Is this at the mouth of a river or estuary ?
It is not at the mouth of any river, but is on the shore of the St. Lawrence. I understand that it is on a point jutting out into the St. Lawrence river. I have never seen the wharf itself.

In the face of all that information, which we have got now after two hours' trying, is it unreasonable that we should ask that if there was a deed it should be produced, as well as the plan and the engineer's estimate on which the item passed the council The ex-minister says there was such an estimate.

There is an estimate of that kind before every work is offered for tender. There is no objection, of course, to bringing down the plans, but it has never been done on such an occasion since I have been in the House.
We have had plans of public works laid on the Table over and over again.

Not after the contract lias been given. Had my hon. friend asked for the plan before the work was awarded his request would have been reasonable. Of course there is no objection of bringing down the plan, but the plans are usually produced when the money is first asked and not after the contracts are given out.
I could state cases of my own knowledge to the contrary, where the plans were brought down after the contracts were let.
There is no objection to that.

Is it unreasonable that we should ask that to-night ? Not one of the requests we have made has been granted, and we ask that the item should stand until a search is made into the department and the information brought down which we require.
Is it fair, after three hours' discussion, to ask for the plans ? I have given a description of the work. In my twenty-three years' experience, after a contract has been let, I

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: have never heard of a request to bring down the plan. I have answered every question ; I have given all the information in the possession of the department.
That is another thing.
We are not superhuman, and cannot give information we do not possess.
You did not tell us who gave you the deed.

Just as soon as the question was put I sent to find out. In the meantime, my hon. friend the ex-Minister of rublic Works told the committee, and I verified his'statement. Tlie property was vested in the Crown, and nobody else could give the deed.
Why did you get a deed ?

I have already explained that while the property belonged to the Crown, there was a doubtful question of right of way, and a deed was got from the owner of the property over which the right of way ran.

When the hon. gentleman was asked for the information, lie refused to give it, and we did not get it until the Minister of Justice came in. What I object to is that we should make this enormous expenditure for the benefit of a private corporation and not of the community generally. To my mind, it has all the indications of a job. The ex-Minister of Public Works objects to my calling it a job, but that certainly is to my mind the most apt description I can give to it. Just fancy spending $60,000 where there is not a post office, where nobody resides except the men working in a saw-mill, and all for the benefit of a member of parliament who was the owner of the timber limits, and who sold them to a corporation at a big profit, which he could not have done unless the government had come to his rescue and built that wharf. I would ask the hon. Minister of Public Works' whether he does not think that we have good reason for our belief that there is a nigger in the fence ? If this deed is not for the property on which the wharf was built, why were we not told that last session ? Now we are told that the deed is only for the right of way to the wharf, and that it was given by a member of this House, but I am satisfied that he would not have given a deed for the right of way if the government had not undertaken to spend $60,000 for his benefit in the erection of this wharf. The building of this wharf made his property more valuable and enabled him to sell it for a much larger amount than he could otherwise have got.

There is no other information that I know of, directly or indirectly, in the possession
