of tlie department that can be given with regard to this matter, and it seems to me very unreasonable, after we have discussed it here during three hours, to ask that the item should again stand over.

I would like to make a proposition to the Minister of Public Works. We are old enough and civilized enough, surely, to understand what we are doing. Here we have been three hours and a half talking about the same thing over and over and nothing done. We should be more reasonable. If one party says :	We will
not give up, and the other party says the same, the result will be we must all stay here till I don't know when. Somebody has got to give up. Now, is it unreasonable to ask the Minister of Public Works simply to jump over this item, and then vote as many others as he pleases. We can vote all the other items for Quebec to-night, and we can take this one up some time next week.
I have already granted that request a dozen times-that the item should be discussed at some future time.
Well, let it stand then. Will the hon. minister agree to that ?
I will carry out the understanding I reached.
Well, now, we are all as contrary as we can be.
I am sorry if my hon. friend (Mr. Morin) is in that humour. I am trying to meet hon. gentlemen opposite and I think they should try to meet me in the same spirit.

In the list left by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) are several items marked to be reserved, and this is the very first one. It seems manifest that that hon. gentleman understood that the items would not go through. But if the hon. Minister of Public Works is determined that it shall go through I am afraid that we shall see the early hours of the morning before it does.
All right.
Go on with your threats.
What would be the use of that to anybody ?

Last year, the Minister of Public Works of that time (Hon. Mr. Tarte) vouchsafed this information in the House, speaking of the hon. member for Gaspfi (Mr. Lemieux) :
He is one of those who came to the government and represented to us that, if there was a wharf built there, large lumbering interests would be fostered and developed. We considered the case and came to the conclusion that it was a meritorious work.
The hon. Minister of Public Works says that he has not this information in his department. I would ask any business man in this House if it is reasonable to suppose that the government entered upon this work without first getting any information about it. Last year we asked for the facts, and we could not get them, nor are we getting them now. We are told in a general way that this expenditure will have the effect of encouraging the lumber industry. Is it anything but reasonable that we should ask that this item be allowed to stand until the hon. member for Stanstead is in his place, he having been associated witli the lumber interest to be developed ? He could give us information which would enable us to judge whether the government is justified in making this expenditure to encourage the lumber industry at that point. If, when the information is given us we conclude that this is not a justifiable expenditure of public money,, we can vote against the item. But why, in the name of decency, should we be pressed to swallow this vote without having the means of judging whether it is a good one or not ? If that is the stand that the hon. Minister of Public Works takes with regard to such items, I, for one, lose my respect for him, though I have hitherto entertained the highest regard for the hon gentleman's fairness. I have discussed this question seriously, and, I think, in a proper way. I have said nothing that I feel like taking back, nothing that an opposition member is not quite entitled to say in view of the circumstances surrounding the item. I have not charged any jobbery or bribery, but I ha*Ve contended, and I think justifiably, that this expenditure was entered upon in an unbusiness like way, seeing that due information was not furnished when it was first proposed. I have protested a hundred times in this House against this way of deciding upon the expenditures of public money. If hon. gentlemen wish public works carried on in their constituencies, the least they can do is to furnish the minister with information which he can lay before the committee and make every vote a business proposition, giving the reasons why, in his opinion, the money should be voted. We point out the serious nature of this expenditure, and it is a serious matter. No man would pretend to say that, at a place where there are only 314 souls, and where there is not even a post office, we are justified in spending .$00,000 without any sufficient reason given. This is business, pure and simple ; and the opposition's part of that business is to investigate ; and, if any rumour justifies us in being suspicious of the matter, it is our duty to ask for an explanation why it is placed in the estimates. Because we ask for that information, is that any reason we should be compelled to stay until daylight? I think we are perfectly justified in asking that this item be allowed to stand until the

lion, member for Stanstead is here to give us the facts we desire to know.

The ex-Minister of Public Works, I think, is about the only-gentleman on that side of the House who knows anything about the locality of this public work. He has passed there on his pleasure yacht on the down trip. Would he tell us what is the nature of the shore there ? It struck me when I saw it, as rather bold and rocky
It is a bluff.

The ex-minister spoke of good soil. My information is that it is a place absolutely unsuited for farming ; that you could not get grain in with a peg awl, and if you did, it would not grow. What settlement is there in rear of this place, or what settlement can be expected ?

The appearance of the place is very picturesque. The leaves, the green trees are charming. The province of Quebec has some rocks, and it has some beautiful plains also. In that locality there are rocks, trees, rivers and scenery which, no doubt, would captivate the poetic mind of my hon. friend. If I were allowed to offer any advice to-night, as the hour is pretty far advanced, I would say that we had better go to bed and discuss this item later on, after we get further information, if there is any. I do not say that there is no more information to be obtained. The site has been given free. My hon. friend complains that it was given free.
Mr. BENNE'JpT. Was there any consideration in the deed ?
Well, the consideration was the public service.

Before we go home, I -would like to recall the attention of the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to an observation he made a few moments ago. I have no knowledge of this particular matter, but I have knowledge of another matter to which the hon. gentleman alluded, and to which I want to call his attention, so that, if he was serious, he may have an opportunity of explaining himself. He said he proposed to stop the jobbery in connection with public works along the shores of the county represented by the Minister of E'inance. I want to know if my hon. friend has any reason to suppose that there is any jobbery in connection with public works along the shores of my county, and if so, I should be exceedingly pleased to have him put his statement in a somewhat more definite form. If he was serious I would be glad to have him enlarge upon it; if he was not serious I will give him an opportunity to withdraw.

I did not use the word ' jobbery ' in relation to the Mr. INGRAM.
Minister in connection with public works along the shores of his county; but I have no hesitation in telling the Minister of Finance here that I consider it is a very extraordinary thing indeed that the Finance Minister of this country should come down and ask for the expenditures that he does annually along the little coves and bays of the shores of his county, where there is no revenue derived from them whatever. I tell the Minister of Finance further that if there is no jobbery in connection with it-I am not here to prove it or to make a charge-but if there is no jobbery in connection with it, it is about the only part of the Dominion of Canada where I have ever seen any public work carried out since he has been on the treasury benches where there has not been more or less of jobbery. In connection with the Public Works Department and other departments of this country, rumour is very current of transactions such as the one I asked the minister about to-night specifically, concerning hemlock and spruce. When the specifications called for spruce, hemlock is put in, in works not a thousand miles from the city of Montreal and from Sorel. I have nothing to retract of what I said.

The question is whether or uot the hon. gentleman said there was jobbery in the public works of the county I represent. That is the question. If the ' Hansard ' does not say that the hon. member used the word ' jobbery, ' then I am wrong and will apologise to him. If the ' Hansard ' does say that the hon. gentleman said there was jobbery, then I ask him to come forward with some evidence, or to acknowledge that he has made a mistake.

1 would ask the hon. member for Victoria to make the same explanation of his charges of jobbery in the neighbourhood of Montreal. He has insinuated that when I was in office I had made changes that were tantamount to jobbery. Well, I invite an investigation on those points. The hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about.
I did not state that the minister was a party to it.

If there was anything wrong, I am responsible for it. If there was jobbery, I am certainly guilty of it, and am responsible. But there was no jobbery, and my hon. friend is just as far wrong as his neighbour was who used the word ' jobbery.' When a member of parliament gets up and charges jobbery, he must be prepared to prove it, otherwise he has no right to use the word. It is no use to take military airs and speak of jobbery. If my hon. friend wants to have an investigation before the Public Accounts Committee of the changes that have been made at Montreal, I will be ready to meet

him. He may call all the officials that are available, and let us have an investigation.

I think it has been clearly established before the country to-night that a member of parliament supporting the Finance Minister in this House, has given a deed of a property to the government after the government had expended $00,000 on a dock in order that he might enhance the value of some other of his property. I think no further proof is required that there has been jobbery in connection with this transaction. I have nothing to retract, and the people of this country, lam satisfied, will open their eyes to the situation. It is, all very well for these gentlemen to get up with their bluffs, they are talking to the wrong individual. We have it admitted that a member of parliament has given a deed. What consideration did he give for the deed ? It was given, I presume, in the form of a wharf. Another lion, member, a Liberal member that I see over yonder, stated that he had sold the property for over $100,000 which cost very little.
Did I state any sum at all ?
The sum of $100,000 was mentioned.
No.
The sum of upwards of $100,000 was mentioned tonight by some hon. member. Will the hon. gentleman tell us what the sum was ?
I do not know what the sum was.

In view of the stand taken by the Minister of Public Works, I am obliged to move that this item be struck out. I regret that I have to take this step, but I am compelled to do so in view of the fact that all the information is absolutely refused, and we have no other alternative. If the hon. gentleman says we are not entitled to know what amount of business is done at this point, or what, amount of business was estimated to be done, if he declines to furnish us with that information or to let the item stand until we can get that information, then there is no other alternative but to move that the item be struck out.

I acknowledge that the committee are entitled to all the information available. I am responsible as the minister of the department, and on my responsibility I have stated over and over again that I have given all the information available. The hon. member will acknowledge on reflection that he has made an unreasonable request, and one outside of my power to grant. By passing this vote we do not deprive him of another opportunity of getting any information that 50
may be had in that direction. If I had understood that there was a desire that the item should stand we would not have objected. But, after the understanding I had with that hon. member and the liberal proposition I made, I thought it was dealing very unfairly with the committee, not to say anything of myself, to press this. I have no objection at all to the vote being taken.

We have the estimates marked by one of the members of the opposition who takes a special interest in matters relating to the province of Quebec. He requests certain items to be allowed to stand. Amongst these is the Grande VallSe item which he requested to stand. Last year when this item was up the hon. gentleman who was interested in getting this item in the estimates was absent. That hon. gentleman was present yesterday and he knew these estimates were to be taken up.
Nobody expected these estimates would be up to-night. I did not expect it at all this afternoon.

In view of the arrangement entered into at three o'clock that after the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) addressed the House, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) was to move the adjournment of the debate, an arrangement which I know was entered into, what then had the House to do for the balance of the evening if it could not take up the Public Works estimates ? The hon. gentleman knew that and yet he absents himself from this House. The hon. minister says that he has no power to force the hon. gentleman to make a speech or to give an explanation. If that is the character of that hon. gentleman, the sooner the House knows it the better, and if the hon. gentleman refuses to get up and state the information which he has in his possession, or repudiate the rumours which have been circulated against him, the House will not have a very high regard for his standing. Let the item stand over until he is in (iis place and if he then refuses to give tlie information, we will not hold the hon. minister responsible for the information we are asking for. I do not see any justification for the hon. minister's course at all, and I believe that he is simply trying to bluff this item through the House.
I do not think the hon. member has any ground for that statement.

I cannot see any other reason. I am obliged to be frank with the hon. minister. If the hon. gentleman could say that we were asking anything unreasonable in respect to this item, I might be willing to change my mind on that point. The hon. gentleman says that ho has no information in the department. I am not ftnd-



ing fault with the hon. gentleman as to that, hut I am finding fault with his attempt to bulldose the item through the committee and not give us an opportunity of hearing the explanation of the hon. gentleman who got this vote put into the estimates.
1 am leaving an opportunity.
You are not leaving ail opportunity.
We on this side are willing to stay.
I do not require any suggestions from the hon. gentleman (Sir. Talbot). I have had as much parliamentary experience as he has.
With a good deal more talk.

And with better effect. I think, than the talk of the hon. gentleman. I wish to say in respect to this item that there is no opportunity of discussing the matter again except on concurrence, and every one knows that during concurrence is no time to debate an item.
I quite agree that if there is any desire to vote, now is the time.
The hon. gentleman knows that on the last day when concurrence is run through there is no opportunity to deviate an item. Then, why not let the item stand over ?
Why not vote now ?
I will take advantage at a later period of doing something in this matter that will take up more time of the House.

The hon. minister made a statement that I do not think he was justified in making. He said that if objection had been taken to this item before the discussion took place, he would not have pressed it. The very moment it was read from the Chair objection was taken and the request was made that in the absence of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Sir. Slonk) it should be allowed to stand. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier gave us a copy of the estimates with a number of the items marked for the specific purpose of allowing these items to stand during his absence. The hon. minister repeats that he has given all the information until the lion. ex-Minister of Public Works comes in and gives us information that wo had not received before and which he believes is in tiie department. The bon. minister tells us that this information is not in the department. We remember that last year when this House remained in session for four hours discussing an item the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) declared again and again that there was no information in regard to Mr. INGRAM.
it, and yet, next day, he brought down all the papers and laid them on the Table. Are we not justified in believing from the information we have about the deed, about the estimates and about the plans and specifications that there are papers in the department which we should see. We are denied the right to see these papers. My hon. friend makes the request that the item should be allowed to stand. The hon. minister says that be was prepared to grant that long ago. But, that is not what he is prepared to grant. He is prepared to force the item through and then he says: I will reserve one item upon which you can have the discussion. That is not what we want. There are many of these items to which we do not object, but to this one item we do object and we want more information before we allow it to pass. Our position is not unreasonable. We have dealt very reasonably with the lion. Minister of Public Works, and I regret to see the obstinacy that he displays now because be has usually been very fair and agreeable. We have been disposed to allow many items to pass that otherwise we would not have allowed to pass so easily but for the fact that we thought he was ready to give us all the information he could. I do not think this should be forced through. I think it is very improper and very unfair and it is not paving the way towards that good feeling that has existed heretofore between the opposition and members of the government.

I have explained so often that I need scarcely repeat that if I had any further information on the matter I would be glad to bring it down and that if lion, gentlemen allow this item to pass we will reserve the right to discuss it at any future time.

There is no doubt in the world that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) deliberately marked certain items that he wished to be held over. If he had only wished the privilege that the hon. Minister of Public Works refers to of reserving one item he would have indicated that but the hon. gentleman deliberately marked a number of items and the distinct understanding was that these items were to be held over, not that they were to be passed and the discussion had upon one item, but that the whole of those items were to be held over and we charge the hon. Minister of Public Works with breaking faith here to-night. This is the first time we have had to do it. He has always kept good faith with this House, but for some unaccountable reason, whether it is the absence of the hon. member who is so seriously involved in this matter I do not know-but undoubtedly for some unaccountable reason he insists on pushing through this item and violating the agreement entered into with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.

I suggested one or two Lours ago that this item should stand. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier was very desirous that he should be present on the occasion of the discussion of this matter, and I think it is a highhanded act on the part of the government that they should carry this item through without having the hon. gentleman here. We are told that the government business must be carried on. We have been here a month without doing any business of Importance. We are now settling down to business and at a very important time when we think that matters affecting the people should be discussed we are simply bluffed and sat upon and told that we are of no importance, and that we, representing the opposition, have no rights in tliis House. Some remarks have been made about jobbery. The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works repudiated the idea that there was any jobbery. The greatest jobbery that was ever perpetrated in Canada was perpetrated in Prince Edward Island in 1900, when the government, without having any appropriation, or having a dollar of money voted by this parliament, expended money at Skinner's Pond for the purpose of gaining votes for their candidate against your humble servant. I charge him now, and I charge the government of Canada witii that. There was not one dollar voted for this expenditure, and yet one month before the election they took money that should go for another purpose, in order to try and corrupt the electors of West Prince. The ex-minister cannot deny it. I have the proof. They talk about cancelling contracts, but they cancelled the contract for a most useful public work at Summerside and there is not one dollar in the estimates to-day to show that they intend to continue that work. A very unkind remark was made imputing ignorance to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes). The hon. gentleman was told that he was quite ignorant about the geography of this locality, whereas the fact is that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) was right and the man who corrected him was wrong.
I have measured (lie distance sxioken of to Restigouche, and it is a little over fifty miles across country. I have been over the whole region, and 1 knew what 1 was talking about.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) was quite right, and the hon. member who contradicted him was wrong. Now, with regard to this work. The government proposes to spend $60,000 on a pier in land where there is no water at all, and while they expend this large amount of money on building a pier where there is no water we have plenty of water around the shores of Prince Edward Island where there is need of a number of piers, and the whole province only gets a vote of $34,000. This place has a population of 314 people and 504
Prince Edward Island has a population of 105,000, and it is contrary to justice and equity that you should spend $61,000 at this little place and only $34,000 for all Prince Edward Island. We are prepared to keep up this discussion until the sun rises tomorrow morning and the best thing the minister eonld do is to hold over this item until the hon. member for Jacques Cartier is present.
Ttem voted: Yeas, 36; nays, 19.
It is time that we should adjourn now.
There are a few items here which perhaps we might pass to-night, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) would consent.
The minister will not get his items through by pursuing these tactics. I have seen staying exhibitions here which were good for one day, and the next day, too.

I hope that my hon. friend will not get angry. I suggested that some unimportant items should be taken up, but I said that if the gentleman who leads the opposition did not wish to do so, then I would not proceed.
I expressed the desire, as plain as the English language could express it, that the committee should now rise.

I should like to add that, judging from the treatment we have received to-night, the Minister of Public Works cannot expect to get many more items through. I wish to say further that the hon. minister and his department have been treated with the greatest courtesy by the members of this House, and I am sorry that he has treated us in the manner he has done to-night.

speechtext:
I consider, Mr. Speaker, the motion which my right lion, friend the Prime Minister has proposed to be an eminently proper one, under the circumstances, and I give it m.v most heartfelt support. In the death of the Hon. Sir Oliver Mowat, a great figure has passed off the stage, a man who linked the present generation with the generation of great men of the past, to whom my right lion, friend has referred. Sir Oliver Mowat truly had a great public career. Great not only in the sense of the unusual success which attended his efforts as a public man, but in this sense also that he has left behind him an honourable name, absolutely unstained. He leaves behind him a name which commands the respect, the esteem and the affection of all his fellow countrymen, regardless of political opinions.

I therefore second the motion which the right hon. gentleman has proposed, and do not think it necessary to speak at greater length, as he has said all, and more than all, that I could say on this occasion.

subtopic: THE DEATH OF SIR OLIVER MOW AT.
speechtext: If I might he permitted, Sir. Speaker, to add my humble testimony to the eloquent tributes which have just been pronounced upon the passing of Ontario's Grand Old Man, I would say that in Sir Oliver Blowat's death Toronto has lost its foremost citizen, Ontario has lost its most highly honoured and cherished son, and the Dominion a patriot whose fidelity to the interests of Canada and of the empire has never faltered. As one of the representatives in this House of the city of which, for more than threescore years, Sir Oliver Mowat had been a resident, I am happy to know and to feel that on this occasion I speak for all parties and creeds and classes in Toronto, when I say that from the moment Sir Oliver Mowat first entered the arena of public life, as a member of the city council, until at the close of a long and useful and honourable career, full of years and of honours, he was called to enter into his eternal rest, he enjoyed the respect and esteem of his fellow citizens. The record of Sir Oliver Blowat's life work will be an incentive and an inspiration to the rising generation, and to future generations of Canadians as well, to strive to emulate his example and to devote themselves to the promotion of their country's interests and welfare. It only remains for me to join most sincerely in the eulogies which have been passed upon the deceased statesman; and on my own behalf as well as for my colleagues, to respectfully tender an expression of our deep sympathy to the bereaved family, whose grief is shared by Canadians from end to end of the Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I submit that the evidence proves conclusively that there is a combine in restraint of trade and for the purpose of increasing prices, bringing it within the limits of the Tariff Act. And, as a representative of the country affected, I ask for action under that Tariff Act; and I ask for action immediately. The ease is that the price of finished lumber-dressed lumber, for flooring, ceiling and siding-has been increased by $9 per thousand feet in the part of "the country I represent with'a the past fourteen months. There may have been some reason for a moderate increase in price, but there is no change in conditions in British Columbia within the last fourteen months that would warrant an increase to the amount of $9 per thousand on this class of lumber. I think it is desirable to call the attention of the House to the facts at this time, when there are thousands and tens of thousands of people entering the territories and settling on the plains. As these people cannot secure the slightest shelter for themselves their families or their stock without buying the necessary lumber, an increase of the cost of lumber to the amount of $9 a thousand feet is such a serious matter as to constitute one of the most effective checks to the tide of immigration that could be given. This is a question in dealing with which we cannot afford to lose time. The people are there. They need the lumber. They need it now. And this precious Western Retail Lumbermen's Association Is holding them up to the extent I have mentioned for this class of lumber. I may point out, for the benefit of the House, that while these gentlemen have a very strong grasp of their business
affairs,' they are not altogether destitute of a sense of humour. They have published, not for general circulation, but for private perusal, a list of members of their association. Now, this lumbermen's association is, in fact, an organization of the mill men, who hold the retail dealers under their thumb, as you have seen by this correspondence. But In this peculiar list that they have published, the mill men figure as ' honorary members ' and the retail men as ' active members.' .So, it would appear as though the dealer, who is at the mercy of the mill man is the active force in carrying out this iniquitous combine. The retailer, of course, comes in direct contact with the unfortunate eousumer, but he is the victim of circumstances as the consumer is ; and it is the mill man, the honourary member, who is really in command, as this correspondence shows.
I have placed this evidence before the House and before the country. It does not admit of contradiction, and it should not be necessary to place it before the House, because the facts are so patent that there is no gainsaying them in any way, shape or manner. An organization which not only increases the price of such a necessity as iumber at such a critical time as the present, but actually; dictates to the people of this country whether they shall do business or shall not do business, is something worthy the immediate attention of this House, and the strongest attention that this Housei can give if. For my part, I take the liberty of saying that, as a preliminary canter in dealing with the question, the best thing to do would be to take the duty absolutely off dressed lumber, as it was taken off rough lumber some years ago for the same reason.

The provision seems only to apply to articles upon which there is a duty. I have now before me the section which the hon. minister invokes. That section is as follows :
That whenever the Governor in Council has reason to believe that as regard to any artiele of commerce there exists any trust, combination, association or agreement of any kind among the manufacturers of such article, or dealers therein, to unduly enhance the price of such article or in any other way to unduly promote the advantage of the manufacturers or dealers at the expense of the consumers, the Governor in Council may commission or empower any judge of the Supreme Court or Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any Superior Court in any province of Canada, to inquire in a summary way into and report to the Gover-

nor in Council, whether such trust, combination, association or agreement exists.
Then follows the provision in regard to the attendance of witnesses, &c. It proceeds :
If the judge reports that such trust, combination, association or agreement exists, and if it appears to the Governor in Council that such disadvantage to the consumers is facilitated by the duties of customs imposed on a like article when imported, then the Governor in Council shall place such article on the free list, or so reduce the duty upon it, as to give to the public the benefit of reasonable competition in such article.
I do not know whether my hon. friends have looked carefully at the schedules of the Tariff Act, and they are so long that I hardly like to trouble the House with them, but the schedule which provides for free lumber is very comprehensive indeed. It seems to me to include almost every kind of lumber that would be required. That particular kind of lumber upon which there is a duty of twenty-five per cent is described as follows :
Boards, sawed boards, planks and deals, planed or dressed on one or both sides, when the edges thereof are jointed or tongued and grooved, 25 per cent.
Then
Lumber and timber manufactured, n.e.s., 20 per cent.	.
That, of course, is coupled with a provision for free lumber covering a whole page of this book with which I will not trouble the House at the present time. It seems to me that the complaint which comes from the west is a striking illustration of one fact which I have had occasion to mention before in this House, namely, that these combines do not always depend on a protective tariff. We have combines in the United States, we have them in free trade England at the present time, we have them in Canada in regard to commodities the greater portion of which come into Canada duty free. I agree entirely with the hon. gentlemen who have said that it might prove a serious handicap to the development of the west, particularly at this juncture, if the price of lumber were to be unduly raised, and I agree with hon. gentlemen who have said that this matter should demand the immediate attention of the government. But, whether or not a remedy is to be found in the suggestions which have been made by these gentlemen is to my mind quite a different question. Mr. Speaker, I think that I may fairly congratulate my hon. friend the leader of the opposition on having delivered last Friday the very mildest criticism upon a budget speech to which it has ever been my good fortune to listen. I do not at all mean to say that in certain other directions the hon. gentleman was not aggressive enough; lint I refer to the budget qua budget simply; and on that I may congratulate him ou having delivered himself of an address which could by no possibility have excited in the slightest degree the susceptibilities of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding). I am aware that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition had his difficulties. It is. I have no doubt, in the recollection of this House how almost six years ago to a day, the predecessor of that lion, gentleman, in his usual fervent fashion, made the very rafters of tills building ring with his denuuciations of the desolation, the wme, the misery and the mis-' chief which my hon. friend beside me was about to inflict on the industries of Canada. That lion, gentleman forelieard the walls of the manufacturers of Canada and foresaw the rain of our industries, and I can understand that the him gentleman who now so worthily fills the place formerly occupied by Sir Charles Tapper, hearing these denunciations in his mind, had his difficulties. He must have contrasted the predictions of 1897 with the realities of 1903, and come to the conclusion proha lily, that tlie less said about the rain and destruction which was then predicted as the result of our policy, tlie better for himself and for hi- party.

1 observe that the hon. gentleman has either developed or inherited a taste for that description of scrap-book literature with which we were so familiar in the time of his predecessor. It is a great honour to me that the hon. gentleman should have devoted so much attention to divers speeches and articles of mine. I hope he reads them constantly; I hope they will do him good, though 1 fear the good seed is falling on stony ground, where it is apt to be choked by the brambles of protection. However, as Cromwell was wont to say, in spite of his malignancy, I trust the day of grace will yet come; but I would advise him as he has a taste for perusing these curiosities of bygone literature, to read, and read carefully, the speeches addressed to this House by his honourable predecessor in the years from 1873 to 1878 and thereafter. If the hon. gentleman will do that, he will And two things : he will find, first of all, that his predecessor, Sir Charles Tupper, was most emphatic in pointing out to the House during the first period to which I have referred, that a government's first duty was to create and ensure prosperity. In the succeeding period, he will find that hon. gentleman invariably gave credit to himself and (he government of which he was a member, for all the prosperity which he alleged, obtained in the country. Were my hon. friend Sir Charles Tupper present, I do not doubt that he would, with equal fervour and energy, with as much loudness and possibly as much consistency and logic explain to the House how it is that, in the eternal fitness ofl things, credit is only due to a government for the prosperity of a country when that government happens to be Conservative.
As I have said, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition had his difficulties. He was confronted with the very largest surplus our country has ever enjoyed and he was not able to put his finger on one single tax which he considered oppressive or unjust. He was not able to suggest the reduction of the duty on one single commodity, rather the contrary. It is true he did suggest that my hon. friend beside me, on one or two occasions, had commented adversely on some of the taxes which are still maintained, but was most careful to say that he himself had no objection to these taxes and had not the slightest desire to advocate the reducing or removing of any one of them. And in like manner, although he had to deal with the very largest expenditure Canada has ever seen, he was particularly carefxil to, say that, so far as regards our expenditure, the only criticism, the only attack, he would level against us was that in certain directions, which he was good enough to specify, we did not spend sufficient money.
When my hon. friend dealt with the fact that while our expenditure was very large, our surplus was very large, we were likewise able to show a volume of trade and commerce larger than ever before, all the criticism which my hon. friend saw fit to indulge in, on that subject, was that in his opinion he thought the people were getting too much for their money. And he was disposed to cut down the purchasing power of the people and make them pay more for the goods they were purchasing than they were called on to pay under the existing tariff.
We can well understand that the hon. gentleman, in dealing with a tariff such as the hon. Finance Minister has presented to the House, finds himself woefully handicapped by his own previous utterances and those of his party. He might try to disguise his feelings, but I fear it was not pleasant to him to find that my hon. friend beside me was able to point to all the indices of prosperity, on which my hon. friend and his party were accustomed to rely in former times as indicating the prosperity of a country and a great many more important ones which they were never able to produce, but which have attended the administration of Canada under a Liberal government. Sir, it was perhaps small wonder that under such circumstances the hon. gentleman should appeal to me. It was small wonder that he should say to me, as he did almost in so many words : ' Owing to my peculiar position I really cannot undertake to criticise the budget of the Minister of Finance, but you might do it.' And he was good enough to intimate that he thought that I might do it well. I am deeply grateful to my hon. friend for his good opinion. I am half disposed to meet my hon. friend half way and I will go this far to gratify him. I will define for his benefit and that of his friends beside him, the conditions under which I might, to quote his words, siug one of my old songs and indulge in some of the criticisms I was aj)t to bestow some years ago on the occupants of these benches when I was in opposition. For instance, if we had to-day an exceedingly unfair and oppressive system of taxation, under which we were practically putting two dollars into private pockets for every one that went in to.the public treasury, I might see my way to deliver myself of some severe criticism. If to-day, I found out trade was utterly stagnant and had been so during a quarter of a century, if it were just at the point where it had started out in 1873, I might concede that there was some ground for criticism. If I found our population growing as slowly as it did in the period of Conservative administration, when, if the truth had been told, it would have been shown that in ten years of Conservative rule the'total growth of Canada was less than what I believe it to be in any one year of Libera! administration, I might have had occasion for fault finding. Were we confronted with three or four years of successive deficits I would be disposed to criticise, and
