speechtext: There was a question of that kind before us about a year and a half ago, when everything was defined as manufactured which was produced by motive power. And I think I stated in my remarks that the term included everything so produced.

Yes, I find that he does define the term ' manufactured goods ' as those produced by motive power. Now I would like to know what he means us to infer. Does he mean us to infer that the $750,000,000 or $800,000,000 worth of goods of which he speaks are what are ordinarily known as manufactured goods; because I strongly suspect that in the list to which he referred he will find a great many things that are not usually included in the term ' manufactured goods.' I find, for instance, in the list which 1 think he must have consulted, that sawmills are put down for $52,000,000 of the $750,000,000 or $800,000,000 of manufactured goods. I think that grist mills which produce flour are put down for something like $42,000,000. I find that sugar, whereof the value of the raw material is $15,000,000, is put down for $17,000,000 of manufactured goods. I think my hon. friend will find that to take these crude statements which are commonly furnished of the gross amount of manufactured goods, and apply them to a discussion of a policy which we may pursue, will lead him into serious error. The actual truth of the matter is, I believe, that these are taken largely from the census of 1891, and that census certainly includes a vast number of articles



which are hardly known as manufactured goods in the ordinary acceptation of the term. If my memory serves me, there are nine or ten millions of cheese included in that list; there are some nine or ten millions of blacksmiths' work included; there are a great many millions included of millinery and dressmaking and a great variety of other things, which no doubt are useful products, but which, under ordinary circumstances, do not fairly fall under the head of manufactured goods.
Then the hon. gentleman goes on to institute an elaborate comparison of the receipts from taxes under the late regime and under the present regime. Here, Sir, I take issue with my hon. friend in toto. I say to my hon. friend that the statements which lie makes are wholly misleading, because he is disregarding a cardinal fact. He has paid no attention whatever to the difference between the real taxation inflicted on the people under a protective tariff, and the actual taxation inflicted on the people under a revenue tariff, even if it be a high one. The difference is this, that substantially the great bulk of the taxes go into the treasury under the present tariff, whereas under the administration which preceded ours an enormous percentage of the taxes which the people of Canada had to pay did not go into the treasury but went to swell the profits of private individuals. The people under our tariff have the satisfaction at any rate of knowing that what is taken out of their pockets goes into the treasury, and can be used for the benefit of the whole people. The hon. gentleman appears to be entirelv unable to u iderstand-although I fancy certain of h's friends, the manufacturers, do understand- that after all is said and done ours is a revenue tariff and theirs a protective tariff. The tariff which ours superseded was a protective tariff, and the best proof of that is the fact that under our regime the exports and imports into this country have grown very largely, especially the imports. The very essence of a protective tariff, as he has shown in other parts of his speech, is to exclude goods and diminish revenue ; the essence of a revenue tariff is to receive goods and to see that such taxes as may be levied upon them go into the treasury and are applied for the benefit of the whole people.
Now, a little later on, I noticed the hon. gentleman made certain statements to the effect that the Minister of Finance at one time or another objected to several of the duties that now exist in our tariff. But the hon. gentleman does not propose to reduce them, he does not propose to abate them, he does not propose to remove one single tax that now presses upon the people. In fact, he tells us that he does not complain of it, he does not propose to reduce it, he considers that the tariff in that respect does not require in the slightest degree anv amendment.
Then he proceeds to dilate at some length
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
on what he calls the percentage of expenditure. Now, I have pointed out that if my contention be correct, if as I say, the taxes which we levy differ from the taxes which were levied by the hon. gentleman's predecessors in this respect, that our taxes go into the treasury and their taxes were divided between the treasury and private individuals, then there is no foundation whatever for any comparison to be made between the taxes levied under the two systems. But, Sir, I entirely deny the accuracy of the hon. gentleman's computation so far as it is based on population. About a year ago I had the honour of laying before this House a variety of statements, all tending to show, in my opinion, that the census of 1891 was an impudent fraud. It will be within the recollection of hon. gentlemen here that yonder table was littered knee-deep with evidence proving most conclusively, I repeat, that the grossest and most palpable frauds had been committed in the census of 1891. I have no doubt, from the examination I then made and have since made, that the census of 1891 exaggerated the then population by several hundreds of thousands- how many it is impossible absolutely to ascertain. I have no doubt whatever that during the four or five years of the serious depression which succeeded 1891, the increase of Canada was very slow, if indeed there was any increase at all. If that be true- and I recommend hon. gentlemen who doubt the facts to examine again the evidence-then I submit that the statements made by the hon. gentleman as regards the per capita expenditure are entirely without foundation. I believe the actual facts of the case are these:	That in 1895 or 1896
the actual population of Canada had barely reached the nominal figures which were stated in 1891; that since that time, owing to the stoppage of the exodus, owing to the enormous development of the Northwest, owing to the tide of immigration that has been flowing into Canada under our administration, the population of Canada has been increasing from 125,000 to 150,000 or perhaps 200,000 a year; and that within these last six or seven years there has been added to the population of Canada not less than 800,000, perhaps 900,000 people. Sir, if the hon. gentleman wishes to go into a computation, I recommend him to revise his statements on that basis, and if he does, he will have very little reason indeed to plume himself on the results of a per capita comparison between the expenditure of 1896-97 and that of 1903.
I note again that the hon. gentleman, in criticising our expenditure, is exceedingly careful to point out that he does not object to a liberal expenditure; he rather desires, in point of fact, that a heavy additional expenditure should be incurred. Well, Sir, he may be right as to some of those matters. It is not my purpose at the present moment to enter into an examination of the

question under that head. But I note that the hon. gentleman, when he comes to deal with one phase of the situation, when he deals with the fact that we imported from the United States a very much larger amount of goods than we exported, I note one remarkable thing, and that is that my hon. friend entirely omits all the coin and bullion, all the gold products of Canada that were exported to the United States. Now, 1 would like to know what my hon. friend's private opinion of that point is. According to our trade and navigation returns we exported roughly $70,000,000 worth of goods to the United States and we imported from them $114,000,000. He arbitrarily deducts $24,000,000 and makes our exports $47,000,000 instead of $70,000,000. Is it the opinion of my hon. friend that Canada is any poorer because Canada parted with a few tons of yellow "dust in return for $24,000,000 of valuable commodities of other kinds. I would like to know what my hon. friend's opinion on that head is.
I was following the example, in making that computation, of a great financier on the other side of the House, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton).

I am afraid that my hon. friend misunderstood the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). However, the hon. member for North Norfolk can answer for that matter himself, but I would like to know if he accepts that. I think an hon. gentleman who is posing as a financial critic ought to explain to us :	Does he consider
that Canada is any the poorer for parting with a few tons of gold dust and getting very many millions of dollars worth of valuable commodities in exchange ? I would like to know. Is that his own opinion?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: My hon. friend from North Norfolk is going to speak in this debate and he will answer the hon. gentleman most fully on that point.

I have no doubt, but, my hon. friend, with very lawyer-like caution and subtlety will not commit himself to an opinion on that point. It bears very materially on the question. To my mind a country is none the poorer because it exchanges a certain amount of gold dust for a large amount of valuable commodities of other kinds. That is my opinion of the subject. I give it without reservation, without fear or favour, without even the fear of the hon. member for North Norfolk. My hon. friend dwelt at considerable length on the fact, which is perfectly true, that there has been a great increase in our trade with the United States, very largely due to the great increase in the growth of our manufactures and in the numerous demands for raw products that our manufacturers have 51i
made upon the United States. But, the hon. gentleman ought to remember this, and all hon. gentlemen might well remember it, that when we are dealing with the question of trade with the United States, when we compare the trade which we carry on with the United States with the trade which we carry on with the mother country, it is a question of geography quite as much as a question of tariff. It is plain to anybody, plain to a demonstration, that that in itself if it were not for our reciprocally barbarous tariffs, our geographical position would naturally induce us to carry on a very great trade with the United States, to our mutual advantage. At this present moment, everybody knows, that in a great many matters it is infinitely easier for our manufacturers and merchants to trade with the manufacturers and merchants of the United States than it will ever be to trade with any country on the other side of the Atlantic. In the greater part of the United States, measured by population it only takes twenty-four hours for a letter from any part of older Canada to reach its destination, and a telegraph or telephone message will reach it in an hour. Moreover, the conditions of manufacture, the conditions of the life of the people in the United States and particularly in the northern states are so closely analagous to those prevailing in Canada that it is exceedingly easy for them to understand the needs of our market; whereas, in the mother country it is not by any manner of means so easy to communicate with us or to supply our wants, and consequently it is no wonder at all that our trade with the United States should increase more largely than our trade with Great Britain.
But, the hon. gentleman went on to deal with the preferential tariff. He went on to analyse the effect of the preferential duty on English goods. He says that the tariff on dutiable goods coming from Great Britain is about 24 per cent, while the tariff on dutiable goods coming from the United States is about 25 per cent, and he draws the deduction, perhaps not unnaturally, that our preference to Great Britain is a matter of very little moment, that our tariff is really, substantially, quite as favourable to the United States as our tariff is to Great Britain. This is a question which will bear a little looking into. I have been at some pains to have the actual effect of this preferential tariff of ours with Great Britain properly analysed. No doubt the hon. gentleman was perfectly correct in one sense. The hon. gentleman has taken our trade and navigation returns, he has looked at the dutiable column, and he has deduced from that that the average duty under the preferential tariff is 24 per cent, whereas had the hon. gentleman condescended to look a little more closely into the matter he would have found that there is only a certain proportion of our imports

from Great Britain which come in under the preferential tariff. The hon. gentleman would have found that such articles as wines and spirits, and I think, tobaccos, are excluded absolutely from the operation of the preferential tariff. If he had desired to know how that tariff operated he ought to have deducted the value of these articles and the amount of taxation which is levied upon them. He ought, in the second place, to have deducted the amount of goods imported from Great Britain, which, for one reason or another, were not permitted the benefit of the preferential tariff, in all, something like $5,000,000 worth, more or less. Had he done so, he would have found that the dutiable imports from Great Britain which enjoyed the benefit of the preferential tariff amounted to $28,730,000 roughly, that the total taxation on these amounted to $5,395,000, and he would have found this further fact, which I commend to his notice, which I commend to the notice of the House, and which I commend to the notice of our English friends, that under the preferential tariff on these $28,730,000 worth, the average duty levied was not 24 per cent, hut 18 8-10 per cent. While I am on the subject, I may just as well say that 1 think, perhaps, it was an unfortunate thing that at the recent colonial conference that that very able man, Mr. Chamberlain, acting on very imperfect information, in my opinion, rather belittled the effect of preferential tariff. Now, I want to call the attention of the House to this fact: The hon. gentleman has recourse to the trade and navigation returns. He takes the average for a number of years and contrasts that with the average for another number of years, and he says: After all is said and done, there has been very little improvement in importations from Great Britain, because, during five years of your administration the average importation has shown very little increase over that of your predecessors. What are the actual facts ? If my hon. friend will turn to the Trade and Commerce Report, he will find that in the year 1890 the dutiable goods- which need only enter into our computation at present-the dutiable goods imported from Great Britain were $33,000,000. That by the year 1897, under the operation of the tariff of these gentlemen opposite, had fallen to $20,000,000. That, since 1S97 has risen from $20,000,000 to $35,000,000.
Now, Sir, the man who tells me-whether he be an Englishman or whether he be a Canadian-the man who tells me, in the face of those figures, that the preferential tariff had no effect whatever in increasing the importation of English goods into Canada, in my humble opinion, knows very little about what he is talking of. I say that the effect has been very marked and very important, and I say that if you choose to look a little below the surface you will find two very im-porant things well worthy of being brought Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
to the attention both of this House and of our English friends and customers. You will find that our trade wjth England in dutiable goods, although relatively smaller than our trade with the United States, is in all human probability much more profitable than the trade which the United States carry on with us. That was a subject which I had occasion to examine into pretty fully during the period that the Joint High Commission was sitting in Washington, and I make the assertion without much fear of contradiction by those who are acquainted with the details, that it will be found that the profit the English merchant derives from the $35,000,000 of goods which he sells to Canada is vastly iu excess of the profit which the American manufacturer derives from the $60,000,000 of dutiable goods which he sells to Canada. More than that, and it is reasonable it should be so, the trade with Great Britain is a natural one, it is not a forced one. The trade with the United States under the peculiar conditions that prevail there is largely artificial and a forced trade, and one thing is very clear about it, that whatever else effect our tariff may have had ; whatever effect our tariff against the United States may have had in some respects, it most assuredly did largely diminish the profits which heretofore have been made by American manufacturers out of their Canadian trade.
Then, Sir, there is another matter also worthy of consideration. In looking at the trade returns of the various countries I find this fact which again I commend to the attention of our English friends. We are at present importing of all kinds of goods from England about $50,000,000 worth. The United States, with a population of 75,000,000, were importing in the years 1899 and 1900 a matter of $90,000,000 and a matter of $100,000,000 worth, respectively. I believe they have done a little more during the past two years, largely in consequence of the disturbed conditions of American trade consequent on the steel and coal strikes. But this result remains, and this result is one worthy of notice : that while the average Canadian family will consume about $50 worth of English goods in the course of the year, the average American family will consume-taking the two years I have spoken of as fair samples-about $6 worth of English goods. Per head, Canada consumes something like seven times as much English goods as do the people of the United States.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) made a reproach against my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and against the government of which he is a member, that in all our trade negotiations we have done nothing. That we had attempted to trade with the United States and we had gained nothing ; that we had attempted to trade with Germany and we had gained nothing ; that we had attempted to trade with France and we
16(19

had gained nothing. Well, Sir, I will tell the hon. gentleman what this government and what the people of Canada have done within the past few years. They have shown the people of the United States, by the best of all object lessons, that we can live without them ; they have shown them that we can increase our trade and commerce in a much faster ratio than theirs ; they have shown them that we can successfully compete with them in the markets of the world if they do not choose to allow us to compete with them in the markets of their own country. And let me tell the House that that knowledge and, what is more, the demonstration of that fact, was an essential underlying factor before we could hope to to secure any favourable conditions of reciprocity with the United States.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Show the Americans that we can do without them ; show the Americans that we are formidable competitors to them ; show the Americans that Canada is growing in trade and commerce at any rate, and probably in population, quite as fast as they themselves are, and you will find that they will be very much more disposed to trade with us, and very much more amenable to reason than we have found them in the past. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has asked what we will do if Canadian farmers leave their farms and go to the United States to find employment in the factories there ; and he gives us to understand, 1 suppose, that those things never happened under the regime of our predecessors, the Conservatives. Well, Sir, I think that I remember when every train from Canada, under the blessed dispensation of the National Policy, was crowded, crammed brimming over with men who were moving from Canada to the United States, and our census returns show that in the seventeen or eighteen years that tire Conservatives held power, the loss of population to Canada- rot counting the immigrants whom they alleged they had brought into the country to the tune of about 886,000-our returns shows that numbered within the ten years from 1881 to 1891, the loss to Canada of Canadians and the direct descendants of Canadians might be counted, not by the ten thousands, but by the millions.
But there are two points on which the hon. gaitleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) dwelt, and on which I desire to say a word or two. The hon. gentleman was good enough to tell us that it was the policy of his party to protect the farmers. That is a laudable, desirable and most important object in which I heartily concur, and I would like to see how the hon. gentleman proposes to do it. We stand here to be instructed ; we desire to know. We are not above, if the hon. gentleman an show us how, taking a useful hint from that hon. gentleman. Bast year the people
of Canada produced about 100,000,000 bushels of wheat, and possibly next year they will produce 200,000,000 bushels of wheat- the chance is that in a very short time they may produce 300,000,000 bushels of wheat. We consume in Canada, all told, something like from 20,000,000 to 30,000,000 bushels a year. Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) be good enough to show me how he proposes by protection to add one ceiit to the value of wheat grown in Canada ? I should like to know. I should like to understand under what conditions, if we grow 200,000,000 bushels of wheat and if we require 20,000,000 bushels for our own use, the hon. gentleman is going to protect the growers of the remaining 180,000,000 bushels. I am open to conviction ; I carry an open mind.
speakername: The MINISTER OE TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Why do you keep 12i cents a bushel on wheat now ?

That is for the hon. gentleman's predecessors to explain; hon. gentlemen opposite do not complain of it. If the hon. gentleman wants my opinion of the matter,
I tell him that it is not of the smallest value to the farmers of Canada. I should like to know in what way the hon. gentleman proposes to protect the Canadian wheat growers. We sell; about $20,000,000 worth of cheese chiefly in the English market. I suppose we consume about $2,000,000 worth in Canada. I would like to know how the hon. gentleman would protect us in that. We sell nearly as much bacon and hams. I would like to know how he proposes to protect us in these articles. The actual truth of the matter is this ; He cannot protect the Canadian farmer, and he knows it well. He cannot add, by any device or means of his in the way of protection, one cent to the value of the wheat grown m Canada. But he can do something else : He can-and he is ready to do it-enormously diminish the value of the purchasing power of the wheat which the farmer raises. That, I grant, lie can do. There his powers for mischief have an almost unlimited field.
Now, Sir, here is an audacious statement- I will give it} in the hon. gentleman's own words :
What is our position with respect to the United States ? We buy from them about $72,000,000 worth of manufactured goods, and we sell to them $6,000,000. We buy from them $28,000,000 of agricultural products and products of animals, and we sell to them of the same articles less than $3,000,000.
Whoever, as I say, undertook to dry-nurse my hon. friend has led him astray. That, while I acquit him of intentionally designing to mislead, is an ill-advised statement. It is quite true, and I make him a present of the fact, that the nominal amount of goods coming under those heads which we imported from the United States in the year 1902 was something like $28,000,-

000; but of what did they consist ? I will give the House one item, perhaps the largest. AVe imported from the United States in 1902 something like $8,663,000 worth of wheat, and we exported some $7,443,000 worth, to the great detriment of the farmers of1 Canada. AVe imported from the United States in the same fashion a variety of other dutiable articles, amounting in all to $14,752,000. Of these we re-exported, almost entirely to England, $7,812,000 worth, leaving of dutiable articles which may be said to have entered to some extent into competition with the products of our farmers, a matter of $6,940,000 worth. Now, I want to go over these importations a little in detail. I want to show how terribly the farmers of Canada have been handicapped by this importation of $23,000,000 which my hon. friend speaks of. The first important item, after breadstuffs, is fruits, of which we imported $1,947,000 worth. I observe that of these an exceedingly largej percentage consists of oranges, which it was no doubt very much to the detriment of the farmers of Canada that we should import. The next largest item, nearly three quarters of a million, consists of raisins, currants, almonds and prunes, which were also imported very much to the detriment of the farmers of Canada, who, I presume, have of late gone largely into the manufacture* of raisins, prunes and almonds. 1 notice, in like manner, when we come to the free list, that the articles which enter into competition with the products of the farmers of Canada, are of a very formidable character. Of dutiable goods, we imported about $14,000,000 worth, the greater part of which was sent across the ocean. AVe likewise imported about $12,000,000 worth of free goods. Of these, the first item is broom corn. I candidly admit that I do not know whether it enters seriously into competition with the products of our farmers or not, and I am open to correction. The next item on the list, a very important one, is bananas, of which we imported $714,800 worth; and the next is pineapples, of which we imported about $90,000 worth, doubtless greatly to the detriment of the1 farmers of Canada. Tiie fact of the matter is, these fruits are not the products of the United States at all. For convenience, we import them through the ports of New York or Boston, as the shortest route to the western markets of the western provinces. Of hemp undressed we imported $G69,000 worth. Of Indian corn we imported $2,480,000 worth, of which we straightway exported to England $1,200,000 worth in the shape of Indian corn, and the other $1,200,000 worth a little later in the shape of fat cattle. Does the hon. gentleman pretend to say that the farmers of Canada were seriously damnified by the importation of this Indian corn which they exported in the two ways I have mentioned ? Are the farmers to be worse treated than our manufacturing friends, to whom we Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
allow the full rebate on everything they export on which they show they have paid the full duty ? AVe imported of flaxseed $1,714,000 worth. I do not think that enters seriously into competition with the products of our farmers, though tobacco may, of which we imported $1,900,000 worth. The next item is furs and skins undressed. Do. my agricultural friends think they were seriously injured by the importation of $1,000,000 worth of undressed furs? Of hides and skins we imported, chiefly from the South American republics,1 through United States ports, $2,174,000 worth, and we exported nearly an equal amount. AVe imported $330,000 worth of raw silk, greatly to the detriment of the farmers of Canada, and $221,000 worth of raw wool and sent out about as much. The actual result is that of the $28,000,000 worth of agricultural and animal products which, according to my hon. friend, we imported from the United States, to enter into competition with the products of the farmers of Canada, if you make a fair analysis, you will find that very nearly one-half were promptly re-exported, giving employment to Canadian ships and Canadian railways, and that the remainder are largely articles, such as bananas, raw silk and the other things I have mentioned, which can by no possibility injure the farmers of the Dominion of Canada.
Briefly, I find that on the $28,000,000 of imports of agricultural products and animals and their products, about five and a half millions, on a fair computation, may go into competition with farm products of Canada while, as the hon. gentleman says himself, we in turn sell the United States about $8,000,000 of similar products. The truth is that along our border of some 4,000 miles, there will always be found a number of places where it is convenient and mutually profitable to interchange products; and were it not for our tariffs we would carry on those exchanges to our mutual profit on a much larger scale, and I fail to see that, on a fair analysis of the case, the farmers of Canada are placed at any such disadvantage, as my hon. friend was, I think, very unfortunately led to suppose. My hon. friend repeats his statement a little later on, and evidently he and his friends intend to use it in their discussions in the country as a proof of the extreme injury done, under this tariff, to the farmers of Canada. But I am convinced that, if a fair examination be made, we will find that we make a reasonable and fair exchange in those products. AVe do not sell our neighbours anything like the quantity of goods, and it would be to our mutual advantage to interchange with tliem to a greater extent. But it is manifestly contrary to the facts to say that at this moment the exchange against us is so unfair that we buy $28,000,000 from the Americans while we sell them but $8,000,000 worth. The bulk of those imports are re-exported, nnd of those that are not, the greater bulk

do not enter Into competition with our farm
products at all, while a large part of the remainder are merely bought from the United States for convenience sake as in the case of hides from South America and bananas and other articles that I have mentioned.
I do not know that it is necessary for me to spend any further time on the speech of my hon. friend. I am afraid that time will hardly permit me to do what I should have liked to do-to analize minutely our expenditure. But I will lay before the House certain facts which, X think, will go far to convince them that we are not after all liable to the charge of gross and undue expenditure and extravagance in the administration of public affairs. Let me take the statement which Mr. Foster laid on the Table of the House in 1896, when he was Minister of Finance. He then computed the requirements of the public service for 1S97 at something like $38,300,000 for his main estimates. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) the other day brought down an estimate something like $50,750,000. There is a difference there and a large difference-a difference of about $12,000,000. If the hon. gentlemen were able to show that we have idly and needlessly added $12,000,000 to the public expenditure, then we would justly be liable to severe censure. But when you come to analyse this expenditure, what do you find ? You find, in the first place, that out of this augmentation of $12,000,000 at least $6,000,000 are directly transferred from one pocket into the other. That $6,000,000 is made up of such items as increase in the sinking fund, extra expenditure on railways and canals, which are recouped by the receipts therefrom, and extra expenditure on the Yukon Territory, which Mr. Foster was not called on to provide, and for which we have received from the start to the present hour, full compensation in the shape of the increased revenue derived from that particular territory. That being the case, the gross expenditure, for which we should he called on to account, is reduced to something like $6,000,000. But to what is this increase of $6,000,000 due ? It has been caused, for the most part, by the necessity of largely extending and increasing such services, our light-house and coast service,' which everybody who knows anything of the condition of Canadian trade admits to be an expenditure that ought to be encouraged as much as possible, and which, as my hon. friends opposite have urged, ought to be enlarged '! That is one large item.
The second is our increased expenditure on immigration, and I venture to say that for every penny we have expended on that head the country stands to receive-and that too, speedily-a dollar in return. Then there is the expenditure for agricultural purposes in various ways. For that also the country has received and is receiving a large return in the continuous increase in our exports of agricultural products. There is also a heavy
increase from North-west administration
rendered necessary by the vast influx of settlers into that country. Is that a wasteful expenditure ? And so it goes all through. I shall not dwell so much on this at present, partly because I have scarcely the time at my disposal and partly because the hon. gentleman himself does not assail our expenditure as extravagant and unnecessary. On the contrary, he admits that large and liberal expenditure is needful and declares that he would be prepared, in many cases, to spend more than we are doing.
But, let me call attention to these three tliiugs. First of all, when comparing the expenditure of 1896-7 with the expenditure of 1903, you would do well to bear in mind that the population of the country has increased very considerably. There has been, by my estimate, an increase of 800,000, or of 900,000 people. In any case, even admitting, which I never will admit-the correctness of the census of 1901, our population has certainly increased 500,000 or 600,000. Consequently a larger expenditure is justifiable and necessary. In the second place, it is well to remember that the income of the Canadian people to-day is fully double what it was seven years ago, and an expenditure is now justified, when you have a volume of trade and commerce of $400,000,000, which might have been unreasonable and extravagant when it was only $200,000,000, with a revenue in proportion. And in the third place, you should bear in mind that coincident with the extraordinary prosperity of Canada, there has been a great increase in the cost of materials and wages all over the country, so that the works executed to-day by the Minister of Public Works and other members of the government must of necessity require a very much increased expenditure. The increase of wages alone must involve a very large additional expenditure compared to what was requisite in 1896. Therefore, taking these three causes into account, you will see that there is little ground for condemning the government on the score of enormous and unjustifiable expenditure. Population has increased, there has been an increase in the volume of trade, our revenue has increased, wages have increased, there has been a great rise in the cost of materials as compared with 1896, to all of which is due the increased expenditure of $6,000,000.
My hon. friend wants to know what I think about surpluses. I have no objection to tell him. There are three excellent uses to which a surplus may be applied. It may in the first place, be applied to the reduction of taxation. In the second place, we may apply it to paying off the public debt, and in the third place we may apply it to the construction of useful and productive public works. AH are good. The question of how a surplus is to be applied is one to be always settled with a due regard to the circum-

stances of the moment and a due consideration as to which of these particular modes is the best to take. It depends upon a great variety of considerations. You may have a young or an old state. It depends upon the position of the people, whether they are prosperous or whether they are in pinched circumstances. It depends lastly, and very largely, on the possibility of rapid development. I have no hesitation in saying, so far as the government of Canada is concerned, we believe, having regard to the present condition of Canada, that the best way we can use our surplus is to open up our new territory, provide means of communication, cheapen transportation, and so avail ourselves of the great advantages of our position. When the question is put : Which is the best for Canada, whether to attempt to increase population and production by the active aid of the government, or to pay off our debt and diminish our taxes, it is a fair question for debate. But, in this case, I think the House and the country will sustain the government in declaring :	Now is the time to
use the advantages which are ours and to develop the great resources we possess. Sir, there is a tide in the affairs of nations as well as of men, and Canada is at the crest of the wave at this moment, and Canada will do well to take advantage of the circumstances of her position.
I desire to say a few words witli regard to the late conference in London, and the demands which were made on Canada. I have already dealt with the question of the preference and have ventured to express my regret that the British ministers who took part in that conference were not sufficiently well advised of the advantage of the preference to British trade. And I am very glad to be assured, as we were by my hon. friend, that the facts were fully brought to their notice before the conference broke up. And I am glad to know, from recent editorial utterances in England, that they are waking up to the fact that the preference is of very real and substantial value to them. There is another question, incidentally connected with the administration of this country and its finances, on which I would like to say a word or two. The request has been made that Canada should co-operate for the defence of the empire. It has been placed before us in several different ways. We have been asked to say what we will contribute to the navy; and we shall be asked what we will contribute to the army that is necessary to defend the empire. There are two policies before us, and it may not be amiss to say a word or two as to which of these policies is, on the whole, the best, not only for Canada but for the empire at large. One body of our advisers seems to think that the best way for Canada to give aid to the empire is to place a large sum of money at its disposal, and ourselves maintain a standing Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
army of larger or smaller proportions. Now, it is possible for Canada, no doubt, to maintain a small standing army-not a very large one. That is possible. The cost will be great. The advantage to Canada will be small. The advantage to the empire will be smaller still. It will be of very little account to the British empire if we are able to put at their disposal one, two, three or four battalions of a little standing army. But there is, in my opinion, a more excellent way, a way far more suitable to the genius of our people, far more likely to promote the real interest of Great Britain, and far more likely to enable us to afford real assistance to the empire should assistance be needed. That way is for us to lay to heart the lessons taught us by the recent Boer war ; to make it, as I would like to see it made, a part of the education of every able-bodied man in Canada, that he should learn some of the elements of drill, and learn how to handle his rifle and become an experienced and trained rifle shot. I believe that for a sum perfectly insignificant, barely half of the cost of the smallest standing army that any one could well propose to maintain, you could have, in a few years in Canada, a body of five hundred thousand riflemen able to give a good account of their enemy at a thousand yards and upwards. And I say that if you but train your people in that fashion you could provide a neucleus of a force through which a most substantial aid could be given to the empire should it ever be imperilled. It is to that I should like to see the energy of the people of Canada and of the Department of Militia devoted. It is an old saying among people of English blood that their first idea, when they have a holiday is to say :	It is a fine day, let
us go out and kill something. That may be rather barbaric, but it is instinctive. There is scarcely a lad of spirit from one end of Canada to the other, but, if he had the opportunity and the bodily strength, would like to become-would even make considerable sacrifices to become-a good rifle shot. I would avail myself of that instinct and that genius of our people, and would endeavour so to train our people that they might be able, in case of need, to put in the field a force which, if they are to judge from the experiences of South Africa, would render the greatest service to the empire, or to ourselves were we, unhappily, called upon to defend our hearths and homes from an invading foe. There is a mode in which we can, I think, without doing violence to our condition, or without interfering in any way with the habits of our people, prepare to render substantial assistance to the mother country. And I am glad to say that the Minister of Militia (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) is already commencing the work and moving in that direction. Were this done, other advantages, advantages of no slight character, would be

likely to flow from it. Every man who knows anything of the training necessary to make a good rifle shot, knows that efficiency is impossible unless one practices the virtues of sobriety and temperance. Moreover, it is one of the things that will go far to instill in our people a spirit of self-reliance, making us respected by other nations as well as by ourselves.
And now, Sir, what is the policy of the opposition, and what is the policy of the government ? My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has told you in his speech and in his motion that his policy is taxes, and more taxes, and yet more taxes. I have pointed out, that it is possible for us to protect some, but it is impossible to protect the whole masses of the people. You may give advantages in this way to the few, but you cannot give advantages to the whole population. I doubt very much if the policy which he proposes, and which some of the manufacturers propose-as the hon. gentleman has stated, not because there is any serious difficulty at the present time, but because they dread that at some future day they may be exposed to undue competition from the United States-would really result in producing any of the consequences they hope for. As I read the signs of the times, there is at this moment, beyond all doubt, some danger of over-expansion and overproduction both here and in the United States. There is some danger of a glutted market. And the best advice that I can give, the best advice that any can give in the House or in the country is, that, under the circumstances, it would be well for all concerned, manufacturers and others, to take stock of the situation, to make use of these fat years to make provision for the lean years which must assuredly come sooner or later-not to over-expand, not to overproduce-to pay off debts, if they have incurred them ; to place ourselves in a position of having good reserves ; to confer (for X am far from objecting to that) with their brother manufacturers and with the chiefs of finance and with the leaders of our banking institutions. They say very truly : Our market is limited, and there is danger of a glut. But the way to avoid a glut is not to go recklessly and without precaution, increasing their productive power, but to make provision in the good times for the possibility they dread that some time or other the slaughter market from the other side may overtake them.
Sir, the policy of the government has been announced by my hon. friend, and it is briefly this :	To deal fairly with all, making ourselves the tool of none ; to insist upon it that those who come to us for aid should explain openly and in the light of day what they desire at our hands, and why they desire it. My hon. friend did well, my hon. friend deserves commendation in that, when the manufacturers approached him, he refused to have any hole or corner
meeting with them, in that he told them : State your case, gentlemen, and it shall have every consideration; but state it openly so that the public may know what you want and why you want it, and that all classes whose interests may be affected may have a chance of being heard before us. Sir, we desire wherever it is possible, to make new territories available ; we desire, wherever it is possible, to help forward all efforts by constructing railroads and other means of communication, in making those territories available. We desire to cheapen transport to the utmost extent that it is possible to do so ; we desire above all to encourage, as far as lies in our power, agricultural and kindred industries, and all other industries. We desire to encourage a well selected immigration ; and I hope and trust-and in that regard I believe that my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, has that likewise much at heart-I hope and trust that the immigration which is now pouring into Canada may be as good in quality as it is great in quantity. I have more than once stated on the floor of this House, and I see no reason to conceal my opinion, that immigrants from old Canada, immigrants from the United States, possessed of capital or even without capital, are far more valuable to us, man for man, than any immigrants that can come here from across the sea. I desire to see above all, the exodus from our own country stopped, and to see the people who in former times went to the United States, remain at home and use their energy, use their ability, use their resources to develop the unbounded territory which is now stretching open to us in the North-west.
For the rest, Mr. Speaker, I say to my hon. friends beside me, I say to my hon. friends opposite me :	Be content to go on
as we have gone ; be content to do as we have done ; and in the next decade it is no idle flight of fancy to say that the man who holds the postition of Finance Minister in 1913, may reasonably expect to come down to this House and tell them that in place of a volume of trade and commerce of $400,000,000, he has a volume of trade of $1,400,000,000 ; that in place of a revenue of $60,000,000, he has a revenue of $160,000,000 ; and it would not surprise me to know that in place of a surplus of $13,000,000, the Finance Minister of the future, if he treads in our footsteps and goes on as we have done, will have an actual surplus of $30,000,000. It is well within the possibilities, it is a thing which has been done again and again in the country to the south of us, in many of the states of the union results equal to these have been actually achieved. Are we Canadians worse, are we Canadians less vigorous, are we less able to make use of our territory than the Americans have proved themselves able, in times past, to make use of theirs ?
Now I put it to you, Sir, and to this House, I put it to the people of Canada, which

policy do you prefer ? Sir, in 1878 the national policy, so-called, was started by these hon. gentlemen, with every conceivable circumstance in its favour. It was coincident with a return of prosperous times, which it had done nothing in the world to produce. Hon. gentlemen had a perfectly free hand. They bad able leaders. They had an absolute majority, a huge majority, an unlimited supply of funds, a perfectly submissive Senate at its back, and a largely gerrymandered constituency to deal with. I have shown you where they had arrived in 1896, I have shown you their four years' deficit, I have shown you their twenty-five years of stagnation, I have shown you our depopulation and disgrace. Sir, compare those seventeen yeai's with our seven years ; compare our surplus of 813,000,000 with their four years' deficits ; compare the million of people we have put into Canada within the last seven years with the miserable showing they had to make in their seventeen years. I say that never since the creation of the world was such an object lesson presented for the consideration of intelligent men as the object lesson which the Trade and Navigation Returns, and the financial returns of the country, show to-day as between the Liberal and Conservative administration. Let us go on in the way we have been going, and I for one, Sir, have no fear whatever of the result.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker-I owe to the courtesy of the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) the privilege of addressing the House to-day. He had been charged by his leader to reply to the speech delivered this afternoon by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). I asked him whether he would be good enough to give way to me on account of the fact that I have some engagements which will keep me away from the House] during the last days of the week and he kindly consented to do so.
The government have resolved to decline to make any changes in the tariff. The hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce have given us the reasons for that decision. There is no doubt whatever that the government feel confident that they are following the proper course. Their motives cannot be impugned. The hon. Minister of Finance, with his usual adroitness and ability, has endeavoured to convince the House that, in point of fact, there was nothing else to be done than what the government are doing. He has told us that the country is prosperous. This is the first reason that he has given Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
us to justify the government in declining to make any general revision of the tariff. He has also informed us that the government have applied for a preference from the British government. The British authorities have not yet replied to that application. The government are desirous of getting a reply before making a general revision of the tariff, so the hon. Minister of Finance has told us. The third reason that has been offered to us is the negotiations that have begun between the United States government and this government with the view of coming, if possible, to a commercial arrangement. These reasons are strong enough in the opinion of the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches to engage them to stay their hands.
Nobody will attempt to deny that this country is prosperous. It would be, indeed, inexplicable that a new country, that a wealthy country like Canada should not be prosperous at the present time. We have had a succession of good crops. There is a wave of prosperity and progress all over the world. We are not the only nation that is prosperous. All the civilized nations of the world are enjoying a great wave of prosperity and progress. The hon. Minister of Finance has proudly told us that by the first of July next, the revenue of this country will have reached the splendid figure of $65,000,000. He also rejoices in the fact that he is in the position to announce a surplus of $13,500,000 on the first of July. There are three main agents of revenue in this country-the customs, the excise and the revenue coming from public works, railways and canals and other works. There are also, to a limited extent, revenues from the sale of lands and other sources. The excise is undoubtedly and exclusively, so to speak, a means of taxation. The customs are a means of taxation when they are applied in a certain way. When they are applied in another way they are both the means of raising revenue and developing the industries of the nation. In 1897, Canada imported for home consumption, $66,220,725 of dutiable goods, $40,397,002 of free goods, a total of $106,617,676. The duties collected on that amount reached a total of $19,891,996. On that amount the average duty paid was 18:613 per cent. In 1902, we imported for home consumption a total of $196,480,190, $118,657,496 of dutiable goods and $77,822,694 of free goods. On that total the average duty collected was 16:466 per cent, while on dutiable goods the average duty paid was 27-265.
There was a total of over $32,000,000 of revenue raised by customs in 1902. This is a very large amount of money. We paid that amount of money because we bought $196,480,190 worth of foreign goods. The total trade of this country in 1902 was $423,910,044. The imports reached the amount of $212,270,158 and the exports amounted to $211,640,286. We imported from the United

States $129,794,147 and we exported to the United States $71,197,684-this of course Includes bullion, foreign goods and everything else. Therefore the balance of trade against us so far as the general Imports and exports are concerned amounts to nearly $50,000,000. As I have said, we imported a total of $196,480,190 for home consumption, and out of that amount we imported from the United States for home consumption $114,774,696, leaving $82,435,494, which we imported for home consumption from other countries. Our total imports from Great Britain for home consumption were $49,022,726, and our total exports of home produce were $196,019,763. The total exports to the United States out of that amount In home produce was $66,607,784; the total exports to Great Britain being $109,347,345. Now, Sir, permit me to call the attention of the House to the composition of the exports of Canadian domestic products to the United States. Out of the $66,607,784 worth that we exported to the United States, there were $33,145,856 of minerals; $4,184,403 of products of the fisheries; $4,139,262 of animals and their produce; $15,517,528 of forest products; $2,555,216 of agricultural products; and $6,024,373 of manufactured products.
Then, we have exported to Great Britain $6,374,877 of products of the fisheries ; $14,154,407 of forest products; $52,687,998 of animals and their products; $27,973,503 of agricultural products, or a total of farm products amounting to $80,661,501. We have exported to Great Britain $7,322,602 of manufactured products. My right lion, friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (lit. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) insisted very strongly this afternoon on the fact that in his opinion the imports of agricultural products to Canada from the United States do not interfere very greatly as yet with the interests of our farming community. That may be so, but we all remember that during the last session of parliament we had a very important and interesting debate in the course of which every one of our friends from the North-west complained bitterly, that the importation of American horses was destroying a large and important industry in the North-west Territories. What is true of that industry is true of others. We are importing large quantities of produce and we are importing large quantities of horses and sheep. We have imported also large quantities of corn. We are all agreed or nearly all agreed that corn is one of those products which should be imported free into a country like this. But, Sir, I ask : whether it would not be a proper policy for this country to adopt to raise the tariff as an average on the farm products of the United States just ns high as our American friends have raised their tariff on Canadian products.
Hear, hear.

Is it not probable that if the Canadian tariff was on the same lines as the American tariff as far as farm products are concerned, that we would develop our farming industry in a direction where capital is afraid to invest now ?
Hear, hear.

In 1902 our exports of manufactured products to the United States amounted to $6,024,373, and we imported of manufactured goods from the United States to Canada to the amount of $69,536,000. It) is an interesting search to look carefully into the American statistics. The last statistics of the United States show that the main bulk of the imports from the United States into this country go to Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, and the Northwest Territories. There are $90,935,713 of imports from the United States dumired into these four provinces. Though the same provinces export to the United States products to the amount of only $27,599,746, leaving a balance of trade of not less than $62,333,967 against these four provinces. The maritime provinces import from the United States $7,841,571, while they export to that country $5,496,697. British Columbia is the only province which has a balance of trade in its favour in its intercourse with the United States, its exports to that country being $9,385,720, as against imports from the United States to the amount of $7,011,930.
These figures, Sir, are not new; but I thought that it was necessary for the argument that I am going to offer to the House, that they should be placed before you. They show that in our commercial intercourse with the United States, our American neighbours have the best of us. It cannot be disputed that they are exporting to this country very large quantities and volumes of their goods of all kinds, while we are exporting to them very little. They do not do us any favour in taking our lumber; they need it. Neither do they do us any favour in taking our minerals; they need them. If they did not require these things, they would not take them. We export to the United States a very limited quantity of agricultural products and a very small volume of manufactured goods. I ask whether that is a state of affairs that is pleasing and advantageous to us. I ask whether it would not be to the interest of this Canadian nation to put an immediate end to such a condition of things. Am I very far from the truth in saying that even those who have been brought up in the ideas of free trade or of a low tariff, would agree with us if they had not some pretext for avoiding the issue ? I want to know if there is a Canadian business man, whatever his political persuasion may be, who will stand up and say that it is a sound condition for a country to have always the balance of

trade against it. Nobody can say that it is a sound state of affairs, and the lion. Minister of Finance has so well felt the strength of that unanswerable argument that he has offered us reasons why the issue should be avoided at the present time. He tells us that the government hope to come to some arrangement with our neighbours. What arrangement, I ask ? Surely the government do not contemplate lowering the tariff on manufactured articles, so far as the United States are concerned. The government have not intimated such an intention, and I do not believe that any government in Canada would venture, in the face of the high tariff of the United States, to regard it possible for this country to lower our tariff in favour of that country. How could we compete with our neighbours in the manufactures ? The' last American census has established that there are ten billions of American and foreign capital invested in American manufactures, that that large capital has produced thirteen billions of manufactured goods in the year 1900, and that the population of wage-earners engaged in those industries is over five millions, or about equal to the whole population of Canada. I ask again how we could compete with such a powerful nation as the United States are to-day ?
But it is represented to us that it will be an advantageous thing for Canada to have reciprocity with the United States in natural products. Let me say first to those who are of that mind, that I do not think they could get it. The protectionist principles and policy are solidly implanted in the minds of the American people-not in the minds of the manufacturers or the workingmen alone, but perhaps more especially in the minds of the farming community. It seems to me that, instead of trying to get reciprocity, our bounden duty to-day should be to adopt a policy of protection for our home products. The United States exported in 1901 $943,811,020 of farm products. How can we compete with a nation equipped, as the American nation is, insofar as its farming industries are concerned. My right hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Sir Richard Cartwright) has told us that we are exporting a good deal of agricultural products. The right hon. gentleman seems not to have taken in account, in comparing our position with that of the United States, the fact that a large part of the agricultural products of the United States are consumed in that country. In point of fact, only about thirty per cent of the wheat grown in the United States is exported. Over seventy per cent of that crop is consumed at home. Not more than twenty-five per cent of American corn is exported. The balance is consumed by the Americans themselves, and what is true of corn and wheat is equally true of other agricultural products. Reciprocity with the United States could not, in my humble opinion, benefit us Hon. Mr. TARTE.
in any way. We could not sell the Americans anything that they do not produce, and if we were to open our gates, they would simply flood our country with the products which they export now to England and elsewhere. In other words, they would destroy many of our farming interests and put us out of business in the export trade. The United States are not a market for our farming community, neither are they a market for our manufacturing community. How much have we exported in manufactured goods during the past year ? In 1901 we exported $16,012,208 worth of manufactured goods. In 1902, we exported $18,000,000 worth. Compare that with the United States. In 1901, the United States exported $412,155,066 worth. In 1901, we exported $24,781,486 worth of agricultural products. In 1902 we exported $37,152,688 worth. I am indeed very sorry that I cannot agree with the hon. Finance Minister and the government when they give us, as a reason for not revising the tariff, that it is inexpedient to do so while we are awaiting the result of negotiations with the United States. We have done a good deal of waiting. Over and over again, during the last twenty-five years, we have endeavoured to come to some understanding with our friends on the other side of the line. The right hon. gentleman at the head of the government, in a very able address to the Manufacturers' Association last year, solemnly promised that wTe would send no more deputations to the United States. We are told that this time it is the United States who are coming to us. Well, I have had a good deal of experience in matters of this kind, and I have a notion that, before such letters as have been read to the House were exchanged, some little understanding took place. However, these letters were very convenient this session, and it was undoubtedly the right of the government to give us that excuse-that pretext, let me call it, in all deference.
The other excuse which has been given us is that the government have applied to the British government for a preference and are awaiting an answer. I thought that they had given us a very clear-cut reply. The right hon. gentleman, the Prime Minister, and some of his colleagues took part in the colonial conference. At that conference they tried to come to some arrangement with the British authorities, and the only result we have is the refusal to-day of the British authorities to admit our cattle. And since the colonial conference took place, we have met also with another refusal-the refusal to permit us to compete for the supply of meat for the British army. If we wait for the British government to give us a preference in their markets, I am very much afraid that the revision of our tariff will not take place until we are much older. Let me say that it has beeu somewhat of a surprise to many of us to find that the

right lion, gentleman and his colleagues pledged themselves at the colonial conference to give to the British islands a further preference on manufactured goods in return for some preference to be given us in another direction.
No.

Yes, the language is very clear. There is a clearly expressed intention in the memo, of the ministers that they are prepared to give a further preference on conditions that are not clearly defined. I feel free to speak-more free than I was formerly-my mind on that point. I do not hesitate one moment to say that we have gone very far, we have gone too far, in the British preference. Perhaps, the first preference was justifiable. I shall explain, later on, under what conditions the British preference was enacted. I do not think the Canadian people would be ready to-day to stand any further preference in favour of British manufactured goods than that which has already been accorded. I hope I am not offensive-I do not mean to be-when I say that the reasons I have discussed for not revising the tariffs this year are diplomatic reasons. The members of the government, nearly every one of them, are unfriendly to a protectionist policy. I do not divulge any secrets in saying this ; they have made their views public and known. I am only commenting on a fact of public notoriety. The large majority of the government are favourable to a low tariff policy.
Hear, hear.

Yes, and it is their right to be so. I grant that they are in perfect good faith. They are in favour of a low tariff, and some of them, if they could, would favour a very low tariff, if not free trade. The real reasons why the tariff was not revised last year, and especially why it was not revised this year, are to be found in the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance. He has told us we should make this country a cheap country to live in. And his sentiments have been echoed by the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) this afternoon. The Minister of Finance told us that we must take good care not to antagonize the masses of the people, especially the great Northwest. He has invited us to the realization of the fact that the control of the affairs of this country is passing from the east to the west. He has told us that if we wish to invite immigration, if we wish to fill up our splendid North-west lands, we must have a tariff as low as it is possible to make it. He believes that a high tariff is inimical to immigration, is inimical to the masses of the people. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is a student of political economy. And I give him credit for entire
loyalty in the expression of his sentiments. Let me say-and it is a pleasure for me to say it-there is no more honourable man than the Minister of Finance. Whatever my differences with him may be on some points, I have always felt, when I was discussing questions of importance with him that I was talking with a man who was always in perfect good faith and loyalty. He thinks, Sir, that a high tariff is inimical to immigration. Will he permit me to offer a comparison to which I would call his attention and the attention of the country. We are supposed to be under a regime of fairly low tariff, under the regime of a revenue tariff, while the United States of America are under the highest protective tariff in the world. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is convinced that a high tariff is inimical to the agricultural interests. Let him compare the result of a high tariff in the United States, with the result of a low tariff-I call it a low tariff in this country. Our tariffs have always been low ; the United States tariffs have always been high. The tariffs of the United States, from the birth of the nation up to to-day, have been, as a rule, twice as high as the Canadian tariffs have been. Now, Sir, so much for agricultural products and immigration. What about population, under the highest protective tariff in the world ? In 1S70 the population of the United States was 38,588,371; on the 1st of June, 1901, it was 77,647,000. In other words, the United States of America have doubled their population during the last thirty years, always under the regime of the highest protective tariff in the world. What have we been doing in this Canada of ours ? We have a great country, as rich in minerals, in farming land, and in every other respect as the United States. In 1870 our population was 3,689,255; in 1891, the census gave us a population of 5,371,315. If our population had increased in the same ratio as the population of the United States we

should have now 7,378,514. In other words, we are short 2,007,199. In 1891 the population of Canada was 4,833,239. From 1891 to 1901 our population increased by only 538,076. In 1891 the population of the United States was 63,884,000. In 1901 the population of the United States was 77,647,000, or an increase of 13,803,036. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. Minister of Finance have spoken in glowing terms of the trade of this country. They have told us that we are forging ahead by leaps and bounds. I am glad to say that this is true. This country is going ahead, but would it not be possible to go ahead quicker than we are going now ? Because a man is prosperous in his business, is that a reason, if he is a man of ability and of courage why he should not endeavour to do better than even in the past ? To judge of the trade of the country it is not out. of place to see how the balance of trade lies ? The balance of trade is to a very large extent the book-keeping of the nation. The hon. minister of Trade and Commerce reminded us to-day that we have had a balance of trade for some years. He has forgotten to tell us that during the last year the balance of trade has been slightly against us. We imported in 1902 $212,270,158 worth. Our exports were $211,640,286. The balance of trade against us was $629,872. We are losing ground. The hon. Minister of Finance knows it, all students of the blue-books and trade of this country know it. We are losing ground year by year. In 1901 our balance of trade was not as high as during the year previous. It was only $6,072,107. In former years it was more. We are losing ground because we are importing too much, because our tariff is not high enough. Why are we losing ground when we have such vast resources at our disposal ? The United States are not losing ground. Look at their balance of trade. I call the attention of the lion. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) to these figures. He is in sympathy with the protectionist policy. He is, I say it again, and he knows it. I know his mind as well as he knows his mind. He is a protectionist as pronounced as I am, not quite as open as I am, but as pronounced as I am. He has done his best to keep the tariff where it is, and I compliment him on his efforts on that account. But it is my special pleasure to call his attention to the splendid results that are achieved elsewhere under a tariff that he would like to see adopted in this country. What are the balances of trade in the United States ? In 1897 the excess of exports over imports was $286,263,144; in 1898, $615,432,676; in 1899, $529,874,813; in 1900, $544,541,898; in 1901, $664,592,826; in 1902, less, but still large, $478,398,453. In the last six years the excess of exports over imports in the United States has been over $2,500,000,000. Why is it so ? Simply for the reason that the United States are keeping up a tariff which on dutiable goods is

49 83 per cent and on free and dutiable goods 28-91 per cent. While the tariff of Canada in 1901 on dutiable goods was 24-835 per cent, and on goods dutiable and free 12-424 per cent. In 1902, on dutiable goods our tariff was 25-182 per cent, and on our total imports 13-207 per cent. The progress of manufactures in the United States has simply been marvellous. When those who, like me, are believers in strong national tariffs speak of manufactures, we seem to annoy some of our lion, friends who do not share our views. The word ' manufacturer ' is obnoxious to them; they are called sharks, they are called thieves, they are called by all sorts of bad names. Let me say immediately that in this discussion the manufacturers of this country enter in a very limited way. There are only a few hundred manufacturers. My bon. friends on the treasury benches have received during the last years the support of as many manufacturers as have my hon. friends on the other side of the House. During the last election in Maisonneuve the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prdfontaine) and his friends made it a point to get the signatures and the names of the manufacturers of the city of Montreal on his nomination paper. This is not a question between the manufacturers and the masses of the people ; we are, I hope, but one people in this country. In 1870 the exports of the domestic manufacturers of the United States amounted to $68,279,704 and in 1901 they amounted to $412,155,066, or 28-22 per cent of the total exports of the United States, the agricultural exports being 64-62 per cent of the total. During the last ten years the number of manufacturers in the United States has increased 44-2 per cent. The value of the products of American manufactures in 1900 was $13,019,251,604. The number of people engaged as wage-earners being 5,310,598, and the capital invested $9,853,630,789. The United States has become the leading exporting nation of the world. Last year the total exports of the United States reached the wonderful amount of $1,487,764,991. England comes next with exports amounting to $1,365,048,400 ; Germany next with $1,338,733,000 and France next with $804,069,SOO. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is proud of his surplus, and he tells us that by July the first he will have a surplus of $13,500,000 ; he has had several surpluses since he has been in office. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would like to know what surpluses they have had in the United States.
In 1900 the total receipts of the United States were $669,595,431 and the total expenditure $590,068,371, leaving a surplus of $79,527,060.
The total receipts of the United States in 1901 were $609,316,530 and the total expenditure $621,598,546, leaving a surplus of $77,717,944 ; or in two years the surplus of the United States amounted to $157,245,040.
Having given those figures, having compared the result of the relatively low tariff of Canada with the high tariff policy of the United States, I want to ask : What the present fiscal policy of this country is and means ? The United States have maintained a tariff, not only for revenue, but for protection. We claim to-day to have a tariff for revenue, and the balance of trade during the last year has been against us. What is our tariff ? Is it not a tax-gathering tariff ? Is it not a stand-by tariff ? Is it not a marking time tariff ? Are we not marking time now ? The tariff of this country is practically the same that was adopted in 1879.
