There was a revision of the tariff in 1897. An inquiry had taken place. The Minister of Finance and some of his colleagues, I was one of them, went into several towns and cities in this couu-

try to consult public opinion and to take consultation with the large interests at stake. Some of us were protectionists. X was then a protectionist, as I am now. My former colleagues will not reproach me with not having done everything I could to keep the tariff as high as possible. I carried on the light to the best of my ability. There was a compromise. The tariff was revised. On the whole, the tariff has not worked badly; it would be going a great deal too far to say that it has; it would not be fair to say so. But I say that the tariff has not worked as well as a stronger and higher tariff would have worked. Of course, if the past utterances of some of my hon. friends of the Liberal party had been carried out, the tariff which is in existencei to-day would not be where it is. We would have simply wrecked and destroyed this country. It was out of the question for any government in 1897 to try to carry out the utterances which some public men had delivered in the past. They were the first to recognize this. It was perhaps a little painful to them; but it seems to me that they were wrong in feeling sorrow, because I have yet to find a man who has been in public life for any great length of time who has not been obliged to change his orientation many times. The revision of the tariff of 1897 has placed it about 2 per cent less high than it was before. We did not do more than that. And) when my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was this afternoon denouncing the former tariff, the tariff that I supported myself, when he was telling us that the tariff enacted in 1S79 and kept on the statute-book up to 1897 had simply allowed the manufacturers to pocket the money of the people, I was saying to myself, if it was so, 1 do not know what it is now. Because there is not [DOT] much difference in the two tariffs; the present tariff is about the same thing. We even raised the tariff in 1897 as against the United States on many articles. Open the tariff book and you will find that on many articles we raised the tariff in order to give the English preference. In keeping our tariff as we have kept it, we have been looking on, while many nations of the world with which we are trading have increased their tariffs. The United States have kept their tariff as high as they could. In 3897 they raised it, not for revenue only, but to encourage their home industries. Last year my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in his budget speech said that he would not revise the tariff that session, because there were reasons why he should not do so. The census returns of manufactures were not available, and the London conference was on. But the words of the hon. Minister of Finance, which I read in the House on another occasion, conveyed to the country the impression that the tariff would be revised this year. The business men of the country took those words as a pledge for a Hon. Mr. TARTE.
revision of the tariff at this present session. The words of the Finance Minister of last year were a great deal more definite on that point than his words of this year. Last year my hon. friend did not argue on principle against a revision of the tariff. He did not argue that the masses would chafe under a higher tariff. He did not point to the people of the west as an obstacle against a revision of the tariff. He simply said, we nnfenot ready now, because of the reasons I have stated; but we realize that conditions have arisen in the world that will make it necessary for us to revise the tariff at some future day. These words, I say, were understood to mean a revision this year. I can appeal to the business men of tin; country-they took the words of the hon. gentleman as a promise. This year my hon. friend does not make any promise of a revision in a short time, but he tells us that he is afraid a revision of the tariff in the direction of protection would bring high prices; he is afraid the people of the North-west would organize against it. Why should the people of the North-west rise and organize against a national tariff more than the people of any other part of the country 7 I want to know that. We are prepared to do anything in reason for the people of the North-west. We would be glad to do it in the future as we have been glad to do it in the past; but they must remain Canadians commercially, as Canadian as we are in the older provinces. My lion-friend the Minister of Finance told us that the manufacturers do not need a revision of the tariff in the direction of further protection-that it is not a higher tariff they require, but more labour and more space. Mr. Speaker, give the manufacturers of this country, the industries of this country, a proper policy, and the labour will be on, and the space will be on. Would my hon. friend the Minister of Finance permit me to tell him that this is the weakest argument he has ever propounded in this Chamber. Why, why, why ! the industries, the manufacturers of this country could not find labour, they could not find space, in a country like this ! They could not find space room in a country like this ! The argument is not worthy of the hon. gentleman's great ability. He tells us that the manufacturers are holding the market. How are they holding it. ? W'e exported to the United States last year $([DOT],000,000 of manufactured goods, and the United States sent to this country $69,000,000 worth. How then are we holding our own ? Where are we ? My hon. friend surely has not weighed the figures which he has before him. Because if he had, it would be impossible for him to use such an argument. My hon. friend has given utterance to expressions which will not be easily understood. He said in his speech :
Later on there might be some changes, that there may be a necessity, at some early day, to make further tariff changes than these which

I now propose, but if so, the extent to which these changes will go and the character of the changes, may, to a considerable degree, depend upon the attitude of certain other countries toward Canada. [DOT]
What is to be the character of the changes . When some people go to ridings where low tariff ideas prevail, the words or my non. friend will be read to the electorate as indicating that the changes will not be towards protection, and when such candidates as the hon. Minister of Marine and isheries (Hon. Mr. Pr5fontaine) will go before the people, they will say :	Now we
have a promise of a change towards protection. I say, without any hesitation, that this is not a policy, it is simply politics. This country wants a definite and clear policy on such an important question.
My hon. friend believes that our manufactures are holding their own. He has in his own province a very important industry- an industry, which, if it were fostered and encouraged and developed as it should be, and as a similar industry is fostered and protected in the United States, would become one of the sources of wealth of Canada.
I refer to the iron industry. Would my hon friend permit me to inform him that during the last six months there have been $25,000,000 lost in that industry. There has been a loss of $25,000,000, direct aud indirect, in connection with the iron industry during the last six months.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) That is because it is protected. That is the reason it has gone down.

If that be so, how is it that the hon. Minister of Pi nance is just adding in his budget an item of protection on steel rails. It Is largely because the iron industry is not protected as it should be, that the depreciation in the stock has been what I have just stated.
That cannot be denied by any one who knows the state of affairs. There are other industries, which are losing money and which went on with their operations, relying upon the words spoken by the hon. Minister of Finance last year. I would not be a prophet of evil, but I have good reasons for knowing that within a short period, unless my hon. friend the Minister of Finance makes further changes in the tariff on other lines, there will be financial difficulties, there will be losses on some industries which my hon. friend well knows. I know that there are in Ontario and the province of Quebec several industries which cannot live under the present tariff. There is one thing that surprises me. This Liberal side of the House is rather empty to-night.
I would like to see it full. But what surprises me is that there arel so many members of parliament on this side who have told me that they share my views, who have written me and told me repeatedly that they share my. views, and who have not been able to impress their views on the govern-52
1 ,say openly, 1 sa3' it from the bottom of my heart, that I fully expected that the Liberal party, with which I have been connected during the last ten years, would ^ carry out the policy it was understood m 1896 they would carry out. I am weighing my words. I know what arrangement, what understanding took place between, some public men. I know what took place. I do not divulge any secrets. I know what we did in the election of 1896 in Montreal. I see within the radius of my eye public men who, at our request, came to the city of Montreal, went to the manufacturers, with the knowledge of the leaders of the party, and told them not only would the tariff not be disturbed, but it would be changed in the right direction when the proper time came. There was no secret about that, i shall not give names. There are men who heal me I am sorry there are not more on those benches-who know that I am perfectly right. I am out of office because I could not stay in office under the present circumstances^ I have had only but pleasant relations with most of my colleagues and have tor the most of them the greatest respect. But I could not possibly stay in office when I knew that the policy we are following now is not the right policy-when I knew what understanding took place formerly. The tariff has worked as well as it could because we _ have been passing through years of prosperity. But after all we have not developed so marvellously. My hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, and my hon. friends from the maritime provinces, should take a lesson from the past. Before confederation they were most of them free traders.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) We are still.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN FARMS AND FARM VALUES.
speechtext:
I know that some of them, very respectable and venerable, are still free traders. We respect their views, but may I ask them to consider the position as it is to-day ? They are losing representation in this parliament. Why ? Because they have lost population. And why have they lost population ? Because they have not sufficient industries. They are very proud of their Sydney works, and we are proud with them, and ready to encourage them. But, if we are to carry out those free trade views to which some of them are still devoutly attached, we would remove the duty on coal and we would not consent to have a duty on steel rails. They would object, and yet when we ask our hon. friends from those provinces to he logical, to give protection to some of our industries, as we are obliged to give protection to their special industry, they reply that they are free traders. They are protectionist where their special industry is concerned, hut they decline to join us in the preparation of the tariff that would cover the whole country.
I am asked what kind of a tariff I would like to have. In point of fact, before I arose



to speak, some of my friends said to me : ^re you going to tell ns what kind of a tariff you would offer to the country if you were in a position to make the tariff ? I have no objection to say what I would do if I were once more ' the master of the administration.' I would have a policy that would favour and protect and foster and develop the manufacturing industries and the farming interest of our country just as effectively as the American tariff protects and fosters and develops the manufacturing industries and the farming interests of the United States. I do not say that that tariff should necessarily be as high as the United States tariff is, but it would be built on the same lines. Let us take a leaf out of their book. It seems to me that it is a very poor consolation for us to hear, in reply to our request for a higher tariff, that the control is passing from east to west. In my humble opinion there should be no east and no west. We should have Canada, and Canada only, in view. The control of the policy of the country must be national, not sectional.
The best markets of this country at present, in my opinion-and it will be so more and more-are the home market and the British market. Let me quote Mr. Carnegie on the value of home markets. This is from his St. Andrew's address :
In economic circles * the law of the surplus as I have ventured to call it, attracts Increasing attention. The manufacturing establishments are Increased year by year until they become gigantic, simply because the more made, the cheaper the product. By giving men constant employment, and having a reputation of never stopping, the best men are attracted and held- an important point. The manufacturer on a large scale can afford to make many contracts in distant parts of the world, and even some at home, at a direct loss in times of depression, knowing that, upon the whole, the result will be less unprofitable by running full than running short time or stopping. Hence, those possessing the most profitable home market can afford to supply foreign markets without direct profits, or even at a loss, whenever necessary. .	. . Politicians give far too much
attention to distant foreign markets, which can never amount to much ; and far too little to measures for improving conditions at home, which would increase the infinitely more important home market.
Our friends in the United States have progressed marvellously, as a whole, under a high tariff, but the farmers have, perhaps, benefited more than any other class of the community. Let me read a few words from the final report of the industrial commission, page 196 :
Tariffs in the United States have been agriculturally justified on the ground of their indirect influence in furnishing home markets for the products of the farm. Alexander Hamilton while secretary of the treasury, in his well-lcno'wn report on the encouragement of manufactures, regarded this relation as a vital feature in his memorable policy. By the creation of manufactures, he pointed out that such a

speechtext:
home market was created. By the diffusion of these manufactures throughout the country the consumer was brought nearer the place of surplus production, and the necessity for distant transportation was thereby eliminated and a near-by market secured more permanently than any foreign market could be.
That is common sense.
Another fact bearing directly on the question of the promotion of agriculture by tariffs is the fact that the level of prices for farm products is determined very largely by the price which the surplus portion of the country s product brings in the world market, where competition with all other countries is active. The retention of an increasing proportion of the farmers surplus for domestic consumption, and the exportation of a decreasing proportion of the crop would tend to the maintenance of a higher level of prices to the farmer under the conditions of a practically exclusive home market. It is this consideration that encourages rural enterprise to produce less of those articles, a part of which have to be sent abroad in competition with all other countries such as grain, and more of those articles which are in increasing demand for domestic use, namely, small fruits, dairy products, poultry, eggs, &c. This implies that diversified and intensive agriculture is necessary for the improvement of farm prices, without coming into competition with foreign producers for so large a part of the surplus crop as has been the case in the past.
Now I wish to ask who is the hon. member within hearing of my voice who will deny-I appeal to the most pronounced free trader-that great centres of population such as Montreal, Quebec, St. John, Hamilton and others are the best markets for the farming community ? Our farmers do not produce for export alone. What pays them better is what they take every day or every week to the market. Who can deny that . If you increase the population of the country, if you develop the industries of the country, you increase at the same time, the home market for the benefit of the farming community. That point cannot be disputed, and still it does not seem to appeal to our low tariff friends. They would rather stand by their theories than grapple with the facts face to face. I have just said a word ot the English market. England is the greatest food importing country in the world. We are not alone in the field. The United States Germany, France, Denmark, in fact all the nations of the world export to England.
Free
lion. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S..) trade England.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN FARMS AND FARM VALUES.
speechtext:
After having been high protection England. She is now free trade England, it is true, but is it not equally true that free trade England is to-day protecting her farming community against Canada ' Is it not a fact that free trade England declines to admit Canadian beef for protection's sake ? Mr. Hanbury has told us that openly. I am reminded that England is free trade. Is there a man in this parliament who would venture to say that

we could practice free trade as England practices it to-day ? If there is a man ready to do that, let him rise in the House and ask parliament to pronounce in its favour. We can export to England nearly everything of which we have a surplus. Let us build up our agricultural interests by a strong tariff ; in other words, let us strengthen the position of our farming community as the Americans have strengthened the position of their farmers. Let us build up a strong basis for our farming interests, and then let us compete in the markets of the world with all other nations. Two things must go together, transportation and the tariff, and those two things should be organized scientifically. We should not delay, we have in the past only been marking time.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce reminded us this afternoon that we have lost several millions of our population. The United States have attracted them. They have crossed over the line and most of them have become American citizens. The maritime provinces have lost more, perhaps, than any other part of the country; my province has lost a great deal. Why have we lost so many of our children ? Because there was on the other side of the line a nation with a strong national policy that had built up its industries. In 1894 the United States, under Mr. Cleveland's administration, lowered their tariff a little, although it still remained very high. Immediately a depression followed and a crisis was at hand for the American people. The Democratic party was defeated, and in 1897 the United States congress reined the tariff. Let me read the heading of it:	' An act to provide for
revenue for the government and to encourage the industries of the United States.' These are plain words, there was no ambiguity as to the object of the tariff of 1897. It was enacted to counteract the evil effects of the tariff adopted under the Cleveland regime. In a very interesting book entitled ' The Elements of National Economy,' Prof. Robert Ellis Thompson speaks in this way of the tariff question of the United States :
Nine times in one hundred years the American people have changed their financial policy, sometimes carried from protection toward free trade by the influence Of *specious theories, but as often driven hack to the policy of protection by hard experience. The two periods of longest continuance in any policy is the protectionist period which followed the establishment of the government (1789-1801) and the protectionist period in which we are now living. Pour times the scaffolding of the tariff has been torn down from the uncompleted edifice of our industrial development, and as often the work has been begun again,-if not from the foundation, yet from a point much less advanced than had been reached under the previous protective tariff. This time it seems to be the nation's purpose that the scaffold shall be kept up till the roof is on.
It is such a policy as that I would like to help build in this country. I would like in-52}
deed that the work be started immediately. This session will not close, I am confident, without that vital question being sifted to the bottom. I for one will do my best to achieve that end. The government has made a change or two in the tariff, but that is not a policy. The government is telling us that they do not know when it will be, in their opinion, advantageous for the country to revise the tariff. They tell us that the character of the tariff has not yet been outlined in their minds.
The hon. leader of the opposition has made a motion which is practically a repetition of the motion he made last year. Let me compliment him on the speech he has delivered. On both sides of the House it is admitted to be one of the ablest utterances that have been made on the question of a tariff in this parliament. It is delightful to hear questions of that importance discussed in such an able manner as the tariff is being discussed at the present time. The Minister of Finance has made an able speech. The right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce has also delivered one of those bright efforts for which we always cheer him, even though we do not share all his views. I do not say that the motion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition meets all my opinions and sentiments, though it goes far my way. His speech is clearer than his motion. His motion has the right ring; but if I am allowed to do so, I would like to supplement it and to make my own position clear before the country by proposing at a later period the following motion :	In
reading it I am giving notice of a motion that will be studied by my hon. friends on both sides of the House. It reads as follows :
This House desires to express the opinion that in order to assure the permanency and the further progress of the existing industries, as well as the creation of many new ones that only wait the proper policy to spring up ; to inspire greater confidence to Canadian, British and foreign capital ; to secure for the farmers now tilling our soil and those that we invite to share the blessing of our institutions and the wealth that Providence has placed at our disposal, the full advantages of a prosperous home market ; to comply with the legitimate desire of the working classes to see their labour rewarded by fair and uninterrupted wages and by comfort in their families ; to render impossible the slaughtering of our markets by the produce of foreign industries, of foreign combines, of foreign agriculture and of cheap labour countries ; to bring about a quicker development and a more rapid expansion of our vast resources ; to promote closer commercial relations between the different provinces of the Dominion and between this Dominion and the mother country ;
It is the bounden and imperative duty of the government to revise and readjust, without delay, the present tariff in such a manner as to leave no doubt as to the determination of the Canadian people to adopt and maintain a fiscal policy adequately and firmly protective of the large national interest at stake. And also to

carry out an energetic transportation policy which will give to our merchandise and products of all kinds commodious, quick and cheap access to the markets of our country and to those of foreign nations trading with us.
This is the motion that I will offer to the House at a future date. I will not discuss to-day the tariff in its details. In other words, I will not discuss the different industries, which, in my opinion, deserve immediate consideration at the hands of this parliament. I hope that this question will be thoroughly discussed at this session of parliament that we may make our views known and when we have placed them before the country, the country will decide. I hope that the government will come to a better understanding of the position. I still hope that they will do so. I have gone over the province of Ontario. I have addressed Liberal audiences at their request. I have found everywhere a strong sentiment in favour of a higher tariff. The members of the government from the other provinces perhaps do not know the strong feeling of the province of Ontario as well as I profess to know it. I know I will be told that the government has carried byelections. We all know what by-elections mean in this country. We all know that they are carried on side issues. We know what a large influence the government has. Perhaps I may be told that the policy lam advocating engenders trusts and combines. My hon. friends who are friendly to the policy of free trade England will be good enough to remember that combines in free trade England have more influence than they have in the United States. There are perhaps more combines in England than in the United States. In the United States combines do not control one-tenth of the manufacturing interests. Therefore, that is no ai'gument. Now, all the nations of the world are equipping themselves. I hold in my hand the tariff recently adopted by Germany. It is practically a prohibitive tariff especially from the farming standpoint. I am glad that the hon. Minister of Finance and the government have at last retaliated against Germany. Why did they not adopt the same policy against the United States ? The tariff of the United States is just as unfair to this country as the tariff of Germany is. If the principle that they are advocating and that they are asking their friends to sanction is sound, is good as far as Germany is concerned, the same principle should be applied as against the United States.
Now, let me say one last word about the North-west Territories and Manitoba. One of the influences-perhaps the main influence-which has prevented the revision of the tariff comes from the North-west Territories. That I happen to know. Our Northwest friends are wrong in their views. We are prepared to give them cheap, easy, commodious transportation. They have never applied in vain to the older provinces. We Hon. Mr. TARTE.
have voted cheerfully all the money they wanted, and we are prepared to do so again -I am speaking for myself. Knowing the sentiment of the province of Quebec I speak as I do. We are prepared to do everything to develop the North-west Territories. Why should they be anxious to buy from the United States more than they buy from us? The older provinces are manufacturing provinces to a very large extent. If we establish cheap transportation between the west and the east why should we not supply the west with our goods ? We are| prepared to increase our transportation facilities by rail and by water. Let us bind this Dominion solidly together. National unity follows commercial intercourse. We are settling the west with foreign elements. Let us have as much intercourse as we can with those foreign elements. Let us trade together, let us unite the country solidly together by a strong Canadian tariff and by a scientific system of transportation. There is no reason why the west should antagonize the east, any more than the maritime provinces should! not join hands with us. If they had more industries in the maritime provinces they would have more population. There are already industries in the west. I will have an opportunity of asking my hon. friends from the west to vote perhaps on certain industries that have applied to me for some protection from the farming standpoint, and from the industrial standpoint. Sir, there should be no west and no east. There must be a united Canada and a Canada united with the British empire. The British isles are our best market. I echo the sentiments that have been expressed in this regard by the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This young Canadian nation cannot be an independent nation for many years to come. We would be gobbled up by the United States; they would simply swallow us at the first difficulty we would have with them. Small nations on the continent of Europe are not in the same position as we are. Because there is a balance of power to be maintained in Europe by the bigger nations between themselves. France or Russia will not allow Germany to swallow up a small nation. But on this continent we would be swallowed up by the United States without any body caring very much for us, if we were an independent nation now. Within ten or fifteen years we may be, we will be I hope, a nation of ten millions or twelve millions people. And unless we have closer relations with England we may have difficulties. Let us begin now the work of making solid the union of this Dominion with the British empire on a commercial basis. Let us bind this Dominion together and let us bind the Dominion with the British empire.

I am in a peculiar position. As I have said, my relations with most of my colleagues have been of a most agreeable character. I have confidence in the integrity, in the honour of most of them. I have worked harmoniously with the great bulk of the Liberal party. I have done what I could for them in days when they were not as strong as they are to-day. I remember very well the days when the Liberal party was scattered to the winds after the Mercier episode in Quebec. My friends, the Liberals from that province were not as strong then as they are now. They found allies in the Conservative party, and let me say to some of them that they have never been loyal to those allies. Let me reproach them on the floor of this parliament for their lack of loyalty and sincerity towards some of us. They know that I am speaking by the book. I for one have been stabbed in the back on more than one occasion, but I forgot all that. A public man must forget and forgive, when he has the true interest of his country at heart. I remained in the government knowing that behind me there were men who were stabbing me in the back. My former colleagues know it just as well as I know it myself. I remained in office for loyalty sake to my leader and to those of my colleagues with whom I was working for the best interest of the country. On the question of the tariff, I could not compromise any longer. It may be said that I am not a good party man, and I stand ready to accept that reproach. If I am asked to give up opinions in which I firmly believe in order to remain in office, I cannot do it. There are things on which a public man cannot compromise ; on which he cannot give up his views. The question of the tariff ; the question of transportation, on which I have spoken in the House so often, are two questions on which I hold strong views that I could not possibly give up. I felt that I was no longer in sympathy with several of my colleagues and I went out of office. I have no ill-will towards them. I do not know if I will remain in Canadian politics. I like my country ; I like Canadian politics ; but life is short and I do not know whether
I will not trust to my luck on another scene. It would not be a disgrace to the French Canadians ; it would not be a disgrace or a bad thing for the French Canadians to have one of their number sitting in the imperial House of Commons.

speechtext: I have been offered a seat in the English House of Commons, which I have not accepted as yet. I do not know what I will do. If I had money I would go, and I think it would not be going back on my native Canada, I would be able to serve her in the imperial parliament as I have served her here. Well, we shall see later on. I give this explanation because I want to close these remarks by saying that in the position which I take I have no personal ends to serve. My ambition is satisfied. I started very humbly in life ; I had the great privilege of being a member of this parliament and of being a minister of the Crown. I cannot go higher in this country or elsewhere. My ambition is altogether satisfied. The position which I take to-day has no other object and no other motive than to serve my country to the best of my ability.
